_comment: Layers of meaning: short notes on one passage, from the plain meaning outward.
section: law-history, prophets-poetry, jesus or letters-revelation, the group a passage is listed in.
kind: plain meaning, quotation, allusion, wordplay, name meaning, pattern, irony, fulfillment or setting.
strength: widely agreed (the Bible itself, a BSB footnote, or words the build can check), commonly held (an openly licensed source in the repo), or some interpreters.
refs: passages the layer rests on. words: Strong's keys the build looks for in those verses, so readers can tap them.
evidence: where a claim comes from (a lexicon, a manuscript, a commentary) and detail the note has no room for, shown at the Deep level. Keep text to 300 characters and evidence to 400.

cites: the sources a note rests on, each { "source": an id on the cite list of config/layer-sources.json, "on": the verse a commentary comments on, "at": the writer and work when it is not a commentary on a verse, "url": a page to read it when the source's own link does not reach it }. Only Bible-believing sources are on that list (Shubhanshu's rule, 2026-10-11), and no note may name one on its avoid list.
Any quotation of four or more words must match the BSB in one of the layer's refs or the passage itself.

reviewed_by: the people who checked the entry. A reviewed passage goes live whole. Otherwise a note goes live once it cites a listed source (a wordplay, allusion, pattern, irony or fulfillment note needs an interpreter, not only a word book), and its passage shows once a live note goes beyond the plain meaning. The rest are drafts and stay out of the published data; ATLAS_LAYER_DRAFTS=1 make data includes them for a local preview.
atlas build checks every rule and stops at the first error.

passages.saying: Now the earth was formless and void
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse describes the earth before God shaped and filled it.
layers.text: Before God shaped and filled the world, the earth was without form and empty, and darkness covered the deep waters. Yet the Spirit of God was already hovering over the waters, ready to bring order and life.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say that wherever tohu and bohu appear together elsewhere, they are taken from this passage. Clarke and Gill on Jeremiah 4:23 note these are the very words of Genesis 1:2, and Barnes and JFB there speak of the land returned to the primeval chaos.
layers.text: Jeremiah later borrows this exact pair when he sees Judah after God's judgment: "I looked at the earth, and it was formless and void." The prophet pictures the ruined land as if it had gone back to the empty darkness before God put creation in order.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call tohu vabohu alliterative nouns. Bullinger's Companion Bible labels the pair the figure Paronomasia, a play on words that sound alike.
layers.text: The words for formless and void are tohu and bohu, two Hebrew words that rhyme. Set side by side, the matching sounds stress how completely empty and shapeless the earth was before God set it in order and filled it.

passages.saying: the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed the breath of life into his nostrils
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: God shapes the first human from the soil and gives him life with His own breath. Human life is both earthy and God-given.

In Hebrew the man is adam and the ground is adamah: the earthling is named after the earth he came from. The pun runs through the story: there was no adam to work the adamah (2:5), and after the fall he will return to the adamah he was taken from (3:19).
Paul quotes this verse, "The first man Adam became a living being," and sets beside it "the last Adam," Christ, who does not only receive life but gives it.
Paul calls Adam "a pattern of the One to come" (the Greek word is typos, a type). As one man brought death to all, one man brings life to all.

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith's lexicon (in TBESG) cites Genesis 2:7 for this verb in the Greek Old Testament
layers.text: After rising, Jesus "breathed on" His disciples and said, "Receive the Holy Spirit." The verb appears nowhere else in the New Testament, and it is the verb the Greek Old Testament uses in Genesis 2:7. A new creation begins with a new breath.

passages.saying: This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: God said, "It is not good for the man to be alone." No animal was a "suitable helper" for him. So God made the woman and brought her to him, and the man's first recorded words are a cry of joy at someone truly like him.

layers.evidence: STEPBible TAHOT: ish (H0376) and ishshah (H0802) both stand in this verse. The Pulpit Commentary renders isha as maness, from ish, though it calls the exact word history of ish obscure. Ellicott and Gill note that English man and woman keep the likeness.
layers.text: In Hebrew, man is ish and woman is ishshah. The man hears himself in her name: she will be called ishshah, "for out of man she was taken." English keeps a faint echo of the pun in man and woman.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: Genesis 29:14 and 2 Samuel 5:1 have etsem, bone (H6106), and basar, flesh (H1320), the two words of Genesis 2:23; the BSB renders the pair flesh and blood. Barnes on Genesis 29:14 calls the phrase a description of kinsmanship drawn from the making of the woman out of the man. The next verse, Genesis 2:24, says the two become one flesh.
layers.text: Bone and flesh was a Hebrew way of speaking of family. Laban tells Jacob, "You are indeed my own flesh and blood," and the tribes say it to David; in Hebrew both say bone and flesh. So the first words about marriage are also words of kinship.

passages.saying: Now the serpent was more crafty than any beast of the field
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.evidence: Genesis itself calls the serpent one of the creatures God had made and does not say more. Later Scripture calls the devil "that ancient serpent" (Revelation 12:9), and Christians have long read the serpent as Satan or as speaking for him.
layers.text: A serpent, one of the creatures God made, comes to the woman with a question that twists God's word: "Did God really say, ‘You must not eat from any tree in the garden?’" God had in fact given them every tree but one.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: arummim, naked (H6174), in 2:25; arum, crafty (H6175), in 3:1; eirummim, naked (H5903), in 3:7. Lexicons list the words separately, but they sound almost the same, and the chapter break hides how closely they sit. Ellicott sets naked (arumim) and subtil (arum) side by side to show the intended contrast.
layers.text: Just before the serpent appears, the couple are arummim, "naked," and not ashamed. The next line calls the serpent arum, "crafty." After they listen to him, "they knew that they were naked." The crafty one leaves them naked.

passages.saying: He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, the Septuagint, the NET Bible notes, classic commentaries, M. H. Woudstra's article on Genesis 3:15, Targum Pseudo-Jonathan, Irenaeus and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: God curses the serpent that deceived the woman and declares lasting hostility between it and the woman, and between their offspring. Her seed will strike the serpent's head; the serpent will strike his heel.

layers.evidence: The count of four uses of shuph is from STEPBible TAHOT; the meaning from TBESH. The NET Bible notes point out that some translations use two different verbs here and so hide the repetition.

cites.at: M. H. Woudstra, Recent Translations of Genesis 3:15, Calvin Theological Journal 6 (1971)

layers.text: "Crush" and "strike" are one Hebrew verb, shuph, found only four times in the Old Testament. Some translations hide the repetition. Both sides strike, but not in the same place: the heel, or the head, where a blow can kill.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch: the idea of seed is in itself indefinite, one descendant or a whole line. The links to Genesis 4:25, 22:18 and 2 Samuel 7:12 follow OpenBible.info cross-references; Gill on Genesis 4:25 traces the promised seed through Seth.
layers.text: "Seed" (zera) can mean one descendant or many, and the verse goes on with a singular "He." Scripture keeps tracing this seed: Seth is "another seed in place of Abel," and zera is the "offspring" promised to Abraham and the "descendant" promised to David.

layers.evidence: The Septuagint of Genesis 3:15 has autos (masculine) after sperma (neuter). M. H. Woudstra, Calvin Theological Journal 6 (1971), thinks the translators felt the personal reference was strong. The NET Bible notes say the Hebrew singular may simply agree with a collective noun.

cites.at: M. H. Woudstra, Recent Translations of Genesis 3:15, Calvin Theological Journal 6 (1971)

layers.text: The Greek Old Testament uses a masculine "He" (autos), though its word for seed is neuter. One scholar thinks the translators heard one person here; others note that the Hebrew "He" may simply match "seed" as a word for a group.

layers.evidence: Ellicott, Barnes and Poole on Romans 16:20 all point back to Genesis 3:15. The Greek verb, syntribo, means to shatter or crush (TBESG).
layers.text: Paul echoes the verse: "The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet." Commentators widely hear Genesis 3:15 here. The feet are the believers' own: the victory of the woman's seed is shared with His people.

layers.evidence: The Pulpit Commentary on Revelation 12:9 identifies the ancient serpent with the one revealed in Genesis 3; Gill on 12:17 speaks of the enmity between the woman's seed and Satan's; Poole on Genesis 3:15 points to Revelation 12:9. OpenBible.info cross-references link these verses too.
layers.text: Revelation names the serpent: the "ancient serpent called the devil and Satan." The dragon goes "to make war with the rest of her children," literally the rest of her seed (sperma). The whole cast of Genesis 3:15 returns in John's vision.

layers.evidence: Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Genesis 3:15 promises a remedy for the heel in the days of King Messiah (Etheridge's English, Sefaria). Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.21.1, about AD 180. The NET Bible note says Christians since Irenaeus have called the verse the protevangelium, the first announcement of the gospel, but reads its verbs as ongoing hostility.

cites.at: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.21.1

layers.text: An old Aramaic paraphrase links the heel's healing to King Messiah, and since the second century Christians have seen Christ, "born of a woman," here. The enmity runs on through history and comes to its head in Him, though the New Testament never quotes the verse directly.

passages.saying: For dust you are, and to dust you shall return
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse closes God's sentence on Adam with hard labor and death.
layers.text: Because Adam sinned, he would have to work hard all his life for his food, until he died. Then his body would go back to the ground, the dust it was made from.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch: formed out of the dust, he shall return to dust again. The Companion Bible points to Genesis 2:7. Gill says man returns to the ground, his original, out of which he was made, and on 2:7 he ties the two verses together.
layers.text: God's sentence points straight back to 2:7, where the LORD God "formed man from the dust of the ground." The same two words, dust (afar) and ground (adamah), return here: what God shaped from the dust will go back to dust in death.

passages.saying: Adam named his wife Eve
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Adam names his wife after the sentence of death, looking to the life that would come through her.
layers.text: After God's sentence, Adam named his wife Eve because all people would descend from her. Though death had entered the world, life would go on through her children.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call Chavvah an old form of the word for life. Gill derives it from chayah, to live. Clarke notes the Septuagint renders the name Zoe, Life. The Companion Bible glosses it Life, Life-spring.
layers.text: Eve's Hebrew name, Chavvah, means life. The verse explains the name with a related word: she would be the mother of all the living (chai). Adam gave her a name of life just after death had been announced.

passages.saying: the man has become like one of Us
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse gives the reason God sent man out of the garden.
layers.text: God declared that man now knew good and evil. To keep him from eating from the tree of life and living forever in his fallen state, God was about to send him out of the garden.

layers.evidence: Wesley says the words were spoken to humble Adam and Eve, so that they would see how wretchedly they had been deceived by following the devil's counsel. Barnes says they did become like God in knowing good and evil, as the serpent had said, but to their own shame and confusion.
layers.text: God's words take up the serpent's promise in 3:5: "you will be like God, knowing good and evil." Some read them as spoken to humble the fallen pair. Man had gained that knowledge, but only through sin and loss, and the echo showed how the devil had deceived him.

passages.saying: I have brought forth a man
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Eve thanks the LORD at the birth of her first son.
layers.text: Adam and Eve had their first child, a son named Cain. Eve gave thanks, saying that with the LORD's help she had brought forth a man.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Eve saw in this birth the beginning of the fulfilment of the promise. Barnes ties her joy to the promise that her seed would bruise the serpent's head. Clarke doubts she took Cain to be the promised one himself.
layers.text: Eve's joy looks back to God's promise in 3:15 that the woman's offspring would crush the serpent. She seems to have seen this birth as that promise beginning to come true, though Cain himself proved to be no deliverer.

layers.evidence: Clarke says Cain signifies acquisition, matching Eve's kanithi, I have gotten. Keil and Delitzsch derive the name from the verb qanah. Barnes says qayin and qanah grow from one root. JFB and Wesley give the meaning possession.
layers.text: Cain's Hebrew name, Qayin, is tied to the verb Eve speaks, qaniti, I have gotten. So his name means something gained, a possession, and it keeps her cry of joy that she had received a son with the LORD's help.

passages.saying: Now Abel was a keeper of sheep
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse records Abel's birth and the callings of the two brothers.
layers.text: Eve gave birth to a second son, Abel. The two brothers took up different work: Abel kept sheep, and Cain farmed the ground.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch gloss Hebel as nothingness, vanity, perhaps a presentiment of his early death. Barnes gives breath, vanity. Gill gives vanity and also suggests a prophetic hint of his violent death. Wesley and the Companion Bible agree on the sense.
layers.text: Abel's Hebrew name, Hevel, means breath or vapor, something that quickly passes away. It is the same word often translated vanity. The name proved fitting, since his life was soon cut short by his brother.

passages.saying: sin is crouching at your door
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: God warns Cain about the sin lying in wait for him and calls him to master it.
layers.text: God told Cain that if he did what was right, he would be accepted. But if he refused, sin was lying in wait at his door, eager to take hold of him, and he must master it.

layers.evidence: Barnes notes the sentence had been used before in Genesis 3:16 of the woman. The Companion Bible cross-refers the words to Genesis 3:16. Some older writers, such as Clarke, read the words of Abel rather than of sin.
layers.text: The end of God's warning uses the same pair of words, desire and rule, that were spoken to the woman in 3:16. The echo ties Cain's trial back to the fall. Here the words describe sin: "it desires you, but you must master it."

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch see an evident allusion to the serpent in sin pictured as a wild beast lurking at the door. Clarke and Bullinger instead take sin here as a sin offering lying at the door.
layers.text: Sin is pictured like a wild animal crouching at the door, waiting to pounce. Some see here a reminder of the serpent in the garden (3:1): the tempter that brought down Adam and Eve now lies in wait for their son.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch read se'et as a lifting up of the countenance, from the contrast of falling and lifting up in 4:5-7: a free, open look is the mark of a good conscience.
layers.text: Cain's face had fallen (4:5-6), and God answers with one Hebrew word, se'et, a lifting up. It is translated accepted, but it pictures the downcast face raised again: if Cain does what is right, he can look up with a clear conscience.

passages.saying: Where is your brother Abel?
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: God questions Cain to draw out a confession of his crime.
layers.text: God asked Cain where his brother was, not because He did not know, but to bring Cain to confess. Cain lied and coldly denied any duty to look after his brother.

layers.evidence: Barnes says the question reminds us of the one put to the hiding Adam and is meant to strike the conscience. Bullinger's Figures of Speech sets the two side by side as the first divine questions in the Bible.

cites.at: E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech Used in the Bible (1898), Anthropopatheia (Condescension)

layers.text: God's question, "Where is your brother Abel?" echoes His first question to Adam, "Where are you?" (3:9). Both use the same Hebrew word for where, and both are asked to reach the conscience. Adam admitted what he had done; Cain answered with a lie.

passages.saying: The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to Me from the ground.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, Strong's, the NET Bible notes, the Mishnah, classic commentaries and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: God looks with favor on Abel's offering, not Cain's. Warned that sin is crouching at his door, Cain kills his brother anyway. When he asks, "Am I my brother’s keeper?" God answers that the blood itself is crying out.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch tie Cain to Eve's word for getting. Ellicott explains hevel as a breath or vapour, and Keil and Delitzsch hear in it a presentiment of Abel's untimely death. TBESH glosses hevel as breath.
layers.text: Cain (qayin) sounds like Eve's "I have brought forth" (qaniti). Abel is hevel, "breath," the word Ecclesiastes uses for "futility," and some hear in it a hint of his early death.

layers.evidence: Teshuqah occurs only in Genesis 3:16, 4:7 and Song of Solomon 7:10 (STEPBible TAHOT); meanings from TBESH. Barnes and Maclaren on Genesis 4:7 note that the same words were first spoken to Eve in Genesis 3:16.
layers.text: God's warning to Cain repeats His words to Eve: "Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you" becomes "it desires you, but you must master it." Same rare noun, teshuqah (desire), found only three times; same verb, mashal (rule).

layers.evidence: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 (Sefaria), paraphrased. Gill notes the plural, bloods, and reports the Jewish reading of Abel's lost posterity, which Poole also gives. Strong's explains the plural of dam as bloodshed.
layers.text: "Blood" is plural here, literally "bloods." Early rabbis read it as Abel's blood and the blood of all the descendants he would have had. Lexicons explain the plural as blood shed by violence, so this is a traditional reading, not the plain sense.

layers.evidence: The Greek verb for speaking is laleo in both verses (TAGNT, TBESG). Ellicott, Gill and Matthew Henry on Hebrews 12:24 draw the contrast between vengeance and mercy.
layers.text: Hebrews says Abel "still speaks, even though he is dead," and that believers have come "to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel." Commentators draw the contrast: Abel's blood cried for vengeance, Christ's speaks mercy.

Jesus names Abel first in a long line of murdered righteous people, "from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah," and John holds Cain up as a warning: "Do not be like Cain, who belonged to the evil one and murdered his brother."

passages.saying: settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explain the presence of the LORD as the place of worship at Eden that Cain left behind.
layers.text: Cain leaves the presence of the LORD and makes his home in the land of Nod, east of Eden. He goes away from his family and from the place where God was worshiped.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Companion Bible glosses Nod as wandering and points back to 4:12; Clarke says nod means the same as nad, a vagabond; Keil and Delitzsch call it a land of flight and banishment. Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Barnes give the same sense. Matthew Henry and Wesley render it shaking or trembling, Henry adding the land of a vagabond.
layers.text: Nod means wandering or flight. The name comes from the same root as nad, wanderer, in God's sentence on Cain (4:12). Cain was told he would be a fugitive and a wanderer, and the land where he settles bears the very name of that sentence.

passages.saying: If Cain is avenged sevenfold, then Lamech seventy-sevenfold
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of Lamech's song (4:23-24); Clarke gives a literal rendering and explains the comparison with Cain.
layers.text: Lamech ends his song to his wives with a claim: if Cain's killer would be punished sevenfold, then anyone who harms Lamech would be punished seventy-sevenfold.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, Gill, Matthew Henry and Clarke all read Lamech's words against God's promise in 4:15. Keil and Delitzsch see defiant arrogance and Henry an abuse of God's patience; Clarke and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown allow that Lamech was reassuring his wives after a killing in self-defense.
layers.text: Lamech takes up God's own promise from 4:15, that Cain will be avenged sevenfold, and inflates it to seventy-sevenfold. God gave that word to protect a guilty man; Lamech's song is often read as a proud boast that turns God's mercy into a license for greater revenge.

passages.saying: God has granted me another seed in place of Abel
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Eve's own explanation in the verse; Gill explains the seed as another son given in Abel's place.
layers.text: Adam and Eve have another son. Eve names him Seth and says God has given her another child in place of Abel, whom Cain killed.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch derive Seth from shith, the appointed one; Gill gives put, placed, set; Bullinger's Companion Bible and Figures of Speech list it as a paronomasia (Sheth, shath). Barnes, Matthew Henry and Wesley agree on the meaning set or placed.
layers.text: Seth is Shet in Hebrew, and Eve explains the name with shat, meaning set or appointed: "God has granted me another seed in place of Abel." The boy's name says that God Himself had set in place a son to take the place of the one Cain killed.

passages.saying: he had a son in his own likeness, after his own image
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; Wesley notes Seth's birth in Adam's 130th year and that he was begotten in Adam's own likeness.
layers.text: When Adam is 130 years old, he fathers a son who resembles him and bears his image, and he names him Seth.

layers.evidence: Clarke notes the words are nearly the same as 1:26; Keil and Delitzsch say Adam passed on God's image as modified and corrupted by sin. Matthew Henry, Wesley, Gill and Bullinger's Companion Bible likewise set the likeness of God beside Adam's fallen likeness.
layers.text: Adam's son is born in his own likeness, after his own image, the same two words used when God said, "Let Us make man in Our image, after Our likeness" (1:26). Adam passes on the image he received, but now as a fallen man, so his son shares his sinfulness as well as his humanity.

passages.saying: May this one comfort us in the labor and toil of our hands caused by the ground that the LORD has cursed.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, classic older commentaries named under each note and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Lamech names his son Noah, hoping he will bring relief from working the cursed ground. When the earth is "full of violence," Noah finds favor with the LORD, builds the ark, and comes through the flood with his family.

layers.evidence: TBESH glosses Noah as rest. Barnes on Genesis 5:29: nuach (rest) and nacham (comfort) are stems not immediately connected, but both point back to a common root. Itstsavon occurs only in Genesis 3:16, 3:17 and 5:29 (STEPBible TAHOT).
layers.text: Noah (noach) means "rest," and Lamech explains the name with nacham, "comfort," a word that sounds like it. His word for "toil," itstsavon, appears only here and in the curse on Eve and Adam (3:16-17).

layers.evidence: The Pulpit Commentary on Genesis 6:8 notes that chen reverses the letters of Noah's name. Word meanings from TBESH.
layers.text: The comfort verb turns to grief: "the LORD regretted that He had made man" (nacham again). Then the story turns on one line: "Noah, however, found favor in the eyes of the LORD." Favor is chen, Noah's two Hebrew letters reversed (נח, חן).

layers.evidence: The dove's rest is manoach. TBESH glosses nichoach as soothing. The Pulpit Commentary on Genesis 8:21 hears in it an allusion to Noah's name.
layers.text: The flood ends in rest-words: the ark "came to rest" (nuach), the dove "found no place to rest," and Noah's offering is a "pleasing aroma," literally a soothing one (nichoach), perhaps a play on his name. Then God says, "Never again will I curse the ground."

layers.evidence: TBESH: tevah is used only of Noah's ark and Moses' basket. Keil and Delitzsch on Exodus 2:3 think the word was probably chosen to call Noah's ark to mind.
layers.text: The word for the ark, tevah, is used only for Noah's ark and for baby Moses' basket. His mother "coated it with tar and pitch" and set it in the Nile, where Pharaoh had ordered Hebrew sons thrown. Some think the word was chosen to recall Noah's ark.

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith's lexicon (in TBESG) explains antitypos in 1 Peter 3:21 as the reality of which the type is the copy.
layers.text: Jesus says the Son of Man will come "as it was in the days of Noah." Peter says eight souls "were saved through water," and "this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you." "Symbolizes" is antitypos: baptism is the reality the flood pictured.

passages.saying: Noah walked with God
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the three descriptions in the verse; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explain that Noah was just by faith and sincere in doing God's will, not sinless.
layers.text: Noah stands apart from the people of his day. He is righteous and blameless, and he lives in close fellowship with God.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Noah resembled Enoch in walking with God, and elsewhere note the phrase is applied only to Enoch and Noah; Bullinger's Companion Bible marks the verb as the same as in 5:22, 24; Gill, Clarke, Barnes and Wesley also compare Noah with Enoch.
layers.text: The words "Noah walked with God" repeat what was said twice of Enoch (5:22, 24). In Genesis these two men alone are described this way. In a corrupt age Noah lived in the same close fellowship with God that Enoch had known before him.

passages.saying: Now behold, I will destroy both them and the earth
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on God's words to Noah; Gill explains that God had determined to end the lives of men and land creatures for the violence that filled the earth.
layers.text: God tells Noah that He has decided to bring an end to all living creatures, because they have filled the earth with violence, and that He will destroy them along with the earth.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch note that because all flesh had destroyed its way it was to be destroyed, and call this plain retribution in kind; Barnes says the words corrupt and destroy are the same in the original.
layers.text: Hebrew uses one verb, shachat, for both the sin and the judgment. The earth was corrupt and people had corrupted their ways (6:11-12), so God says, "I will destroy both them and the earth," with that same verb. Those who ruined their way would themselves be ruined.

passages.saying: all the fountains of the great deep burst forth
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own wording: water broke out from below the earth and poured from the sky above.
layers.text: On a dated day in Noah's six hundredth year the flood began. Water burst up from the springs of the great deep below the earth, and the floodgates of the heavens opened above, so that the earth was flooded from beneath and from above.

layers.evidence: Clarke says the waters above and below the firmament, separated on the second day of creation (1:7), were united again. Wesley says God removed the bounds He set for the sea at creation, so the waters covered the earth as at first (1:9). Barnes says the land that rose from the waters on the third day was submerged again.
layers.text: The flood undoes the order God set up at creation. The waters He had divided above and below the expanse (1:7), and the seas He had gathered so that dry land appeared (1:9), now rush back together and cover the land again.

passages.saying: everything that had the breath of life in its nostrils died
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's description of land creatures that breathe through the nostrils.
layers.text: Every breathing creature that lived on dry land died in the flood, except those kept safe in the ark. The description leaves out the creatures that live in the water.

layers.evidence: Barnes ties the phrase to Genesis 2:7, saying nishmat chayyim, breath of life, is the expression used there for man's life, and reads this verse as the death of all mankind outside the ark.
layers.text: Some hear in the words breath of life and nostrils an echo of Genesis 2:7, where God breathed the breath of life into the first man's nostrils. On this reading, the life God gave mankind at creation is cut off in the flood for all outside the ark.

passages.saying: Never again will I curse the ground because of man
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own words, literally I will not add to curse the ground.
layers.text: Pleased with Noah's offering, the LORD resolves never again to curse the ground because of man or to destroy all living creatures as He did in the flood, even though the human heart is bent toward evil from youth.

layers.evidence: Wesley says God cursed the ground at the first entrance of sin (3:17), added to that curse by the flood, and now resolves to add no more. Gill sets this promise beside the curse laid on the ground for the sin of Adam.
layers.text: This promise looks back to Genesis 3:17, where God told Adam that the ground was cursed because of him. Both verses speak of the ground and of a curse because of man. After the flood God resolves never again to curse the ground in this way.

layers.evidence: Clarke on 5:29 derives the name Noah from nuach, to rest, calls Lamech's words prophetic, and points to this verse, where God smelled a savor of rest and promised not to curse the ground again. Wesley, Gill and Bullinger's notes on this verse also say the Hebrew reads a savour of rest, though without the link to Noah's name.
layers.text: When Noah was born, his father hoped he would bring relief from the hard work of farming cursed ground (5:29). Noah's name comes from the word for rest, and the pleasing aroma here is literally an aroma of rest. Some see Lamech's hope answered here, as God promises not to curse the ground again.

passages.saying: Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain words of God's blessing to Noah and his sons.
layers.text: After the flood God blesses Noah and his sons and tells them to have many children and fill the emptied earth again. The growth of families is His gift.

layers.evidence: Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Keil and Delitzsch, Wesley and Barnes all call this a renewal of the blessing given at creation. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes it is given again in the very same words as Genesis 1:28.
layers.text: God blesses Noah with the same words He spoke over the first man and woman in Genesis 1:28. With the old world gone, mankind makes a fresh start under the blessing given at creation.

passages.saying: for in His own image God has made mankind
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own words, which give both the penalty and its reason.
layers.text: Whoever murders a person is to pay with his own life at the hands of men. The reason is that every human being is made in the image of God.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Gill, Wesley and Matthew Henry explain the reason as the image of God in which man was made, marred by the fall but not lost, so that murder dishonors God. Barnes says the reason shows what it means to be created in the image of God.
layers.text: The reason given looks back to creation, when God created man in His own image (1:27). Sin has marred that image but not erased it, so to kill a person is to strike at one who bears God's likeness.

passages.saying: May God expand the territory of Japheth
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Noah's words of blessing over his son Japheth.
layers.text: Noah prays that God will give Japheth's descendants wide room to spread, that he may dwell in the tents of Shem, and that Canaan will serve him.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Noah starts from the meaning of the name and sums up his blessing in japht, from a root meaning to be wide. Barnes says the original plays on the word Japheth, which signifies enlargement. Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists yapht and l'yephet as a paronomasia.

cites.at: E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech Used in the Bible (1898), Paronomasia (Rhyming-Words)

layers.text: In Hebrew the blessing plays on Japheth's name: yapht (may He make wide) and Yephet (Japheth) sound alike. Noah takes the name, which carries the sense of enlargement, and turns it into a prayer that his descendants would spread far and wide.

passages.saying: One was named Peleg, because in his days the earth was divided
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own reason for the name; Keil and Delitzsch take the dividing as the scattering of peoples after Babel (11:8).
layers.text: Eber had two sons. One was named Peleg, because in his days the earth was divided, and the other was named Joktan.

layers.evidence: Clarke derives Peleg from palag, to divide; Bullinger's Figures of Speech glosses the name as division; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the name was given in memory of that event, Wesley gives the dividing as the reason for the name, and Barnes lists the root as divide.

cites.at: E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech Used in the Bible (1898), Ellipsis (Omission)

layers.text: Peleg means division. It comes from the Hebrew root palag, to divide, the same root as the verb that follows: in his days the earth was niflegah, divided. The boy's name kept alive the memory of that great dividing.

passages.saying: Come, let us make bricks and bake them thoroughly
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself; Clarke explains that stone was scarce in that district, so brick and bitumen took its place.
layers.text: With no stone at hand, the settlers in Shinar decided to make bricks and fire them hard. They used brick in place of stone and tar in place of mortar.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Companion Bible calls the repeated roots (brick bricks, burn a burning) a polyptoton emphasizing their determination; Keil and Delitzsch note that the added word for burning intensifies the verb.
layers.text: In Hebrew the builders repeat each root: nilbenah levenim, let us brick bricks, and nisrephah lisrephah, let us burn them to a burning. The doubled words stress how determined they were to make their own building stone.

passages.saying: Come, let Us go down and confuse their language
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explains that the word for language is literally lip, a confusion of speech that split them by dialect.
layers.text: The LORD announces that He will go down and confuse the people's language, so that they can no longer understand one another.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call God's havah (go to) an ironical imitation of the same word in 11:3 and 11:4; the Companion Bible sets the LORD's coming down in contrast with the builders' call in 11:4.
layers.text: The LORD's words begin with the same Hebrew word the builders used twice, havah, come (11:3, 11:4). The builders called each other to come and build a tower reaching the heavens; the LORD answers with His own Come, let Us go down, and their plan falls apart.

passages.saying: That is why it is called Babel, for there the LORD confused the language of the whole world
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, the NET Bible notes, the Septuagint, classic commentaries, BibleProject, Gregory of Nazianzus and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: After the flood, people who share one language build a city with "a tower that reaches to the heavens" to make a name for themselves and avoid being scattered. The LORD confuses their language and scatters them anyway.

layers.evidence: The NET Bible note on Genesis 11:9 gives the Babylonian meaning, gate of God. TBESH glosses Babel as confusion by mixing.
layers.text: The text explains the name by a pun on balal, "confused." In Babylonian, bab-ili meant "gate of God," but in Hebrew Babel sounds like confusion. The city that called itself God's gate is remembered for scrambled speech.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch on Genesis 11:7 call God's words an ironic imitation of the builders; Ellicott sees irony in God taking up the phrase they used twice. Havah from TBESH.
layers.text: The builders say "Come" (havah) twice: "Come, let us make bricks" and "Come," they said, "let us build." God answers in kind: "Come, let Us go down and confuse their language." Commentators hear irony: God takes up their own words.

layers.evidence: BibleProject (What's So Bad About Babel?) sets the builders' bid to make a name for themselves against God's promise to make Abram's name great.

cites.at: BibleProject podcast, What's So Bad About Babel?

layers.text: Babel's builders want to "make a name for ourselves"; one chapter later God promises Abram, "I will make your name great." A great name is given, not seized.

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith's lexicon (in TBESG): in the Greek Old Testament syncheo stands for balal, Babel's verb. The Septuagint also calls the city Synchysis, Confusion. Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 41.16 (On Pentecost).

cites.at: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 41 (On Pentecost) 16

layers.text: At Pentecost the crowd "came together in bewilderment," each hearing "his own language." Behind "bewilderment" is syncheo, the Greek Old Testament's verb for Babel's confusion. An early Christian writer saw one Spirit bringing the languages back into harmony.

layers.evidence: Hebrew safah (lip, language), shem (name) and puts (scatter), as tagged in STEPBible TAHOT. Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary on Zephaniah 3:9 read the verse as a reversal of Babel.
layers.text: Zephaniah promises Babel undone: God will "restore pure lips to the peoples, that all may call upon the name of the LORD," and His "scattered people" will bring offerings. Lip (Babel's word for language), name and scattered all come from Genesis 11.

passages.saying: and all the families of the earth will be blessed through you.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, the Septuagint, the NET Bible notes, Matt Champlin's Themelios article, classic commentaries and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: God calls Abram to leave his country and his father's household for a land He will show him, and promises him a great nation, a great name, and a blessing that will reach "all the families of the earth."

layers.evidence: Matt Champlin, Themelios 42.1, counts both and quotes James McKeown, who calls Genesis 12 the turning point from cursing to blessing. Word data from STEPBible TAHOT and TBESH.

cites.at: Matt Champlin, A Biblical Theology of Blessing in Genesis, Themelios 42.1

layers.text: Before Abram the heavy word is "cursed" (arar), five times: the serpent, the ground, Cain, the ground again, and Canaan. Now God speaks blessing five times in two verses. The story turns from curse to blessing.

layers.evidence: Name meanings from TBESH. Paul quotes Genesis 17:5 in Romans 4:17; the father of us all is his own line in 4:16.
layers.text: Later God renames him. Abram, "exalted father," becomes Abraham, father of a multitude, "for I have made you a father of many nations." Paul quotes the line and calls Abraham "the father of us all," of everyone who shares his faith.

layers.evidence: TBESG: proeuangelizomai, to announce good news beforehand, used only in Galatians 3:8. Ellicott, Gill and the Pulpit Commentary note that Paul joins Genesis 12:3 to 18:18. The NET Bible note says the Hebrew could also mean will bless themselves; the Septuagint, like Paul, reads it as passive.
layers.text: Paul says Scripture "foretold the gospel to Abraham": "All nations will be blessed through you." "Foretold the gospel" is one Greek word, found only here. Paul's "all nations" comes from Genesis 18:18; this verse has "all the families."

layers.evidence: Ellicott on 1 Kings 4:20 reads it as the promise of countless descendants (Genesis 22:17) fulfilled. Peter quotes the promise to Abraham in Acts 3:25.
layers.text: Near: by Solomon's day Israel was "as numerous as the sand on the seashore," as promised (22:17). Far: the blessing for all families comes in Christ, first to Israel, Peter says, and then "to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus," as Paul puts it.

layers.evidence: Poole on Galatians 3:16: seed is a collective noun that is also used of a single person.
layers.text: Paul presses the word: the promise says "to your seed," not "to seeds," meaning One, who is Christ. Zera can mean one or many, and Paul uses both senses, ending the chapter: "if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed."

passages.saying: well watered like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; Keil and Delitzsch explain that Lot chose what looked like the best part of the land.
layers.text: Lot looked over the Jordan valley and saw that it was richly watered, as lush as the garden of the LORD and like Egypt. The verse adds that this was before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the garden of Jehovah is the garden He planted in paradise; Clarke compares the streams that watered paradise; Gill names the garden of Eden, well watered by a river; Wesley glosses it simply as paradise.
layers.text: The garden of the LORD points back to Eden, the garden God planted and watered with a river (2:8-10). Lot chose a valley that looked like paradise, yet the verse adds that the LORD later destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.

passages.saying: Do not be afraid, Abram. I am your shield, your very great reward
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; Keil and Delitzsch explain the shield as protection from all enemies and the reward as God richly repaying Abram's trust.
layers.text: After Abram's battle to rescue Lot, the LORD speaks to him in a vision. He tells Abram not to fear, because God Himself is his shield and his very great reward.

layers.evidence: Gill says that though Abram refused any reward for rescuing the captives, he would be no loser, for God Himself would be his reward. The Companion Bible says God's role as shield was already shown in the events of 14:13-24.
layers.text: These words answer chapter 14. Abram had just defeated the kings and then refused even a thread from the king of Sodom (14:23). Now the LORD says He is Abram's shield and his very great reward, so Abram loses nothing by trusting Him.

passages.saying: the heir of my house is Eliezer of Damascus
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Abram's own words here and in verse 3 about having no offspring.
layers.text: Abram tells God that every gift means little while he has no child. As things stand, his household and all he owns will pass to his servant Eliezer of Damascus.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say meshek, possession, is chosen on account of its assonance with Dammesek, and that ben meshek means one who takes possession, that is, an heir.
layers.text: In Hebrew Abram calls his heir ben meshek, literally son of possession, and then names Damascus, Dammesek. The word meshek seems to have been chosen because it sounds like Dammesek, so the heir's title and his home city ring together.

passages.saying: you shall name him Ishmael, for the LORD has heard your cry of affliction
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the angel's words to Hagar at the spring in the wilderness.
layers.text: The angel of the LORD tells Hagar, who has run away from Sarai, that she will bear a son. She is to name him Ishmael, because the LORD has heard her misery and her cries.

layers.evidence: Clarke derives Yishmael from shama, he heard, and El, God. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Keil and Delitzsch give the meaning God hears, and Wesley God will hear, each tying it to the reason given in the verse.
layers.text: Ishmael, Yishmael in Hebrew, means God hears. The angel gives the reason in the same breath: the LORD has heard (shama) Hagar's affliction. Every time the boy's name was spoken, it would remind her that God had listened to her.

passages.saying: You are the God who sees me
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Hagar's own words and the reason she gives for them.
layers.text: Hagar realizes that the one who spoke to her is the LORD Himself. She gives Him a name, the God who sees me, amazed that out in the desert God had seen her and she had seen Him.

layers.evidence: Gill, Wesley and Clarke take El Roi as Thou God seest me and read the well as the well of the Living One who sees me. Keil and Delitzsch read God of seeing and well of the seeing alive, and the Companion Bible gives well of living after seeing.
layers.text: Hagar calls the LORD El Roi, the God who sees me, and the well is then named Beer-lahai-roi. Both names come from ra'ah, to see. The well's name is read as well of the Living One who sees me, or as well of living after seeing, since Hagar saw God and lived.

passages.saying: your name will be Abraham, for I have made you a father of many nations
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of God's promise, which speaks of the future as already done.
layers.text: God changes Abram's name to Abraham as a seal of His covenant. He speaks as if it were already done, because His promise is certain, even though the promised son had not yet been born.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Keil and Delitzsch, Wesley, Matthew Henry, Gill and the Companion Bible give Abram as high or exalted father and Abraham as father of a multitude. Clarke notes that the exact derivation of the longer name is debated.
layers.text: Abram means exalted father. God renames him Abraham, understood as father of a multitude, and gives the reason in words that echo the new name: av hamon goyim, father of many nations. The name itself became God's pledge of what He would do.

passages.saying: do not call her Sarai, for her name is to be Sarah
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on God's words here and the promise of a son by her in the next verse.
layers.text: God tells Abraham that his wife Sarai will now be called Sarah. For the first time He makes clear that the promised son will be born to Sarah herself.

layers.evidence: Gill, Keil and Delitzsch, Matthew Henry, Wesley and the Companion Bible all give Sarah as princess. Keil and Delitzsch tie the name to her becoming the mother of kings of nations, and Wesley calls her a princess of multitudes.
layers.text: Sarah means princess, and her old name, Sarai, is usually explained as my princess or princely. The new name fits the promise that follows: she will be the mother of nations, and kings of peoples will descend from her.

passages.saying: Then he laughed and said to himself
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on Romans 4:19-20, which says Abraham did not waver in unbelief.
layers.text: Abraham bows facedown and laughs as he wonders how a man of a hundred and a wife of ninety could have a child. His laugh is best understood as joyful amazement at God's promise, not scorn.

layers.evidence: Clarke says our Lord evidently alludes to this joy in John 8:56, Wesley and Matthew Henry say this was when Abraham rejoiced to see Christ's day, and Gill on John 8:56 sees some reference to Abraham's laughter. Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on John 8:56 point to other moments as well.
layers.text: Jesus said that Abraham "rejoiced that he would see My day." Many Bible teachers link those words to this moment, when Abraham laughed for joy at the promise of the son through whom the Messiah would come. Others also point to other scenes in his life.

layers.evidence: Clarke notes that yitschak is the same word as vaiyitschak, he laughed, in this verse. Gill says the name came from Abraham's laughter, not Sarah's, and Keil and Delitzsch give Isaac as laughter with reference to Abraham's laughing.
layers.text: The Hebrew for he laughed here is vayyitschaq. Two verses later God tells Abraham to name the son Isaac, Yitschaq, from the same word, meaning laughter. The boy's name would keep alive the joyful laugh with which Abraham first heard the promise.

passages.saying: After I am worn out and my master is old
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the LORD's response in verses 13 to 15.
layers.text: Listening at the tent door, Sarah laughs to herself at the promise of a son, since she is worn out with age and Abraham is old. Unlike Abraham's joyful laugh, hers comes from doubt, and the LORD questions it in the next verse.

layers.evidence: Gill on this verse says Peter seems to have respect to it in 1 Peter 3:6, and Wesley and the Companion Bible tie the two together. On 1 Peter 3:6, Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown point back to Genesis 18:12, and Barnes says Peter probably drew on this instance.
layers.text: In her thoughts Sarah calls Abraham adoni, my master or my lord. Peter points back to this verse when he writes that Sarah "obeyed Abraham and called him lord," holding up her respect for her husband as an example for Christian wives.

passages.saying: I will go down to see if their actions fully justify the outcry
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown read God's going down to see as language after the manner of men, used to show that His judgment is just and not rash. Wesley likewise says God speaks here after the manner of men, not because anything is in doubt to Him.
layers.text: The LORD tells Abraham He will go down to Sodom and Gomorrah to see whether their deeds are as bad as the outcry against them. God already knows everything; He speaks in human terms to show that His judgment is just and never made on hearsay.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible notes link the two verses both ways: on 18:21 it points to Genesis 11:7 as a time of judgment, and on 11:7 it says this going down is always in judgment and compares 18:21. Both verses use the Hebrew verb yarad, go down.
layers.text: God says, "I will go down to see." He spoke the same way at Babel: "Come, let Us go down," and then He confused the builders' language. Some see God's coming down in both places as marking a time of judgment on human sin, first at Babel and now at Sodom.

passages.saying: though I am but dust and ashes
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse's own words, read by Wesley and Gill as Abraham's humility before God.
layers.text: Abraham keeps pleading for Sodom, but he knows his place. He is amazed at his own boldness in speaking to the Lord, since he is only a frail, mortal man, dust and ashes, before the great and holy God.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech says Abraham is alluding to the creation of man from the dust in Genesis 2:7. Gill explains dust as man's origin and end: out of the dust, and back to it (compare Genesis 3:19). All three verses use afar, dust.

cites.at: E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech Used in the Bible (1898), Meiosis (A Be-Littleing)

layers.text: Dust looks back to creation, when "the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground," and to God's word that man will return to dust. Speaking to his Maker, Abraham remembers what he was made from.

layers.evidence: Clarke notes aphar vaepher are words very similar in sound. Bullinger lists the phrase as a paronomasia (a play on like-sounding words) both in Figures of Speech and in the Companion Bible notes. Afar (dust) and efer (ashes) differ by one letter.

cites.at: E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech Used in the Bible (1898), Paronomasia (Rhyming-Words)

layers.text: Abraham calls himself dust and ashes, in Hebrew afar va-efer. The two words sound almost the same, a near rhyme that stresses how small and frail he is before the Lord he dares to address.

passages.saying: is it not a small place? Then my life will be saved.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The plain sense of Lot's plea in 19:17-22, as Keil and Delitzsch explain it.
layers.text: The angels tell Lot to flee to the mountains, but he pleads that he cannot get that far. He asks to escape instead to a nearby town, arguing that it is only a small place, so that his life will be saved.

layers.evidence: Gill says the town was called Zoar from Lot's use of the word little, which Zoar signifies; Clarke glosses Tsoar as Little, formerly Bela; Keil and Delitzsch say Bela received the name Zoar because Lot called it little. Mits'ar and tso'ar both come from the root tsa'ar, be small.
layers.text: Twice Lot calls the town mits'ar, "a small place." His plea gave the town its new name: "That is why the town was called Zoar," tso'ar, meaning small. Until then it had been called Bela (14:2).

passages.saying: The older daughter gave birth to a son and named him Moab.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The narrative of 19:30-38, as Gill and Keil and Delitzsch explain it.
layers.text: After Sodom's fall, Lot's two daughters made him drunk and each conceived a son by him. The older daughter named her son Moab. He became the father of the Moabites, a nation that lived beside Israel and often troubled it.

layers.evidence: Gill reads Moab as if me'av, from the father; Keil and Delitzsch call it another form of those words, and the Septuagint adds her words, from my father. Clarke and Gill render Ben-ammi son of my people; Gill says the link is less plain there. Keil and Delitzsch say the names immortalized the boys' paternity.
layers.text: The older daughter names her son Moab, which sounds like me'av, from the father. The younger names hers Ben-ammi, son of my people, a son of her own kin. Both names keep the memory that the boys were fathered by Lot, their mothers' own father, Moab most plainly.

passages.saying: God has made me laugh, and everyone who hears of this will laugh with me.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, the Septuagint, the NET Bible notes, Targum Onkelos and classic commentaries.

layers.text: God promised a son to Abraham, who was about a hundred, and to Sarah, who was ninety and had never had a child. Both laughed at the thought. Then Sarah bore a son "at the very time God had promised," and Abraham named him Isaac.

layers.evidence: TBESH: Isaac means he laughs. Sarah's words make a last, joyful play on the name: literally, God has made laughter (tsechoq) for me, and all who hear will laugh (yitschaq). Keil and Delitzsch hear an evident allusion to his name; Barnes says this is no longer the laugh of doubt.
layers.text: Isaac, yitschaq, means "he laughs," and God Himself chose the name. Abraham laughed at the promise; Sarah denied it, "I did not laugh," and the LORD said, "but you did laugh." Now her laughter is joy, and everyone who hears "will laugh" (yitschaq) with her.

layers.evidence: Septuagint of Genesis 18:14. Luke 1:37 has ouk adynatesei para tou theou pan rhema, literally no word will be impossible (TAGNT, TBESG). Bengel and Jamieson, Fausset and Brown on Luke 1:37 point back to Genesis 18:14.
layers.text: The LORD answered Sarah's laugh: "Is anything too difficult for the LORD?" The Greek Old Testament asks whether any word is impossible with God. Pointing Mary to barren Elizabeth, Gabriel answers in nearly the same Greek: "no word from God will ever fail."

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Genesis 21:9: the same verb as laugh in 21:6, in an intensive form. Ellicott, Gill and the Geneva notes tie the mocking to Paul's word persecuted in Galatians 4:29.
layers.text: Even the trouble that follows uses the name's verb: Ishmael's "mocking" is tsachaq, "laugh," in a stronger form. Paul calls it what it was: "the son born by the flesh persecuted the son born by the Spirit."

layers.evidence: Barnes on Romans 4:19 compares Abraham's age in Genesis 17:17.
layers.text: The New Testament makes this birth the model of faith. Abraham was "fully persuaded that God was able to do what He had promised," and Sarah "considered Him faithful who had promised." Believers, "like Isaac, are children of promise."

layers.evidence: Targum Onkelos on Genesis 17:17 has vachadi, and he rejoiced (Aramaic, Sefaria). Gill ties John 8:56 to the laughter and to Isaac's name; the Pulpit Commentary reports others who point to Isaac's birth, and Barnes and Poole point to the offering of Isaac.
layers.text: Jesus said, "Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see My day. He saw it and was glad." An Aramaic paraphrase turns Abraham's laugh (17:17) into joy. Some tie Jesus' words to that laughter; others point to Isaac's birth or to his offering on Moriah.

passages.saying: the son whom Hagar the Egyptian had borne to Abraham was mocking her son
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The narrative of 21:8-10, as Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explain it.
layers.text: At the feast held when Isaac was weaned, Sarah sees Ishmael, the son Hagar bore to Abraham, mocking her young son Isaac. This leads her to ask Abraham to send Hagar and Ishmael away.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, quoting Hengstenberg with approval, say Isaac, the object of holy laughter, was made the butt of unholy wit: he did not laugh (tsachaq) but made fun (metsacheq). Gill says Ishmael was laughing at Isaac's name. The Companion Bible notes the Hebrew means laughing.
layers.text: The word for mocking, metsacheq, comes from tsachaq, to laugh, the root of Isaac's name, he laughs. Isaac's birth brought holy laughter (21:6), but Ishmael turns that laughter into scorn, laughing at Isaac and his name.

passages.saying: So that place was called Beersheba
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse itself gives the reason for the name: the two men swore an oath there.
layers.text: Abraham and Abimelech made a covenant at the well Abraham had dug, and both swore to keep it. Because of that oath, the place was named Beersheba.

layers.evidence: Gill and Keil and Delitzsch give Beer as well and sheba as seven, from the seven lambs; Clarke and Wesley render the name well of the oath. Keil and Delitzsch say the Hebrew verb to swear means literally to seven oneself.
layers.text: Beersheba means well of seven. Abraham gave seven ewe lambs as a witness that the well was his, and there the two men swore an oath. In Hebrew the verb to swear (nishba) is built on the word for seven (sheva), so the name recalls both the seven lambs and the oath.

passages.saying: and go to the land of Moriah
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: It rests on the plain wording of God's command, which names the son in ever closer terms.
layers.text: God tests Abraham by telling him to take Isaac, his only son whom he loves, to the land of Moriah and offer him there as a burnt offering on a mountain God would show him.

layers.evidence: Gill derives Moriah from the verb to see and points to 22:14; Keil and Delitzsch read it as the shown of the LORD, from ra'ah and Yah; the Companion Bible gives shown or provided by Jah. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch say the name is used ahead of the event.
layers.text: Moriah is taken to come from the Hebrew verb ra'ah, to see, joined to Yah, a short form of the LORD's name. It means something like shown or provided by the LORD. The name fits what happens there, for in verse 14 the LORD sees to it and provides, and He is seen on His mountain.

passages.saying: God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering, my son.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: God tests Abraham by asking for Isaac, then stops his hand and provides a ram to offer in Isaac's place.

"Provide" is the Hebrew verb ra'ah, "to see." Abraham names the place "The LORD Will Provide" (literally "will see"), and the saying grows: "On the mountain of the LORD it will be provided," or more literally, it will be seen. God sees the need and meets it.

Moriah is named in only one other verse: Solomon builds the temple "on Mount Moriah, where the LORD had appeared" (the same verb, ra'ah). Most readers take it as the same place, so the mountain of the substitute ram becomes the place of Israel's sacrifices.
Hebrews says Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead, and that "in a sense" (literally "in a parable") he received Isaac back from death.

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith's lexicon (in TBESG) notes that the Greek Old Testament often renders yachid with this word. Gill on Genesis 22:2 makes Isaac a type of the Son of God, the dear Son of his love.
layers.text: "You have not withheld your only son" returns in Paul's "He who did not spare His own Son" (Romans 8:32). The Greek Old Testament calls Isaac Abraham's "beloved" son, a word it often uses for yachid, "only," and Isaac has long been read as a picture of God's beloved Son.

Isaac carries the wood up the hill as Jesus carries His cross, and "God Himself will provide the lamb" is answered by "Look, the Lamb of God." These are old Christian readings; the New Testament does not draw them itself.

passages.saying: And Abraham called that place The LORD Will Provide
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: It rests on the naming in the verse, which follows God's providing of the ram in Isaac's place.
layers.text: After God provided a ram to be offered instead of Isaac, Abraham named the place The LORD Will Provide, and it became a saying that on the mountain of the LORD it will be provided.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch give the name as the LORD will see, meaning He will provide, and tie it to Abraham's words in 22:8; Wesley, Matthew Henry and the Companion Bible say the same. Gill, Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch read the saying as the LORD will be seen or appear.
layers.text: In Hebrew the name is YHWH yir'eh, the LORD will see, meaning He will see to it and provide. It answers Abraham's word to Isaac in verse 8 that God would provide the lamb, with the same verb. The saying that follows uses it again: on the LORD's mountain He will be seen, or it will be provided.

passages.saying: May your offspring possess the gates of their enemies.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: It rests on the words of the farewell blessing as Rebekah leaves to marry Isaac.
layers.text: As Rebekah leaves home to marry Isaac, her family blesses her: may she become the mother of a vast number of people, and may her descendants overcome their enemies.

layers.evidence: Gill says the blessing seems to have respect to God's promise to Abraham in 22:17, which the family may have learned of from Abraham's servant. Keil and Delitzsch note the wording is almost the same as 22:17 but doubt it was borrowed.
layers.text: The family's blessing uses almost the same words as God's oath to Abraham after Moriah, that his offspring would possess the gates of their enemies (22:17). They may have heard of that promise from Abraham's servant, and God would carry it on through Rebekah's children.

passages.saying: covered with hair like a fur coat; so they named him Esau
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: It rests on the verse's description of the firstborn twin at birth.
layers.text: The first of Rebekah's twins was born reddish and so hairy that he looked wrapped in a fur coat, and he was named Esau.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch give Esau as the hairy one; Barnes gives hairy, or made; Gill says the name came chiefly from his hairiness; Wesley and Clarke take it as made or perfected, as if he were already full grown. All tie the name to how he looked at birth.
layers.text: Esau's name was drawn from how he looked at birth. Its exact sense is uncertain: some take it as hairy or covered, for his thick hair, and others as made or fully formed, as if he were born already like a grown man.

passages.saying: his brother came out grasping Esau’s heel; so he was named Jacob
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: It rests on the verse's account of the second twin's birth and Isaac's age.
layers.text: The second twin was born holding on to his brother Esau's heel, and so he was named Jacob. Isaac was sixty years old when the twins were born.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Keil and Delitzsch on Hosea 12:3 all take it as recalling Jacob's birth in Genesis 25, and Wesley on Genesis 25:26 says the same. Keil and Delitzsch note Hosea's verb is formed from the word heel.
layers.text: Centuries later the prophet Hosea recalls this birth, saying Jacob took his brother by the heel in the womb (Hosea 12:3). Hosea's verb for grasping the heel ('aqav) is formed from the same word, so it echoes Jacob's name.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, Gill, Clarke, Barnes, Wesley and the Companion Bible all derive Jacob from heel. Keil and Delitzsch and Clarke add that the verb came to mean to outwit or supplant, and Gill and Keil and Delitzsch point to Esau's words in 27:36.
layers.text: He came out holding his brother's heel ('aqev), so he was named Jacob (Ya'aqov), the heel-holder. The same root came to mean to trip someone up or supplant him, and Esau later plays on the name when Jacob takes his blessing (27:36).

passages.saying: Let me eat some of that red stew, for I am famished.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: It rests on the verse and the story around it, where Jacob is cooking lentil stew.
layers.text: Esau came in from the field worn out and begged Jacob for some of the red lentil stew he was cooking. The writer adds that this is why Esau was also called Edom.

layers.evidence: Gill, Keil and Delitzsch and Matthew Henry say Edom, red, comes from the red stew; Wesley and the Companion Bible give Edom as red, and Bullinger notes the doubled red. Barnes says the name came from his red skin at birth and was renewed by this red red; the Companion Bible also points to 25:25. Gill rejects the birth link.
layers.text: In Hebrew Esau asks for that red, red stuff (ha-adom ha-adom), and from this he was also called Edom, which means red. Some also see the name fitting the red color he had at birth (25:25).

passages.saying: So he named the well Esek, because they contended with him.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: It rests on the verse's account of the quarrel over the well Isaac's servants dug.
layers.text: The herdsmen of Gerar claimed the water of a well that Isaac's servants had dug, so Isaac named the well after the quarrel.

layers.evidence: Gill, Wesley, Barnes, Keil and Delitzsch and the Companion Bible give Esek as contention or strife; Keil and Delitzsch and Barnes give Sitnah as opposition and Rehoboth as breadths or room, explained by Isaac's words in 26:22. Matthew Henry calls the first two Contention and Hatred.
layers.text: Isaac names each well for what happened there. Esek means strife, and it shares its root with the verb translated contended in this verse. The next well, Sitnah, means opposition. The third, Rehoboth, means broad places, because, he said, the LORD has made room for us.

passages.saying: he called it Shibah, and to this day the name of the city is Beersheba
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the account of Isaac's treaty with Abimelech and the new well in 26:26-33.
layers.text: On the day Isaac and Abimelech swore peace, Isaac's servants found water in the well they had dug. Isaac named it Shibah, and the town kept the name Beersheba, which it had first received in Abraham's day (21:31).

layers.evidence: Gill, Keil and Delitzsch, Barnes and the Companion Bible all give Shibah as oath; Gill and Keil and Delitzsch tie it to the oath just sworn, and Barnes also glosses it seven. Gill and Barnes render Beersheba the well of the oath, and Keil and Delitzsch say the name renews the Beersheba of 21:31.
layers.text: Shibah means oath, and the same word can also mean seven. Isaac gives the well this name because he and Abimelech had just sworn an oath to each other (26:31). So the town is Beersheba, well of the oath, renewing the name from Abraham's day.

passages.saying: May those who curse you be cursed, and those who bless you be blessed
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Isaac's spoken blessing over Jacob in 27:27-29.
layers.text: Thinking he is blessing Esau, Isaac blesses Jacob with rule over peoples and over his own brothers, and with blessing for all who bless him and a curse on all who curse him.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the wording is moulded on Genesis 12:3; Gill says the same blessing was pronounced on Abraham; Wesley calls it part of the blessing of Abraham, and Clarke, quoting Bishop Newton, says the promise made to Abraham is here repeated to Jacob.
layers.text: Isaac closes with the words God first spoke to Abram in 12:3: blessing for those who bless him and a curse on those who curse him. The promise given to Abraham is now passed down to Jacob.

passages.saying: Is he not rightly named Jacob? For he has cheated me twice.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Urged on by his mother, Jacob, disguised as his brother, tricks his blind old father into giving him the blessing meant for Esau. Esau "let out a loud and bitter cry" and remembers that Jacob already got his birthright for a meal.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: aqev, heel (H6119), and Ya'aqov (H3290) in 25:26; Ya'aqov and vaya'qeveni, he has supplanted me (H6117), in 27:36. Gill explains supplanting as putting one's foot under another's heel to trip him up.
layers.text: Jacob, ya'aqov, was born holding his twin's heel, aqev, and named for it. Esau turns the name into an accusation. Behind "cheated me" is aqav, a verb built on heel: to grab by the heel, trip up, overreach. Jacob has tripped him up twice.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: bekhorati, my birthright (H1062), and birkhati, my blessing (H1293), in the same breath. The consonants are b-k-r and b-r-k. Craig Keener: Esau's complaint plays on the Hebrew words for birthright and blessing.

cites.at: Craig Keener, Jacob gets Esau's blessing

layers.text: Esau's complaint holds a second pun: "He took my birthright, and now he has taken my blessing." Birthright is bekhorah and blessing is berakhah: the same three letters, b-k-r and b-r-k, with two swapped. His two losses sound almost alike.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: Jeremiah 9:4 has aqov ya'qov (H6117 twice), the verb of Genesis 27:36, in a form spelled like the name Jacob. Ellicott, Barnes, Gill and Poole on Jeremiah 9:4 hear a play on the name; the Pulpit Commentary doubts it.
layers.text: Centuries later Jeremiah warns, "do not trust any brother, for every brother deals craftily." In Hebrew, deals craftily is aqov ya'qov, and ya'qov is spelled like the name Jacob. Many hear the old family story in it: every brother acts like a Jacob.

passages.saying: your dwelling place shall be away from the richness of the land
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Follows the BSB and the Companion Bible in reading the Hebrew as away from; Gill and JFB took it as a share in the richness.
layers.text: When Esau begs for a blessing too, Isaac tells him that his home will lie away from the rich land and the dew of heaven. His lot would be harder than Jacob's.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call it a play upon the words: the same expression as 27:28, but the from that meant some of there means away from here. The Companion Bible reads it the same way. Gill and JFB instead read it as a share in the richness, as the KJV does.
