layers.text: Isaac repeats the very words of Jacob's blessing (27:28), the richness and the dew of heaven, each with the small Hebrew prefix mi, from. For Jacob it meant a share of these gifts. For Esau it means away from them. One little word turns the blessing around.

passages.saying: And Jacob had a dream about a ladder that rested on the earth with its top reaching up to heaven, and God’s angels were going up and down the ladder.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESH, the Septuagint, the NET Bible notes, Genesis Rabbah, classic commentaries, a Ligonier devotional by Derek Thomas and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Fleeing the brother he cheated, Jacob sleeps in the open with a stone under his head and dreams of a ladder, or stairway, joining earth and heaven. The LORD renews Abraham's promise: "Look, I am with you, and I will watch over you wherever you go."

layers.evidence: Name meaning from TBESH.
layers.text: Jacob wakes afraid: "This is none other than the house of God; this is the gate of heaven!" So he names the place Bethel, "house of God," though until then the town had been called Luz.

layers.evidence: Literal wording of Genesis 11:4 from the STEPBible TAHOT word glosses. Babylon as gate of God from the NET Bible note on 11:9. The contrast of Babel and Bethel is Derek Thomas's (Snakes and Ladders, Ligonier).

cites.at: Derek Thomas, Snakes and Ladders (Ligonier devotional)

layers.text: Babel's tower was to have, literally, its top in the heavens; Jacob's stairway has "its top reaching up to heaven," the same Hebrew words. Babylon's name meant "gate of God"; Bethel is "the gate of heaven." At Babel people reach up; at Bethel God reaches down.

layers.evidence: Genesis Rabbah 68:12 (Sefaria), paraphrased. Gill on John 1:51 reports this Jewish reading (citing Bereshit Rabba 68) beside Jesus' words.
layers.text: The last word, bo, can mean "on it" or "on him." An ancient Jewish commentary records two rabbis disagreeing: the angels went up and down the ladder, or on Jacob. When Jesus retells the dream, a person stands where the ladder was: "on the Son of Man."

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on John 1:51 calls Christ the real ladder, and Ellicott notes that ascending comes before descending, as in Jacob's vision. OpenBible.info cross-references link the verses.
layers.text: Jesus tells Nathanael, "you will all see heaven open and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man," in the dream's own order: up first, then down. Jesus Himself is now the stairway between heaven and earth.

layers.evidence: Name meaning from TBESH. Dolos in the Septuagint of Genesis 27:35, where the Hebrew has mirmah, deceit (TAHOT). Ellicott on John 1:47 hears the contrast: Nathanael lives up to the name Israel and has none of Jacob's guile.
layers.text: Jacob means "heel holder" or "supplanter"; Esau says, "he has cheated me twice." Jesus calls Nathanael "a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit," nothing of the old Jacob. John's Greek even uses dolos, the Greek Old Testament's word for Jacob's deceit.

layers.evidence: Under Strong's numbering, Genesis 32:28 and Hosea 12:3 are the verb's only two uses (STEPBible TAHOT). Jamieson, Fausset and Brown tie Hosea's power with God to the name Israel.
layers.text: Hosea retells Jacob's life: "In the womb he grasped his brother’s heel, and in his vigor he wrestled with God," and "he found Him at Bethel." "Wrestled" is sarah, the verb inside the name Israel (32:28). The heel-grabber who met God at Bethel became Israel.

passages.saying: This is none other than the house of God
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Jacob's words after the dream of 28:12-15.
layers.text: Waking from his dream of the stairway, Jacob is filled with awe. He realizes that God is present in this place, which is like God's own house and a gateway between heaven and earth.

layers.evidence: Gill, Keil and Delitzsch, Wesley, Clarke, JFB and the Companion Bible all give Bethel as house of God, and Gill ties the name to Jacob's words in 28:17. Gill, Clarke and Wesley give Luz as almond.
layers.text: Jacob calls the place beit Elohim, the house of God, and the next morning he names it Bethel (Beit-El), which means house of God (28:19). The town had been called Luz, almond tree, but Jacob's new name keeps the memory of what God showed him there.

passages.saying: Why have you deceived me?
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the account of Jacob's wedding in 29:21-25.
layers.text: After the wedding night Jacob finds that Laban has given him Leah instead of Rachel, the bride he worked seven years for. He confronts Laban for deceiving him.

layers.evidence: Gill, Wesley and Matthew Henry each tie Laban's trick back to Jacob's deception of Isaac, Gill calling it a righteous retaliation in Providence and Wesley and Henry saying that, however unrighteous Laban was, the Lord was righteous.
layers.text: Jacob once deceived his blind father by claiming to be Esau (27:19). Now, in the dark, he is deceived himself and given one sister in place of the other. The deceiver is repaid in kind, and God's justice is at work even through Laban's wrong.

passages.saying: The LORD has seen my affliction
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Leah's own words at the birth in 29:31-32.
layers.text: Leah, the less loved wife, gives birth to her first son. She takes him as a sign that the LORD has noticed her sorrow, and she hopes that now Jacob will love her.

layers.evidence: Clarke, Keil and Delitzsch, Gill, Wesley and Matthew Henry all give Reuben as see, a son, and Clarke links it to raah, the LORD has seen, in Leah's explanation.
layers.text: Reuben means see, a son! Leah gives the reason in the same breath: the LORD has seen my affliction, and the Hebrew for seen is ra'ah. The name holds her thanks that God saw her when she felt unseen and unloved.

passages.saying: the LORD has heard that I am unloved
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Leah's words at the birth in 29:33.
layers.text: Leah bears a second son. She sees him as God's answer to her pain, a gift from the LORD who knows she is unloved.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Keil and Delitzsch and the Companion Bible all give Simeon as hearing, matching shama, heard, in Leah's words; the Companion Bible marks it as a paronomasia, a play on words.
layers.text: Simeon (Shim'on) means hearing and echoes shama, heard. Leah names him this because the LORD has heard that she is unloved. Every time his name is spoken, it recalls that God listens to the overlooked.

passages.saying: Now at last my husband will become attached to me
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Leah's words at the birth in 29:34.
layers.text: Leah bears a third son and hopes that, with three sons, her husband will at last be bound to her in love.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Keil and Delitzsch, Wesley, Matthew Henry and the Companion Bible all give Levi as joined or attachment; the Companion Bible and Bullinger's Figures of Speech mark yillaveh and Levi as a paronomasia.
layers.text: Levi means joined or attached. It echoes yillaveh, will be joined, in Leah's hope that her husband will now become attached to her. The name carries her longing to be truly joined to Jacob.

passages.saying: This time I will praise the LORD.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, the NET Bible notes and classic older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Laban tricked Jacob into marrying Leah, and Jacob "loved Rachel more than Leah." But "When the LORD saw that Leah was unloved, He opened her womb." She bore four sons in a row, and each name came out of her pain and her hope.

layers.evidence: Name meanings from the NET Bible notes and TBESH. The NET notes call Leah's explanation of Reuben a popular etymology, not an exact one, and say the meaning of Levi is debated.
layers.text: Each name echoes her words. Reuben, "look, a son": "The LORD has seen my affliction." Simeon, "heard": "the LORD has heard that I am unloved." Levi sounds like lavah, "to join": "my husband will become attached to me." Some are puns, not exact meanings.

layers.evidence: Both verses have happa'am (STEPBible TAHOT). The NET Bible notes gloss Judah as he will be praised; Keil and Delitzsch, as the one for whom the LORD is praised.
layers.text: Her third and fourth sayings share a Hebrew word, happa'am, "this time" (in 29:34 the BSB has "Now at last"). The third hopes Jacob will be joined to her. The fourth does not mention him: "This time I will praise the LORD." Judah means "praised."

layers.evidence: The NET Bible note on Numbers 18:2 calls yillavu a wordplay with Levi and links it to Leah's hope in Genesis 29:34.
layers.text: The pun on Levi returns when God gives the Levites their work: they are to "join you and assist you" (join is yillavu). Leah hoped her husband would be joined to her; her son's tribe is joined to the priests to serve at God's tent.

layers.evidence: TBESG derives Ioudaios from Ioudas, Judah. Bengel and Gill on Romans 2:29 hear an allusion to Judah's name; Bengel compares Genesis 49:8.
layers.text: The word "Jew" (Ioudaios) comes from Judah. So when Paul says a true Jew is one inwardly, whose "praise does not come from men, but from God," some commentators hear a play on Judah, "praise."

layers.evidence: Barnes on Genesis 29:35: the wife who came first but was not preferred is the mother of the seed.
layers.text: God's answer to the unloved wife went far beyond what she asked. Through Levi she became the mother of Israel's priests, and through Judah of its kings. Matthew's genealogy of "Jesus, who is called Christ" runs through "Judah and his brothers."

passages.saying: God has vindicated me; He has heard my plea and given me a son.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Gill explains that Rachel saw the birth as God's approval and the answer to her prayer, and counted Bilhah's son as her own.
layers.text: Rachel, still childless, had given her servant Bilhah to Jacob so that Bilhah's child would count as her own. When Bilhah bore a son, Rachel took it as God ruling in her favor and answering her prayer, and she named the boy Dan.

layers.evidence: Gill on Genesis 49:16 calls the words an elegant paronomasia or allusion to the name of Dan. Keil and Delitzsch say Dan would act according to his name. Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists Dan and yadin in 49:16 and compares Rachel's dananni in 30:6.

cites.at: E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech Used in the Bible (1898), Paronomasia (Rhyming-Words)

layers.text: Jacob's dying blessing plays on this same name: "Dan shall provide justice for his people." Dan and yadin, he will provide justice, share the root din. The son of a servant would live up to his name as a full tribe of Israel.

layers.evidence: Gill: Dan signifies judgment, and the reason lies in the first clause of the verse. Clarke: dan, judging. Keil and Delitzsch: Dan, i.e., judge, because God had judged her. The Companion Bible marks dananni and Dan as a paronomasia.
layers.text: Dan means judge. Rachel's words "God has vindicated me" are in Hebrew dananni, he has judged me, from the same root din, to judge. The boy's name sums up her claim that God had heard her case and ruled for her.

passages.saying: In my great struggles, I have wrestled with my sister and won.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Gill reads the struggle as Rachel's earnest prayer to have children as her sister had.
layers.text: When Bilhah bore a second son, Rachel spoke of it as the result of a long, hard struggle with her sister Leah, who already had four sons. She felt she had finally prevailed, and she named the boy Naphtali.

layers.evidence: Gill: Naphtali signifies my wrestling, and he sees striving in prayer. The Companion Bible: wrestlings of El, i.e. mighty wrestlings, a polyptoton and paronomasia. Keil and Delitzsch: my conflict, wrestlings of prayer. Clarke notes the root pathal means to twist or entwine.
layers.text: Naphtali means my wrestling. Rachel says literally, with wrestlings of God I have wrestled (naftule Elohim niftalti). Naftule, niftalti and Naphtali all come from the root patal, to twist or wrestle. Wrestlings of God may mean mighty struggles, as translated here, or wrestling with God in prayer.

passages.saying: Then Leah said, “How fortunate!” So she named him Gad.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch explain that jealousy of Rachel moved Leah to use the same means and give her maid to Jacob.
layers.text: Leah had stopped bearing children, so she copied Rachel and gave her servant Zilpah to Jacob. When Zilpah bore a son, Leah counted it as good fortune for herself and named the boy Gad.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch: Gad means good fortune, from begad in the written text or ba gad in the Masoretic reading; the Septuagint has with good fortune (Clarke). Gill and Wesley take gad as a troop of children, and Clarke weighs both.
layers.text: Leah's cry is one Hebrew word, begad, with good fortune (the Hebrew margin reads ba gad, fortune has come), and the name Gad repeats it. Here gad is taken as good fortune; older English Bibles read a troop comes, as if Leah looked for a band of sons.

passages.saying: How happy I am! For the women call me happy.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Gill explains that the women around Leah would count her happy for her many children.
layers.text: Zilpah bore Leah a second son. Leah felt blessed and expected the women around her to call her happy as the mother of so many sons, so she named the boy Asher.

layers.evidence: Clarke: beoshri, in my happiness, therefore she called him asher, happiness. Keil and Delitzsch: Asher, the happy one. The Companion Bible sets be'ashri, 'ishshruni and Asher side by side as a paronomasia. Gill and Wesley agree that Asher means happy.
layers.text: Asher means happy or blessed. Leah's words use the same root twice: be'oshri, in my happiness, and ishruni, they call me happy. The boy's name gathers up her joy in a single word.

passages.saying: Reuben went out and found some mandrakes in the field.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch explain that mandrakes were used in the ancient world to promote child-bearing, which is why Rachel wanted them.
layers.text: During the wheat harvest young Reuben found mandrakes and brought them to his mother Leah. Rachel, still childless, begged for some, most likely because people then believed the plant helped a woman conceive.

layers.evidence: Gill: the mandrakes seem to have their name dudaim from love, and the later births are ascribed to the Lord hearing Leah and Rachel. Clarke: the original word means loves. Keil and Delitzsch call them love-apples and say fruitfulness came from God, not from them.
layers.text: The Hebrew word for mandrakes, duda'im, seems to come from dod, love, so they were love plants. That is probably why Rachel wanted them. Yet the story goes on to show that children came because God listened, not because of the plant.

passages.saying: God has rewarded me for giving my maidservant to my husband.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Gill explains that Leah counted the son as God's payment for the night she had hired with the mandrakes.
layers.text: Leah had bought a night with Jacob from Rachel with Reuben's mandrakes. God listened to her and she bore a fifth son. She saw him as God's reward for giving her servant to Jacob, and she named him Issachar.

layers.evidence: Clarke: Issachar is compounded of yesh, there is, and sachar, wages. Keil and Delitzsch: there is reward (written text) or he brings reward (Masoretic reading). Gill and Wesley tie the hire to the mandrakes; the Companion Bible marks hire and Issachar as a paronomasia.
layers.text: Issachar is built on sakhar, wages or hire, and is read as there is a reward. Leah had told Jacob, "I have hired you" (sakhor sekhartikha), and now she says God has given her her wages (sekhari). The name recalls both the bargain and the gift.

passages.saying: This time my husband will honor me
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Leah's own words at the birth of her sixth son.
layers.text: Leah gives birth to her sixth son. She thanks God for a good gift and hopes that, now she has borne Jacob six sons, her husband will at last honor her. She names the boy Zebulun.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the name is formed with a play on the sound of zabad, to give or endow, beside zabal. The Companion Bible marks the repeated dowered and dowry (zevadani zeved) as a figure of speech (polyptoton).
layers.text: Leah's words ring with the same sounds. God zevadani zeved, has given me a good gift, and now my husband yizbeleni, will honor me. The name Zebulun echoes both halves of her thanks.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Keil and Delitzsch, Wesley and the Companion Bible all give Zebulun the sense dwelling, from zabal in yizbeleni (will honor me, or will dwell with me). The Companion Bible adds that the word also carries the sense to honour.
layers.text: Zebulun means dwelling. It is built on zabal, the word Leah uses when she says her husband will honor her, which older versions render dwell with. The boy's name carries her hope that Jacob would now stay close to her.

passages.saying: God has taken away my shame
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Rachel's words at the birth of her first son.
layers.text: After long years of barrenness, Rachel at last conceives and bears a son. She says that God has taken away her shame, the disgrace a childless wife carried in her day.

layers.evidence: Gill, Keil and Delitzsch and Wesley all say the name points both to asaph, take away (verse 23), and to yasaph, add (verse 24). Clarke gives Joseph as adding and, with Keil and Delitzsch, sees the prayer answered in Benjamin's birth.
layers.text: Joseph (Yoseph) looks two ways. It echoes asaph, God has taken away my shame, and it means he adds, for Rachel prays, "May the LORD add to me another son". God answered that prayer when Benjamin was born.

passages.saying: Laban called it Jegar-sahadutha, and Jacob called it Galeed
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the two names given to the covenant heap.
layers.text: Jacob and Laban make a covenant and pile up a heap of stones to stand as its witness. Each man names the heap in his own language, Laban in Aramaic and Jacob in Hebrew.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Keil and Delitzsch and Wesley all say the two names mean the same thing, heap of witness, one in Aramaic (Chaldee or Syriac) and one in Hebrew. Laban's words in verse 48 give the reason: the heap (gal) is a witness (ed).
layers.text: Both names mean heap of witness. Laban's Jegar-sahadutha is Aramaic, and Jacob's Galeed is Hebrew, from gal (heap) and ed (witness). Laban explains it himself: "This mound is a witness between you and me".

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Gilead sounds so like Galeed that the two are surely connected. Gill (on verse 21) says the name was given afterward from this heap, and Clarke (on verse 21) thinks the same likely. The Companion Bible glosses Gilead differently, as perpetual fountain.
layers.text: The region's name, Gilead, sounds like Galeed, and it very likely comes from this heap of witness. That is why the account can already speak of the hill country of Gilead in verse 21, using the name the place later bore.

passages.saying: May the LORD keep watch between you and me
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Laban's prayer as the covenant is made.
layers.text: The heap gets a second name, Mizpah. Laban asks the LORD to keep watch over both men when they are apart and cannot see each other, so that neither breaks the covenant.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Keil and Delitzsch, Wesley and the Companion Bible all give Mizpah as watch or watchtower, tied to the verb in Laban's prayer, the LORD watch between me and thee.
layers.text: Mizpah means watchtower or lookout. It comes from the same root as Laban's prayer that the LORD keep watch (yitsef) between them. The place was named to remind both men that God would be watching.

passages.saying: This is the camp of God
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Jacob's words when the angels of God meet him.
layers.text: On his way home to face Esau, Jacob is met by angels of God. He calls them God's camp and names the place after them, a sign that God was guarding him on the road.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Keil and Delitzsch, Wesley and the Companion Bible all explain Mahanaim as two camps or two hosts. Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch take the two as the angels' host and Jacob's own; Gill and Wesley also allow two companies of angels.
layers.text: Jacob says this is God's camp (machaneh) and names the place Mahanaim, two camps. Many explain the two as God's camp of angels beside Jacob's own company, so the name marks that he did not travel alone.

passages.saying: Jacob divided his people into two camps
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Jacob's fear and his plan in verses 7 and 8.
layers.text: When Jacob hears that Esau is coming with four hundred men, he is terrified. He splits his people and animals into two groups, so that if Esau attacks one, the other can escape.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible notes that two camps here is the same word, and perhaps the same idea, as God's camp in verse 2. In Hebrew, lishnei machanot (into two camps) in verses 7 and 10 sits beside the place name Machanayim, two camps.
layers.text: Jacob's two camps (machanot) use the word camp from verse 2, where God's camp met him and he named the place Mahanaim, two camps. Some see a link: now in fear he makes two camps of his own, and in prayer says, "now I have become two camps".

passages.saying: crossed the ford of the Jabbok
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the account of Jacob's night crossing.
layers.text: In the night Jacob takes his two wives, his two maidservants and his eleven sons across the ford of the Jabbok, a stream that runs west into the Jordan.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on the wrestling verse (32:25 in Hebrew numbering, 32:24 in English), note the rare verb for wrestle and say the river evidently took its name Jabbok from this wrestling. The Companion Bible instead glosses Jabbok as pouring out.
layers.text: The stream's name, Yabboq (Jabbok), may be meant to sound like the rare verb ye'aveq, wrestled, used two verses later when a man wrestles with Jacob there. Some hold that the river was even named after this struggle.

passages.saying: Your name will no longer be Jacob, but Israel
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.evidence: Genesis calls him a man; at Peniel Jacob says, "I have seen God face to face" (Genesis 32:30); Hosea 12:4 calls him the angel. Christians have read him as an angel, as God appearing in human form, or, as many since the early church, as the Son of God before His birth. Jewish tradition often sees him as Esau's guardian angel (Genesis Rabbah 77:3). The text leaves it a mystery.
layers.text: Alone at night, about to meet the brother he cheated, Jacob wrestles a mysterious man until dawn. Hip struck, he still says, "I will not let you go unless you bless me." He is given a new name and a blessing, and says, "I have seen God face to face."

layers.evidence: TAHOT: Yisra'el (H3478) and sarita, you have struggled (H8280), in this verse. TBESH gives God prevails; Ellicott and Gill explain the name as a prince of God, one who prevails with God, as the verse does by Jacob's own struggle.
layers.text: Israel, yisra'el, is explained by the verb in the verse, sarita: "you have struggled with God and with men, and you have prevailed." Jacob, named for a heel, now carries a name that remembers his struggle with God, and so do his descendants.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: Yabboq (H2999) in 32:22; Ya'aqov (H3290) and vaye'aveq, he wrestled (H0079), in 32:24. The verb avaq occurs only here and in 32:25 in the whole Hebrew Bible. Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary note that the verb was chosen for its likeness to the name Jabbok.
layers.text: The scene is full of sound-alikes. Jacob (ya'aqov) crosses the Jabbok (yabboq), and a man wrestles (ye'aveq) with him. The verb for wrestle appears only in this scene. Three similar words tie Jacob, the river and the struggle together.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: Hosea 12:3 has aqav (H6117), the verb Esau uses in Genesis 27:36, and sarah (H8280), the verb of Israel's name in Genesis 32:28; 12:4 adds bakhah, he wept (H1058), and vayyitchannen, he sought favor (H2603). Hosea 12:2 frames the retelling as a charge, and 12:6 calls the people back. Most read Jacob as the one who wept; some take it to be the angel.
layers.text: Hosea retells the story in a charge against Jacob's descendants. Jacob "struggled with the angel and prevailed; he wept and sought His favor." Genesis never mentions the tears. Then Hosea calls them, "you must return to your God."

passages.saying: I have seen God face to face, and yet my life was spared
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Jacob's own reason for the name, given in the verse.
layers.text: After wrestling through the night, Jacob names the place where it happened. He marvels that he has seen God face to face and still lived.

layers.evidence: Gill, Wesley and Matthew Henry all explain Peniel as the face of God, named because Jacob saw God face to face there. Gill also notes the spelling Penuel in the next verse.
layers.text: Peniel means face of God (peni, face of, and El, God). Jacob gave the place this name because there he saw God face to face, and his words use the same Hebrew word for face (panim).

passages.saying: that is why the place was called Succoth
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own account of what Jacob built there.
layers.text: After parting from Esau, Jacob travels on and stays a while at a place where he builds a house for himself and shelters for his livestock.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown all say Succoth means booths and was named from the shelters Jacob put up there. Wesley says the same.
layers.text: Succoth means booths or shelters. The place takes its name from the shelters (sukkot) Jacob made for his livestock, so the name is simply the Hebrew word for what he built there.

passages.saying: he arrived safely at the city of Shechem in the land of Canaan
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the Hebrew word shalem, which the BSB renders safely.
layers.text: After the long journey from Paddan-aram, Jacob arrives safe and sound at Shechem in the land of Canaan and camps just outside the city.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch read shalem as safe, not a town name, and call it an evident allusion to in peace in 28:21, Jacob's vow now fulfilled. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown suggests shalem means Jacob arrived safe and sound, a tribute to the God who promised his return (28:15), though most writers take Shalem as a town, as Gill does. Clarke and Wesley also read safely here.
layers.text: Jacob arrives safely (shalem). At Bethel God had promised to bring him home (28:15), and Jacob had vowed to return in peace, beshalom (28:21). His safe arrival shows the promise kept and the prayer answered.

passages.saying: There he set up an altar and called it El-Elohe-Israel
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse, which closes Jacob's journey home with worship.
layers.text: Now settled near Shechem in Canaan, Jacob sets up an altar to worship God and gives it a name that confesses who God is to him.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Jacob named the altar this way according to his vow in Genesis 28:21, to give glory to the God of Israel for keeping him while he was away.
layers.text: Some see the name answering Jacob's vow at Bethel, where he said that if God brought him home safely, "then the LORD will be my God" (28:21). Back in the land, he names his altar for God as the God of Israel.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke and Wesley all read the name as God, the God of Israel, and tie it to Jacob's new name Israel. Keil and Delitzsch and Matthew Henry give the same meaning.
layers.text: El-Elohe-Israel means God, the God of Israel. Jacob uses the new name Israel that God had just given him at the Jabbok (32:28), and so acknowledges the mighty God as his own God.

passages.saying: who answered me in my day of distress
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Jacob's words in the verse, with his flight from Esau and his fear at the Jabbok in view.
layers.text: Jacob calls his household to go up with him to Bethel. There he will build an altar to the God who answered him in trouble and stayed with him wherever he went.

layers.evidence: Gill, Keil and Delitzsch, and Wesley all link this day of distress and this altar to the vow Jacob made at Bethel (28:20-22). In Hebrew the two verses share the words for with me, the way and go.
layers.text: These words look back to the vow Jacob made at Bethel as he fled from Esau. He asked God to be with him on the journey he was taking (28:20) and promised that the stone would be God's house. Now he says God has been with him, and he goes back to keep his word.

passages.saying: he called that place El-bethel
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the reason the verse itself gives for the name.
layers.text: Back at Bethel, Jacob builds the altar God told him to make. He names the place for the God who had revealed Himself to him there years before, when he was fleeing from Esau.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, Wesley, Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown all render El-bethel as God of Bethel. Matthew Henry sets Beth-el, the house of God, beside El-beth-el, the God of the house.
layers.text: El-bethel means God of Bethel, and Bethel means house of God. Jacob now names the place not only as God's house but for the God he met there.

passages.saying: was buried under the oak below Bethel
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on the mourning that the tree's name records.
layers.text: Deborah, who had nursed Rebekah, dies and is buried under an oak below Bethel. Her death is deeply mourned, and the tree is named for that grief.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke and Wesley all give the meaning oak of weeping, from the mourning over Deborah. Keil and Delitzsch and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown agree.
layers.text: Allon-bachuth means oak of weeping (allon, oak, and bakhut, weeping). The tree was named for the tears shed over Deborah, a faithful old servant of the family.

layers.evidence: Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown both give bee as the meaning of Deborah; Gill adds that Josephus says the same.
layers.text: The nurse's name, Deborah, is the Hebrew word for a bee.

passages.saying: you will no longer be called Jacob. Instead, your name will be Israel
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on God's words in the verse, spoken at Bethel after Jacob's return.
layers.text: God appears to Jacob again at Bethel. He tells him that Jacob, the name he was given at birth, is no longer to be his name. From now on he will be called Israel.

layers.evidence: Gill, Wesley, and Keil and Delitzsch all say God here confirms the name Israel already given at Genesis 32:28.
layers.text: God here repeats the new name first given at the Jabbok, where Jacob wrestled through the night and heard, "Your name will no longer be Jacob, but Israel" (32:28). Now, as God appears to him again at Bethel, that name is confirmed.

passages.saying: I am God Almighty. Be fruitful and multiply.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of God's promise to Jacob at Bethel.
layers.text: At Bethel God appears to Jacob again, calls Himself God Almighty, and renews His promise. Jacob's family will grow into a nation and a company of nations, and kings will come from his line.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the title El Shaddai here points back to God's words to Abram, and that the promise of offspring points back to Genesis 17:6 and 17:8. Wesley, on 17:1, notes God used the same name to Jacob in 35:11.
layers.text: God greets Jacob with the name He first used to Abraham, “I am God Almighty” (El Shaddai), and repeats His promise that kings would come from Abraham's line. The words tie Jacob to the covenant God made with Abraham in chapter 17.

passages.saying: she named him Ben-oni. But his father called him Benjamin.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain account of Rachel's death in childbirth and the two names.
layers.text: Rachel dies giving birth to her second son. With her last breath she names him Ben-oni, but Jacob gives the boy another name, Benjamin.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Matthew Henry and Wesley explain Ben-oni as son of my sorrow. Clarke, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Henry and Wesley give Benjamin as son of the right hand, one dearly loved. Keil and Delitzsch prefer son of good fortune for Benjamin.
layers.text: Ben-oni means son of my sorrow, a name drawn from Rachel's pain as she died. Jacob renamed the boy Benjamin, son of the right hand, meaning a dearly loved son and a support at his side, so his name would not keep the grief alive.

passages.saying: You have broken out first!
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain account of the birth of Tamar's twins.
layers.text: Tamar gives birth to twins. One baby puts out his hand first but draws it back, and his brother is born first instead. That brother is named Perez.

layers.evidence: Clarke, Keil and Delitzsch, Gill and Wesley all tie the name Perez to the words about the breach at his birth. Keil and Delitzsch explain the breach as breaking through by pressing forward.
layers.text: When the baby pushes ahead of his twin, the cry is, “You have broken out first!” The Hebrew verb is parats, to break through, and the boy is named Perez (Perets), meaning breach or one who breaks through, after the way he was born.

passages.saying: Now Joseph was well-built and handsome
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording about Potiphar's trust in Joseph.
layers.text: Potiphar trusts Joseph so fully that he leaves everything he owns in Joseph's care and thinks of nothing but his own meals. The verse ends by noting that Joseph was well-built and handsome.

layers.evidence: Clarke, on 39:6, gives the Hebrew as beautiful in his person and beautiful in his countenance, and notes that the same expressions are used of Rachel at 29:17. Barnes, on 39:1-6, renders the phrase beautiful in form and look, points to 29:17, and says it prepares the way for what follows.
layers.text: In Hebrew Joseph is yepheh toar and yepheh mareh, beautiful in form and beautiful in appearance. The same pair of phrases describes his mother Rachel in 29:17, so the wording recalls her. His good looks also set the scene for the temptation that follows.

passages.saying: Pharaoh will lift off your head and hang you on a tree.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Joseph's plain interpretation of the chief baker's dream.
layers.text: Joseph explains the chief baker's dream. Within three days Pharaoh will have him put to death and his body hung on a tree, where the birds will eat his flesh.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch note that 40:19 uses the same words as 40:13 but adds away from thee, meaning beheading, and that on the birthday Pharaoh lifted up both heads in very different ways. Gill says both heads were lifted up, yet in a different sense.
layers.text: In Hebrew Joseph uses the same phrase, lift up your head, for both dreamers. For the cupbearer it means Pharaoh will restore him (40:13). For the baker Joseph adds from off you, so it means he will be beheaded. On Pharaoh's birthday both heads were lifted up, in opposite ways.

passages.saying: God has made me forget all my hardship
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Joseph's own explanation of the name he gives his firstborn.
layers.text: Joseph names his firstborn son Manasseh, giving thanks that God has made him forget all his hardship and his father's household.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke and Wesley explain Manasseh as forgetfulness, Clarke deriving it from nashah, to forget. Keil and Delitzsch render it causing to forget and note that the verb form nashshani was chosen for its likeness in sound to the name.
layers.text: The name Manasseh (Menashsheh) means one who makes to forget. It comes from nashah, to forget, and Joseph explains it with a matching word: God nashshani, has made me forget. The name thanks God for easing the pain of his years of trouble.

passages.saying: God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Joseph's own explanation of the name he gives his second son.
layers.text: Joseph names his second son Ephraim, thanking God for making him fruitful in Egypt, the land where he had suffered as a slave and a prisoner.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke and Wesley explain Ephraim as fruitfulness, Clarke deriving it from parah, to be fruitful. Gill notes the dual ending, and Keil and Delitzsch render it double fruitfulness.
layers.text: The name Ephraim (Ephrayim) comes from parah, to be fruitful, the same verb Joseph uses when he says God has made me fruitful (hiphrani). Its form suggests double fruitfulness: God blessed Joseph in Egypt, the very land of his suffering.

passages.saying: they bowed down before him with their faces to the ground
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself and on 42:8, which says the brothers did not recognize Joseph.
layers.text: Joseph now rules Egypt and oversees the sale of grain to everyone who comes. His brothers, who had sold him as a slave years before, arrive to buy food and bow low before him, not knowing who he is (42:8).

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on 42:6 all say this bowing fulfils Joseph's dream; Keil and Delitzsch on 42:9 say the sight reminded him of the sheaves and stars. The same Hebrew verb for bowing down (shachah) is used in 37:7, 37:9 and 42:6.
layers.text: The brothers bow to the ground before Joseph, just as their sheaves bowed down to his sheaf in his dream (37:7). The dream they hated, and tried to defeat by selling him, comes true without their knowing it, and in verse 9 Joseph remembers his dreams.

passages.saying: When Joseph saw that his father had placed his right hand
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on 48:18, where Joseph tells his father that Manasseh is the firstborn.
layers.text: Jacob, blessing Joseph's two sons, lays his right hand, the hand of greater honor, on Ephraim, the younger. Joseph is displeased and tries to move it to Manasseh, his firstborn.

layers.evidence: Gill on 48:17 says the patriarchal blessing was thought to belong to the firstborn but did not always go to them, as in Jacob's own case. Gill on 48:20 and Clarke on 48:14 also list Jacob over Esau among the times the younger was set before the older.
layers.text: Joseph expects the firstborn to get the greater blessing. Yet Jacob himself was a younger son who received his father Isaac's blessing ahead of his older twin Esau, a blessing that made him master over his brothers (27:29). Now Jacob in turn sets the younger grandson ahead of the older.

passages.saying: I give the ridge of land that I took from the Amorites
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own words.
layers.text: Jacob gives Joseph one portion of land more than his brothers receive, land he says he took from the Amorites with his sword and bow.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Jacob used shekhem as a play upon the word Shechem; Gill says the word is Shechem and the city is referred to enigmatically; Clarke reads one shechem or one shoulder and links it to the field bought in 33:19. Wesley and Keil and Delitzsch note Joseph's burial there.
layers.text: The word for ridge of land is shekhem, literally shoulder, which is also the name of the town Shechem. Jacob plays on that name, for at Shechem he had bought a plot of ground (33:19). Joseph's bones were later buried in that plot, and it became his descendants' inheritance (Joshua 24:32).

passages.saying: Uncontrolled as the waters, you will no longer excel
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on 49:3, which names Reuben as Jacob's firstborn.
layers.text: Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, should have held the place of honor. Jacob calls him uncontrolled as water and says he will no longer excel, because he went up to his father's bed and defiled it.

layers.evidence: Gill on 49:4 and Keil and Delitzsch on 49:3 both tie these words to Reuben lying with Bilhah in 35:22, and Clarke on 49:4 sends the reader to his note on 35:22. 1 Chronicles 5:1 also says Reuben lost the birthright because he defiled his father's bed.
layers.text: Jacob points back to the time Reuben slept with Bilhah, his father's concubine (35:22). Back then the record says only that Israel heard about it. Now, at the end of his life, Jacob names that sin as the reason Reuben loses the firstborn's place of honor.

passages.saying: Simeon and Levi are brothers; their swords are weapons of violence.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the curse that follows in 49:6-7.
layers.text: Jacob says Simeon and Levi are brothers alike in spirit, who used their swords for violence. He wants no part in their plans and curses their fierce anger (49:6-7).

layers.evidence: Gill and Keil and Delitzsch on 49:5, and Matthew Henry's Concise on 49:3-7, all link these words to the slaughter at Shechem in 34:25. In 49:6 Jacob says they killed men in their anger, with the same Hebrew verb for killing (harag) as 34:25.
layers.text: Jacob looks back to the day Simeon and Levi took their swords, went into the city of Shechem, and killed every male to avenge their sister Dinah (34:25). Jacob had rebuked them then (34:30), and now he condemns their anger in his final words.

passages.saying: Judah, your brothers shall praise you.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own words.
layers.text: Jacob gives Judah the blessing of leadership. His brothers will honor him, his hand will be on the necks of his enemies, and his father's sons will bow down to him.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call yoducha a play upon Yehudah, like Leah's word in 29:35; Gill, Clarke, Wesley and Matthew Henry's Concise all say Judah's name means praise and that Jacob builds on it. Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists the verse as a play on words.
layers.text: The name Judah, Yehudah, is built on the Hebrew verb for praise (yadah). Leah named him saying, "This time I will praise the LORD" (29:35). Jacob now plays on the name: your brothers shall praise you, yoducha. The son for whom God was praised will be praised by his brothers.

passages.saying: The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the staff from between his feet, until Shiloh comes and the allegiance of the nations is his.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, the NET Bible notes, classic commentaries, the Dead Sea Scroll 4Q252, Targum Onkelos, the Talmud, Justin Martyr and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: On his deathbed Jacob blesses his sons. Judah, the fourth, receives the royal line: "your father’s sons shall bow down to you," and the ruler's staff will stay with his tribe until a coming one receives the obedience of the nations.

layers.evidence: Name meaning from TBESH. Keil and Delitzsch and the Pulpit Commentary on Genesis 49:8 note the play on yadah, to praise.
layers.text: "Judah, your brothers shall praise you" plays on his name, which means "praised." At his birth Leah said, "This time I will praise the LORD," and named him Judah. The verb is yadah both times.
The near fulfillment came with David, of the tribe of Judah: "Judah prevailed over his brothers and a ruler came from him," and God promised David, "your throne will be established forever."

layers.evidence: TBESH: the meaning is uncertain. Ellicott gives Sheloh, whose it is, among several readings; the NET Bible's rendering follows the ancient versions. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch on Genesis 49:10 hear Jacob's words in Ezekiel 21:27 and see the Messiah in them.
layers.text: No one is sure what "Shiloh" means. A favored reading, though not certain, is shello, "whose it is." Ezekiel seems to echo it: "until the arrival of Him to whom it belongs." Older commentators see the Messiah there.

layers.evidence: Dead Sea Scroll 4Q252 5:3 (Intertextual Bible translation; dated there to 160 to 60 BC). Targum Onkelos on Genesis 49:10 has meshicha, Messiah, whose is the kingdom (Aramaic, Sefaria). Talmud, Sanhedrin 98b, paraphrased.
layers.text: Jewish readers heard the Messiah here too. A Dead Sea Scroll from before Jesus' birth reads it as the coming of the righteous Messiah, the branch of David. An Aramaic paraphrase names the Messiah outright, and in the Talmud one school says Shiloh is his name.

layers.evidence: Poole, Barnes and Gill on Revelation 5:5 link it to Genesis 49:9, as do OpenBible.info cross-references.
layers.text: Revelation takes up Jacob's lion: "Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed." Then John sees "a Lamb who appeared to have been slain." The King from Judah wins by being slain; as Hebrews says, "our Lord descended from Judah."

layers.evidence: Hebrew ayir (colt) and aton (donkey) in both verses (STEPBible TAHOT, TBESH). Gill on Genesis 49:11 notes that some read it of Christ, when Zechariah 9:9 was fulfilled in Matthew 21:2. Justin Martyr, First Apology 32, about AD 155.

cites.at: Justin Martyr, First Apology 32

layers.text: "He ties his donkey to the vine, his colt to the choicest branch." Zechariah's king rides "on a colt, the foal of a donkey," the same two Hebrew words. Matthew finds "a donkey tied there, with her colt"; an early Christian writer saw Jacob's colt in it.

passages.saying: Dan shall provide justice for his people
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and on 30:5-6, which tell of Dan's birth to Bilhah.
layers.text: Dan was the son of Rachel's servant Bilhah, yet Jacob says his tribe will provide justice for his people as fully as any other tribe of Israel.

layers.evidence: Gill calls the words an elegant paronomasia on the name Dan, Keil and Delitzsch say Dan will act according to his name, and Clarke says the name signifies judgment. Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists the verse with 30:6.
layers.text: The name Dan comes from din, to judge. Rachel named him when she said, "God has vindicated me" (30:6), using that same verb. Jacob now plays on the name: Dan yadin, Dan shall provide justice for his people. The son whose birth showed God judging for Rachel will himself bring justice.

passages.saying: Gad will be attacked by raiders, but he will attack their heels.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of raiders attacking Gad and Gad striking back, as Wesley explains it.
layers.text: Jacob foretells that bands of raiders will attack the tribe of Gad, but Gad will strike back and chase them off. The tribe would often have to fight, yet in the end it would win.

layers.evidence: Gill calls the verse a paronomasia, an allusion to the name of Gad almost in every word; Clarke points to a most singular alliteration in the original; Keil and Delitzsch say the name Gad reminds Jacob of gud, to press, and gedud, the pressing host, and call the blessing a triple alliteration.
layers.text: Jacob builds this blessing out of the sound of Gad's name. In Hebrew it runs gad gedud yegudennu, ve-hu yagud akev: Gad, a raiding band (gedud) will raid him (gud), but he will raid at their heels. Four of its six Hebrew words echo gad.

passages.saying: Joseph is a fruitful vine
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the vine image, which Jamieson-Fausset-Brown read as the great growth of Joseph's tribes.
layers.text: Jacob pictures Joseph as a fruitful vine planted by a spring, its branches climbing over a wall. His descendants, the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, would grow large and spread.

layers.evidence: Gill ties the fruitful bough to Joseph's children, one of whom he called Ephraim from his fruitfulness; Wesley explains the line with the words of Genesis 41:52, that God had made him fruitful in the land of his affliction. Both verses use the verb parah.
layers.text: The word for fruitful here comes from parah, to be fruitful. Joseph used the same verb when he named his son Ephraim, saying, "God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction." Jacob's blessing picks up that name and that thanks.

passages.saying: Thus the place across the Jordan is called Abel-mizraim.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own explanation of how the place got its name.
layers.text: Jacob's funeral procession, which included many great men of Egypt, mourned so deeply at the threshing floor of Atad that the Canaanites watching named the place Abel-mizraim.

layers.evidence: Gill and Wesley both give the name as the mourning of Egypt, or of the Egyptians. Keil and Delitzsch read abel as meadow, with a play upon the word for mourning. The verse itself ties the name to the mourning the Canaanites saw.
layers.text: The Canaanites saw the great mourning, in Hebrew evel, and named the place Abel-mizraim. Abel sounds like the word for mourning, so the name is heard as mourning of Egypt, though abel can also mean a meadow. The name kept the memory of Egypt's grief for Jacob.

passages.saying: As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TBESH, the NET Bible notes, Genesis Rabbah, classic older commentaries named under each note and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: After Jacob dies, Joseph's brothers fear he will finally pay them back for selling him into slavery. Joseph weeps and tells them not to be afraid: their evil plan had been God's plan to keep many people alive.

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Genesis 50:20 notes that the same verb is used for both, contrasting the two purposes. Chashav from TBESH.
layers.text: "You intended" and "God intended" are one Hebrew verb, chashav, to plan. The repetition sets human purpose against God's: one event had two authors with opposite aims, and God's aim stood.

Joseph had said it when he first revealed himself: "it was to save lives that God sent me before you," and "it was not you who sent me here, but God." The psalm tells it from heaven's side: "He sent a man before them," "Joseph, sold as a slave."

layers.evidence: Matthew Henry on Genesis 38:25 sets Tamar's words to Judah beside Judah's words to his father in 37:32, as Genesis Rabbah 85:11 (Sefaria) had. The Pulpit Commentary on 42:7: treated them as strangers is the same root, nakar, that means recognize. Word data from STEPBible TAHOT and TBESH.
layers.text: "Examine it," the brothers tell Jacob, showing him the bloody robe. "Please examine them," Tamar tells Judah, sending his seal and staff. Both are haker-na, and each man "recognized" (nakar). Later Joseph "recognized them," but "they did not recognize him."

layers.evidence: The NET Bible note on Genesis 37:31 points out that Jacob had deceived his own father with two young goats.

cites.at: An Inconsolable Father, Tabletalk devotional (Ligonier), no writer named

layers.text: The deceiver is deceived the same way. Jacob once fooled his blind father with goat skins; now his sons fool him with Joseph's robe dipped in a goat's blood.

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Acts 7:9 sees the same envy leading their descendants to hand over Jesus.
layers.text: Stephen tells Joseph's story as a pattern: "Because the patriarchs were jealous of Joseph, they sold him as a slave into Egypt. But God was with him." He ends with "the Righteous One" whom his hearers betrayed, as their fathers had betrayed Joseph.

layers.evidence: Gill on Genesis 50:20 draws the comparison with the cross.
layers.text: The cross has the same shape. Peter says Jesus "was delivered up by God’s set plan and foreknowledge, and you, by the hands of the lawless, put Him to death." Human evil and God's saving purpose meet in one event, though Acts does not mention Joseph.

passages.saying: she got him a papyrus basket and coated it with tar and pitch
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself, read with the rescue that follows in Exodus 2:4-10.
layers.text: When Moses' mother could no longer hide her baby from Pharaoh's order to drown the Hebrew boys, she made a basket of papyrus reeds, sealed it with tar and pitch, put him inside, and set it among the reeds at the edge of the Nile.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the word tevah (ark) is probably meant to call to mind the ark in which Noah was saved; Bullinger's Companion Bible compares Genesis 6:14. Clarke and Barnes note the word is used only for Noah's ark and Moses' basket.
layers.text: The word for Moses' basket, tevah, is the word used for Noah's ark, and the Bible uses it for nothing else. Both are sealed to keep out the water. The baby who will one day lead Israel out is kept safe from the deadly Nile in a little ark, as Noah was kept safe from the flood.

passages.saying: She named him Moses and explained, “I drew him out of the water.”
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TBESH, the NET Bible notes and classic older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Pharaoh ordered every Hebrew baby boy thrown "into the Nile." One mother set her son in a basket "among the reeds along the bank of the Nile," and Pharaoh's own daughter found him, "had compassion on him," and raised him: "he became her son."

layers.evidence: Ellicott, Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary on Exodus 2:10: the name is probably Egyptian, Mesu, meaning born or son. I drew him is meshitihu, from mashah (STEPBible TAHOT). Keil and Delitzsch say the Hebrew explanation is a theological interpretation, not an etymology.
layers.text: Moses (Mosheh) is most likely an Egyptian name, from a word meaning "born" or "son." In Hebrew it sounds like mashah, "to draw out," and the princess makes it a Hebrew pun: "I drew him out of the water." It is a play on sound, not the name's origin.

layers.evidence: The NET Bible notes on Exodus 2:10 read Mosheh as an active form, the one who draws out, and cite Isaiah 63:11. The TBESH gloss, drawn, gives the sense of the pun, not the form. Keil and Delitzsch, quoting Kurtz, call the name an unintended prophecy: the one drawn out became the drawer out.
layers.text: The Hebrew form is active: Mosheh means one who draws out, not one drawn out. The name became an unintended prophecy: the baby drawn from the Nile led Israel through the sea. Isaiah remembers "the days of Moses" and "He who brought them through the sea."

layers.evidence: Mashah occurs only in Exodus 2:10, 2 Samuel 22:17 and Psalm 18:16 (STEPBible TAHOT). Keil and Delitzsch on Psalm 18:16 link the verb to Moses drawn from the Nile; Gill offers it as one of two readings, the other a drowning man.
layers.text: Mashah, "draw out," occurs only three times: here, and twice in David's song of rescue: "He drew me out of deep waters." Each time the verb comes with water. Some commentators think David may be recalling Moses, or simply picturing a drowning man.

layers.evidence: Matthew Henry, Gill, Poole and the Pulpit Commentary on Acts 7:35 see Stephen setting Moses beside Jesus as a type of Christ.
layers.text: Stephen retells this life as a pattern. The man Israel rejected with "Who made you ruler and judge over us?" is "the one whom God sent to be their ruler and redeemer." Commentators see Stephen setting Moses beside Jesus, whom his hearers had also rejected.

layers.evidence: Barnes on Hebrews 11:24 ties it to Moses' adoption by Pharaoh's daughter (Exodus 2:10); Acts 7:21-25 also recalls it.
layers.text: Hebrews recalls the adoption: "By faith Moses, when he was grown, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter." The prince drawn from the river "chose to suffer oppression with God’s people" and "valued disgrace for Christ above the treasures of Egypt."

passages.saying: Moses rose up to help them and watered their flock
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its setting at the well in Midian (Exodus 2:15-19).
layers.text: At a well in Midian, shepherds drove away the seven daughters of the priest of Midian who had come to water their father's flock. Moses, a fugitive from Egypt, stood up for them, rescued them, and watered their flock himself.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Moses won his welcome in Midian by doing as Jacob had done in Genesis 29:10; Bullinger's Companion Bible compares Genesis 29:10 at the word helped. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also likens Moses' winning of his wife to Jacob's.
layers.text: Moses meets his wife much as Jacob met Rachel. In each story a man far from home comes to a well, steps in for a shepherd's daughter or daughters, and waters the flock. Each time the stranger is taken into the family and marries a daughter of the house.

passages.saying: I have become a foreigner in a foreign land
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its setting in Midian (Exodus 2:15-21).
layers.text: In Midian, Moses' wife Zipporah gave birth to a son. Moses named him Gershom, because he was living as a foreigner, far from Egypt where he grew up and from the land promised to his people.

layers.evidence: Clarke says Gershom is literally a stranger; Gill, a desolate stranger; Wesley, a stranger there. Keil and Delitzsch derive it from garash, to drive out, and say Moses explains the name by its sound with ger, stranger.
layers.text: The name Gershom sounds like ger, the Hebrew word for a foreigner or sojourner, and Moses explains it that way: he has become a foreigner in a foreign land. The name may also come from garash, to drive out, which fits a man living in exile.

passages.saying: appeared to him in a blazing fire from within a bush
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its setting at Horeb, the mountain of God (Exodus 3:1-6).
layers.text: At Horeb, the mountain of God, the angel of the LORD appeared to Moses in flames of fire coming from a thorn bush. Moses saw that the bush was on fire, yet the fire did not burn it up.

layers.evidence: Clarke (on Exodus 3:1 and 19:1) says Sinai may take its name from the seneh, the bush of Exodus 3:2. Gill says Sinai was named for the bushes that grew on it and Wesley for its many thorny bushes; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says it was so called from the seneh bush.
layers.text: The Hebrew word for this bush, seneh, sounds like Sinai, the mountain where God would later meet all Israel and give the law. Older Bible scholars held that Sinai was named for its thorn bushes, and some thought it was named for this very bush where God appeared.

passages.saying: I AM WHO I AM. This is what you are to say to the Israelites: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESH, Strong's, the Septuagint, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: At the burning bush Moses asks what to tell Israel when they ask God's name. God answers, "I AM WHO I AM," then calls Himself the LORD, the God of their fathers, and says, "This is My name forever."

layers.evidence: TAHOT tags ehyeh as hayah, to be. Poole calls Jehovah a word of the same root and meaning as I am; the Pulpit Commentary derives it from hava, to be, and renders it The Existent. Strong's: the self-existent or eternal One. The gloss the existing One is TBESH's.
layers.text: The answer plays on the name. "I AM" is ehyeh, from hayah, "to be." The next verse gives the name YHWH, "the LORD," which most scholars derive from the same verb, with a sense like "the existing One."

layers.evidence: Pulpit, Barnes and Gill on John 8:58 point to Exodus 3:14. The Septuagint of Exodus 3:14 reads ego eimi ho on, I am the One who is, but the Hebrew is ehyeh (TAHOT). In Isaiah 43:10 the Septuagint has ego eimi for ani hu, I am He.
layers.text: Jesus says, "before Abraham was born, I am!" and His hearers "picked up stones to throw at Him." Many hear the name from the bush, ego eimi, "I am," in the Greek Old Testament, and Isaiah's "I am He," ani hu in Hebrew: an echo that does not depend on Greek.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Gill and Bengel on Revelation 1:4 call it a paraphrase of the name Jehovah; Ellicott calls the break in grammar intentional, and Bengel ties it to the undeclined Hebrew name. TAGNT: the critical texts read apo ho on
layers.text: Revelation greets the churches "from Him who is and was and is to come," which commentators call a paraphrase of the name given to Moses. John even breaks Greek grammar, leaving "Him who is" (ho on) unchanged after "from," as if the Name could not change.

Jesus finds the resurrection in this same scene. At the bush God called Himself "the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob," long after they had died, and Jesus concludes: "He is not the God of the dead, but of the living."

layers.evidence: Ellicott on John 18:6 hears the name I AM in the answer; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Gill see Christ's divine majesty overpowering them; Barnes finds no proof of miraculous power.
layers.text: When soldiers come for "Jesus of Nazareth," He answers "I am He" (ego eimi), and "they drew back and fell to the ground." Some commentators hear the divine name again; others think the men were simply overawed.

passages.saying: Israel is My firstborn son
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESG (Abbott-Smith), the Septuagint, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: God sends Moses to tell Pharaoh, "Israel is My firstborn son," and to let God's son go. Pharaoh refuses, and at the last plague the LORD "struck down every firstborn male in the land of Egypt."

layers.evidence: Pulpit on Matthew 2:15: Hosea's words rest on Exodus 4:22, and the Messiah's experience parallels the nation's. Ellicott: they refer to the history of Israel. Poole: Israel's going out was a type of Christ's going into Egypt.
layers.text: Hosea looks back on the exodus: "out of Egypt I called My son." Matthew sets this beside the child Jesus' stay in Egypt and calls it "fulfilled." It first meant Israel's past; commentators see Matthew reading Israel's story as a pattern for the Messiah's.

layers.evidence: Septuagint of Exodus 4:19 and Matthew 2:20 (TAGNT) share the words tethnekasin gar, hoi zetountes and ten psychen. Ellicott, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Pulpit Commentary on Matthew 2:20 trace the wording to Exodus 4:19.
layers.text: The angel tells Joseph to go home, "for those seeking the Child’s life are now dead," the words God spoke to Moses in Midian: "all the men who sought to kill you are dead." In the Greek Old Testament the two sentences are almost word for word the same.

layers.evidence: Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 8:3, 6:16 and 6:13. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Matthew 4:4 sets Israel's forty years beside Jesus' forty days, and Bengel notes that all three sayings were first spoken to Israel in the wilderness.
layers.text: Israel, God's son, was tested forty years in the wilderness, disciplined "just as a man disciplines his son." Tested forty days, Jesus hears "If You are the Son of God," and answers three times from Deuteronomy. Where the first son failed, this Son stands.

layers.evidence: Abbott-Smith (in TBESG): exodos, a going out, used of death in Luke 9:31 and 2 Peter 1:15. Barnes: perhaps an allusion to Israel's departure from Egypt; Gill: the name of the second book of Moses; Ellicott calls the word remarkable for a death.
layers.text: On the mountain Moses and Elijah talk with Jesus about "His departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem." The Greek word is exodos, as in "the exodus of the Israelites." It can just mean death, but with Moses there, many hear a new exodus.

layers.evidence: Exodus 13:2 and 13:15. Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown on Luke 2:23 tie the law to the sparing of Israel's firstborn in Egypt.
layers.text: Because God spared Israel's firstborn when Egypt's died, every firstborn son belonged to the LORD and had to be redeemed. Luke quotes this law when Mary's firstborn is presented at the temple: "Every firstborn male shall be consecrated to the Lord."

passages.saying: when I see the blood, I will pass over you
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: On the night of the last plague each household kills a lamb and puts its blood on the doorframe, and the LORD passes over the marked houses.
The feast is named for the act: pesach (Passover) comes from pasach, "to pass over." The text explains the name itself: "It is the Passover sacrifice to the LORD, who passed over the houses."
Paul writes, "Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed," and Peter calls Him "a lamb without blemish or spot," like the unblemished lamb the law required.

When the soldiers do not break Jesus' legs, John says Scripture was fulfilled: "Not one of His bones will be broken." The words fit the Passover rule and also Psalm 34:20; commentators discuss which John means, and some think both.

In John, Jesus is sentenced on "the day of Preparation for the Passover," when the lambs were slaughtered, and at the cross a sponge is lifted to Him on hyssop, the plant used to put the blood on the doorframes.

The lamb runs from Egypt to the end of the Bible: "Look, the Lamb of God" and the Lamb at the center of the throne "who appeared to have been slain." These draw on the Passover lamb and on Isaiah's servant "led like a lamb to the slaughter."

passages.saying: It is the Passover sacrifice to the LORD, who passed over the houses
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse with the children's question in Exodus 12:26.
layers.text: When their children ask what this ceremony means, the Israelites are to answer that it is a sacrifice to the LORD, who passed over their houses in Egypt and spared their homes when He struck down the Egyptians. Then the people bowed down and worshiped.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch derive pesach from the verb pasach, to pass over or spare. Clarke and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (on Exodus 12:11) say the feast is named for the LORD passing over Israel's houses; Gill and Barnes say the same.
layers.text: The feast's name, Pesach (Passover), comes from the verb pasach, to pass over, and this verse puts the two side by side: it is the Passover because the LORD passed over Israel's houses. The word carries the idea of sparing, for He spared every home marked with the lamb's blood.

passages.saying: they could not drink the water there because it was bitter
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse.
layers.text: After days without water, Israel came to Marah and found water at last, but it was too bitter to drink. The verse adds that this is how the place got its name.

layers.evidence: Wesley and the Companion Bible give Marah the meaning bitterness or bitter. Clarke and Gill say the place was named from its bitter water, as the verse itself says. Hebrew marah and marim, bitter, share the same root.
layers.text: Marah means bitter. The water there was marim, bitter, so the place was named Marah. In Hebrew the name and the reason for it sound almost the same, so the name itself remembers the bitter water.

passages.saying: It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: In the desert, the hungry Israelites find thin flakes on the ground after the dew lifts, like nothing they have seen before. Moses tells them it is bread from the LORD. They will eat it for forty years, until they reach Canaan.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: man, what? (H4478B), in 16:15, found only here, and man, manna (H4478A), in 16:31. The same verse then uses the ordinary Hebrew word for what, mah, in "they did not know what it was." The naming story is the Bible's own explanation.
layers.text: When they first see it they ask, man hu (said mahn hoo), "What is it?" And the food keeps the question as its name: they "called the bread manna," man in Hebrew. For forty years Israel's daily bread was called What-is-it.

passages.saying: He named the place Massah and Meribah
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse and the story of Exodus 17:1-6.
layers.text: Moses named the place where God gave water from the rock after the people's sin there. They had quarreled with Moses and tested the LORD by doubting whether He was with them at all.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Matthew Henry, Wesley and the Companion Bible all explain Massah as temptation or testing and Meribah as strife or contention, matching the two reasons the verse gives.
layers.text: Each name matches one of the two reasons in the verse. Massah means testing, because the people tested (nasah) the LORD. Meribah means quarreling, because they quarreled (riv) with Moses. The place kept the memory of their sin.

passages.saying: Moses built an altar and named it The LORD Is My Banner
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse after the victory over Amalek in Exodus 17:8-13.
layers.text: After Israel defeated Amalek, Moses built an altar to thank God for the victory and gave it a name that gave the credit to the LORD.

layers.evidence: Clarke, Gill, Barnes, Wesley, Keil and Delitzsch and the Companion Bible all give the name as Jehovah my banner. Gill, Clarke and Matthew Henry link the banner to Moses' hands and rod held up during the battle.
layers.text: The altar's name, YHWH Nissi, means the LORD is my banner. A nes was a pole or flag raised high for soldiers to rally around. Moses had held up his hands with God's staff through the battle like a raised banner, and the name says the LORD Himself is Israel's banner who gave the victory.

passages.saying: The other son was named Eliezer
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse and Moses' escape from Pharaoh in Exodus 2:15.
layers.text: Moses' second son was named to remember how God had rescued Moses when Pharaoh sought to kill him. The name was a lasting thank you for God's help.

layers.evidence: Gill and Wesley both explain Eliezer as my God is help and connect it to Moses' rescue from Pharaoh, as the verse itself does.
layers.text: Eliezer means my God is help. Eli means my God, and ezer means help. Moses explains the name with the same word: the God of his father was his helper (ezer) and saved him from the sword of Pharaoh.

passages.saying: Therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and set it apart as holy
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the fourth commandment, Exodus 20:8-11.
layers.text: This verse gives the reason for the Sabbath command. The LORD made the heavens, the earth, the sea and everything in them in six days and rested on the seventh, so He blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy.

layers.evidence: Gill says the command draws on what was recorded in the creation account. Keil and Delitzsch and Wesley both point to Genesis 2:3, where God rested on the seventh day and blessed and sanctified it. Both verses use the words for seventh, blessed and made holy.
layers.text: The reason given for the Sabbath points back to the first week. In Genesis 2:3 God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it He rested from His work. Exodus names the same rest, blessing and holiness, so the Sabbath Israel kept was rooted in the day God set apart at creation.

passages.saying: place the Bread of the Presence on the table before Me
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse with Leviticus 24:5-9, which describes the loaves.
layers.text: God told Moses to keep special bread on the golden table in the tabernacle at all times. The loaves were set before the LORD and replaced with fresh ones each Sabbath, so the table was never empty.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible and Bullinger's Figures of Speech name the play panim lephanai a paronomasia. Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch say the bread was called bread of the face because it lay before God's face, and Gill says the same.
layers.text: In Hebrew the bread is lechem panim, literally bread of the face, and it is to lie lephanai, before My face. The same word for face is used twice, so the bread's name tells where it belonged: always in the LORD's presence.

passages.saying: See to it that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG (Abbott-Smith), Strong's, the Septuagint, the Mishnah, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.
