layers.evidence: The Companion Bible, on the words I will be, gives the Hebrew 'ehyeh and says to compare Exodus 3:14, where the same word is part of God's title Jehovah.
layers.text: In Hebrew, so will I be with you uses ehyeh, I will be, the same word God used at the burning bush when He told Moses His name, I AM WHO I AM (Exodus 3:14). Some hear in it the God who made Himself known to Moses there now promising the same presence to Joshua.

passages.saying: the fear of you has fallen on us
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown note the panic of the Canaanites alongside Rahab's firm conviction.
layers.text: Rahab tells the two spies she knows the LORD has given Israel the land. She also knows that terror of Israel has fallen on her people and that everyone in the land is losing heart.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the wording of Rahab's report is tied to Exodus 15:15-16 to show that the song at the Red Sea was now fulfilled; Gill says the inhabitants melt as Moses had predicted in Exodus 15:15. Both passages use emah (dread), nafal (fall) and mug (melt).
layers.text: Rahab's words echo the song Moses and Israel sang after crossing the Red Sea, which said the people of Canaan would melt away and dread would fall on them (Exodus 15:15-16). Rahab uses the same Hebrew words, emah (dread) and namogu (melted), so what Israel sang has come true.

passages.saying: you have tied this scarlet cord in the window through which you let us down
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, Strong's, 1 Clement, Justin Martyr, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Rahab, a prostitute in Jericho, hides Joshua's two spies and asks them to spare her family. They tell her to tie a scarlet cord in her window and gather everyone inside, and when the city falls, Joshua spares her household.

layers.evidence: TAHOT tags 2:18 and 2:21 as tiqvah, cord, and 31 other verses, Hosea 2:15 among them, as hope; the rope in 2:15 is chevel. Strong's counts one word, TBESH two. Ellicott: the cord and the rope are different words. Bullinger (Companion Bible) on 2:18: Hebrew hope, put by metonymy for the line that was its token. 1 Clement 12: redemption for all who believe and hope in God.

cites.at: Clement of Rome, First Epistle to the Corinthians 12

layers.text: The cord in the window is not chevel, like her rope, but tiqvah, which means "cord" only here and in 2:21. Over 30 other times it means "hope" ("a gateway of hope"). An early church letter saw in this cord redemption for all who hope in God. Dictionaries differ on whether it is one word or two.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: both verses end in the heavens above and on the earth below with the same words (mimmaal, mitachat); the openings differ. Barnes and Keil and Delitzsch on Joshua 2:11 cite Deuteronomy 4:39
layers.text: Rahab confesses that "the LORD your God is God in the heavens above and on the earth below," the confession Moses told Israel to take to heart (Deuteronomy 4:39). In Hebrew the closing phrase is identical. A Canaanite outsider confesses Israel's own creed.

layers.evidence: Matthew Henry, Gill and Barnes on Joshua 2:18 compare the scarlet cord with the Passover blood
layers.text: The terms echo the first Passover. Egypt: "None of you shall go out the door of his house until morning." Jericho: "If anyone goes out the door of your house," his blood is on his own head. A sign on the house, the family inside, and judgment passes over.

layers.evidence: 1 Clement 12 (Lightfoot translation); Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 111. Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary trace the reading through the early church fathers

cites.at: Clement of Rome, First Epistle to the Corinthians 12
Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 111

layers.text: Early Christian writers saw Christ's blood in the scarlet cord: it showed that redemption would come through the Lord's blood to all who believe and hope in God. The New Testament does not draw this link.

layers.evidence: Pulpit on Matthew 1:5: generally taken as Rahab of Jericho, though the Old Testament says nothing of the marriage; Bengel agrees, and Ellicott notes the silence. Gill: a Gentile in Christ's line. TBESG marks the identification as uncertain
layers.text: Hebrews counts "the prostitute Rahab" among the faithful, and James says she was "justified by her actions." Matthew names a Rahab as Boaz's mother, a Gentile in Jesus' line; most take her to be this one, though the Old Testament records no such marriage.

passages.saying: It backed up as far upstream as Adam
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The commentaries read the verse as a plain report of the miracle at the Jordan.
layers.text: The water flowing down the Jordan stopped and backed up far upstream near the town of Adam, while the water below was cut off toward the Dead Sea. So the people crossed over opposite Jericho, on a riverbed God had emptied.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown explains the heap here by pointing to Exodus 15:8 and Psalm 78:13. Bullinger's Companion Bible sets the way cut through the sea (Exodus 14) beside the way through the river (Joshua 3). Joshua 4:23 itself compares the two crossings.
layers.text: In Hebrew the Jordan's waters rose up in one heap (ned). The same word is used for the Red Sea waters in the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15:8, translated wall there). The river crossing echoes the sea crossing, as Joshua 4:23 says outright.

passages.saying: What do these stones mean to you?
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The commentaries agree the twelve stones were a lasting memorial of the crossing.
layers.text: The twelve stones taken from the riverbed were to stand as a sign. When children in later years asked what the stones meant, their parents would tell how the LORD stopped the Jordan so Israel could cross.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on this passage, send the reader to Exodus 13:14, Exodus 12:26-27 and Deuteronomy 6:20-21 for the wording of the children's question. The Hebrew shares the verb ask and the word machar, in the future, with Exodus 13:14.
layers.text: Some note that the children's question is worded like those children were to ask about the Passover (Exodus 12:26) and the redeeming of the firstborn (Exodus 13:14). As those customs taught each new generation about leaving Egypt, these stones would teach them about crossing the Jordan.

passages.saying: circumcised the sons of Israel at Gibeath-haaraloth
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The commentaries take the verse as Joshua ordering the circumcision of the generation born in the wilderness.
layers.text: Joshua had flint knives made and had the men of Israel circumcised, renewing the covenant sign that the generation born in the wilderness had not received.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, Gill and Barnes all explain the name as the hill where the foreskins from this circumcision were left, and Keil and Delitzsch and Barnes say they were buried there. Keil and Delitzsch and Gill add that the place was called this afterward because of what happened there.
layers.text: Gibeath-haaraloth means hill of the foreskins, from givah (hill) and orlah (foreskin). The place was named for what was done there, since the foreskins cut off in this mass circumcision were left at that spot, most likely buried there.

passages.saying: Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The commentaries link the removal of the reproach to the circumcision just carried out.
layers.text: Once the people were circumcised, the LORD told Joshua that He had taken away the disgrace Israel had carried from Egypt. The place where this happened was named Gilgal from then on.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Wesley and Bullinger's Companion Bible all explain Gilgal as rolling, named from God's word gallothi, I have rolled away, in this verse.
layers.text: God says, I have rolled away (gallothi, from galal, to roll), and so the place is called Gilgal, which means rolling. The name kept alive the memory of the day God rolled away Israel's disgrace.

passages.saying: Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The commentaries explain that the ground was holy because of the presence of the Commander who appeared to Joshua.
layers.text: The Commander of the LORD's army told Joshua to take off his sandals, because the ground was made holy by His presence. Joshua did as he was told.

layers.evidence: Clarke, Wesley, Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown all tie this command to God's words to Moses at the bush in Exodus 3:5. The Hebrew of the two commands is nearly word for word the same.
layers.text: These are nearly the same words God spoke to Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:5). Moses heard them before leading Israel out of Egypt, and Joshua hears them before leading the fight for Jericho and the land, a sign that God would be with Joshua as He was with Moses.

passages.saying: Achan son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The commentaries note that one man sinned but the guilt was counted against the whole nation.
layers.text: Achan of the tribe of Judah secretly took some of the things from Jericho that had been devoted to the LORD. Because Israel was one people under the covenant, his sin was counted against the whole nation, and the LORD's anger burned against Israel.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown note that 1 Chronicles 2:7 calls Achan Achar, trouble. Keil and Delitzsch and Barnes say the n became r so the name would play on akar, the verb Joshua uses in Joshua 7:25.
layers.text: In 1 Chronicles 2:7 Achan's name is spelled Achar, with r in place of n, so that it matches akar, to trouble. That verse calls him the one who brought trouble upon Israel, using the same verb Joshua spoke against him in Joshua 7:25.

passages.saying: Why have you brought this trouble upon us?
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The commentaries read Joshua's words as a sentence showing that Achan's punishment came from God.
layers.text: Joshua tells Achan that because he brought trouble on Israel, the LORD will bring trouble on him that day. Then all Israel stoned him to death, and they stoned the others and burned their bodies.

layers.evidence: Clarke says Joshua's question refers to the meaning of Achan's or Achar's name. Keil and Delitzsch point out that Joshua uses akar both for Achan's sin and for his punishment, and that the valley's name refers back to this.
layers.text: Joshua uses one verb twice, akar, to trouble: Achan troubled Israel, so the LORD will trouble Achan. The word echoes Achan's own name, which 1 Chronicles 2:7 spells Achar, and it gives the Valley of Achor its name in the next verse.

passages.saying: that place is called the Valley of Achor to this day
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The commentaries explain the pile of stones as a lasting warning.
layers.text: Israel heaped a great pile of rocks over Achan, still standing when the book was written, as a warning to others. With the sin dealt with, the LORD turned from His burning anger, and the place was named the Valley of Achor.

layers.evidence: Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Wesley and Keil and Delitzsch all give Achor as trouble and tie the name to the trouble of verse 25. Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown note that Isaiah and Hosea name the valley again (Isaiah 65:10; Hosea 2:15).
layers.text: Achor means trouble. The valley was named for the trouble Achan brought on Israel and the trouble the LORD brought on him (verse 25). Later prophets name this valley again in promises of blessing (Isaiah 65:10; Hosea 2:15).

passages.saying: Joshua did not draw back the hand that held his battle lance
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself and the LORD's command in verse 18.
layers.text: At the LORD's command in verse 18, Joshua had held out his battle lance toward Ai. He did not lower it until everyone in the city had been devoted to destruction.

layers.evidence: Gill says Joshua kept his hand out just as the hand of Moses was held up until Amalek was beaten by Joshua (Exodus 17:12). Jamieson-Fausset-Brown suggests Joshua kept up the same devout spirit Moses showed in lifting up his hands. Clarke mentions the comparison but doubts any figurative meaning here.
layers.text: This recalls the battle with Amalek in Exodus 17. There Moses kept his hands raised until sunset while Joshua fought below, and Israel prevailed. Now Joshua himself keeps his hand stretched out until the victory is complete.

passages.saying: Hebron used to be called Kiriath-arba, after Arba
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its repeat of Joshua 11:23.
layers.text: Hebron was once called Kiriath-arba, after Arba, the greatest man among the Anakim. With the great battles over, the land had rest from war while it was divided among the tribes.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Bullinger's Companion Bible notes give Kiriath-arba as city of Arba, and Keil and Delitzsch say the name was given when Arba took the town. Clarke adds that the words can also be read city of the four, though he grants from Joshua 15:13 that Arba was a man's name.
layers.text: Kiriath-arba means city of Arba. The verse explains the name: the town was called after Arba, the greatest man among the Anakim, a people known for their size and strength. The word arba is also the Hebrew number four, but the verse ties the name to a man.

passages.saying: So the Reubenites and Gadites named the altar Witness
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the tribes' explanation in verses 26 to 29.
layers.text: The tribes east of the Jordan named the altar they had built after its purpose. It was not for sacrifices but stood as a witness that the LORD is God of all Israel, on both sides of the river.

layers.evidence: Gill, Wesley and Matthew Henry say Ed signifies a witness, and Keil and Delitzsch call the wording at once a name and an explanation. Clarke, Barnes and Bullinger note that most Hebrew copies lack ed right after altar; Clarke would supply it, while Barnes and Bullinger read the name from the words that follow.
layers.text: The altar was named Witness, in Hebrew ed. In the Hebrew the name and its reason run together: they named the altar, for "It is a witness between us that the LORD is God." It stood as proof that the eastern tribes shared Israel's faith.

passages.saying: a scourge in your sides and thorns in your eyes
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the condition set out in verse 12.
layers.text: Joshua warns that if Israel mixes with the nations left in the land, the LORD will stop driving them out. Those nations will trap Israel and torment it until Israel is lost from the good land God gave.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Joshua's threat is founded on Numbers 33:55 (with Exodus 23:33 and Deuteronomy 7:16), and Bullinger's notes on Numbers 33:55 compare Joshua 23:13. Gill sends readers to his note on Numbers 33:55 for the thorns, and Keil and Delitzsch, on Judges 2:3, treat the two verses as one threat.
layers.text: Joshua is repeating the warning God gave through Moses in Numbers 33:55, that those left in the land would become "barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides." He reuses its Hebrew words for thorns (tsanin) and sides (tsad), though here the thorns are in the eyes and a scourge is in the sides.

passages.saying: devoted the city to destruction. So it was called Hormah
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and Judah's promise to Simeon in verse 3.
layers.text: Judah kept its promise to help Simeon. Together they defeated the Canaanites of Zephath and destroyed the city completely, as something devoted to the LORD, and the city was renamed Hormah.

layers.evidence: Gill says what Israel vowed near Arad was now fulfilled; Barnes says the destruction then vowed was now accomplished; Keil and Delitzsch say the ban on the king of Arad's land (Numbers 21:2) was now carried out on Zephath, which was part of it. Clarke takes it as the same event as Numbers 21.
layers.text: This carries out the vow of Numbers 21:2, when Israel promised the LORD to devote to destruction the cities of the Canaanite king of Arad. Zephath lay in that king's land, and now Judah and Simeon fulfill the old vow there.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the town received the name Hormah, that is, banning, from the ban carried out on it. Gill says it was named from the destruction made of it, and Bullinger's Companion Bible notes gloss Hormah as utter destruction.
layers.text: The verb for devoting to destruction is charam, and the city's new name, Hormah, comes from the same root. It means something like banned or utter destruction, so the city's name kept the memory of what was done to it.

passages.saying: they will be thorns in your sides
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the charge in verse 2.
layers.text: Because Israel disobeyed God's command to make no covenant with the Canaanites and to tear down their altars, the LORD says He will no longer drive them out. They will trouble Israel, and their gods will lure Israel away.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the words point back to the threat of Numbers 33:55 and Joshua 23:13, that sides is short for thorns in your sides, and that the snare clause follows Exodus 23:33. Gill refers to Numbers 33:55, and Bullinger compares both verses, noting that some copies read adversaries.
layers.text: The angel repeats warnings Israel had already heard. The Hebrew says only that the Canaanites will be in your sides, short for the thorns in your sides of Numbers 33:55, a warning Joshua repeated in Joshua 23:13. Their gods becoming a snare echoes Exodus 23:33.

passages.saying: So they called that place Bochim
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the weeping in verse 4.
layers.text: After the people wept at the angel's rebuke, they named the place Bochim and offered sacrifices there to the LORD for the sins they had committed.

layers.evidence: Gill and Barnes give Bochim as weepers and Clarke as weepings or lamentations; Keil and Delitzsch say the place received its name from the weeping. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Bullinger's notes also give weepers.
layers.text: Bochim means weepers. The place was named for what happened there: when the angel of the LORD rebuked Israel, the people lifted up their voices and wept (bakah), and the name is built on that same verb.

passages.saying: Ehud son of Gera, a left-handed Benjamite
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the Moabite rule described in verses 12 to 14.
layers.text: When Israel cried out under Moabite rule, the LORD raised up Ehud, a left-handed man of Benjamin, to deliver them. Israel sent him to bring its tribute to Eglon, king of Moab.

layers.evidence: Gill notes that Benjamite signifies a son of the right hand, though Ehud was left-handed, and that the Hebrew says shut up in his right hand. Keil and Delitzsch explain the phrase as hindered in the use of his right hand and say it is mentioned so plainly because of what follows.
layers.text: Ehud is a Benjamite, ben-yemini, and Benjamin means son of the right hand. Some note the irony that the Hebrew calls him a man shut up in his right hand (yemino), that is, left-handed. The detail matters: his left hand will draw the sword hidden on his right thigh.

passages.saying: O LORD, when You went out from Seir
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The song addresses God directly and recalls His earlier appearings for Israel.
layers.text: Deborah's song turns to speak to the LORD and remembers a time He marched out from Seir and Edom for His people. The earth shook, and the sky and the clouds poured down water before Him.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call the allusion to Moses' blessing unmistakable and see the victory as a renewal of the LORD's coming at Sinai, and Clarke sees an allusion to the giving of the law. Gill and Barnes refer it instead to the LORD leading Israel past Edom toward Canaan.
layers.text: Deborah's words here echo Moses' blessing, "The LORD came from Sinai and dawned upon us from Seir," and the next verse names Sinai itself. She praises the new victory as the same God who shook Sinai coming again to help His people.

passages.saying: Surely I will be with you
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The promise answers Gideon's objection in the verse before.
layers.text: Gideon has just said his clan is the weakest and he is the youngest. The LORD answers that He will be with Gideon, and Gideon will strike down the whole Midianite army as easily as one man.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call the scene suggestive of the call of Moses and point to Exodus 3:12 for this promise, as the Companion Bible also does. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown note that Gideon resembles Moses in his excuse and in asking for a sign. The Hebrew in both verses is ki ehyeh immakh.
layers.text: When Gideon objects that he is too small for the task, the LORD gives him the promise He gave Moses at the burning bush, "I will surely be with you," in the same Hebrew words. Like Moses, Gideon then asks for a sign.

passages.saying: called it The LORD Is Peace
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse records the altar, its name, and that it remained in Ophrah.
layers.text: Gideon built an altar to the LORD on the spot where the LORD had appeared to him, and gave it a name. The altar was still standing in Ophrah when the book was written.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke and Barnes all say the name repeats the word of peace (shalom) the LORD spoke to Gideon in verse 23.
layers.text: The altar's name, Yahweh shalom, means The LORD Is Peace. Gideon took it from what the LORD said when he feared he would die for having seen Him: "Peace be with you. Do not be afraid, for you will not die."

passages.saying: So on that day Gideon was called Jerubbaal
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The name grows out of Joash's challenge in the verse before.
layers.text: After Gideon tore down Baal's altar, the townsmen wanted him dead. His father told them to let Baal defend himself, and from that day Gideon was given a new name.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch all give the meaning let Baal contend, from the verb riv used in verses 31 and 32. Keil and Delitzsch add that it soon became an honorable title when Baal could do him no harm.
layers.text: Jerubbaal means Let Baal contend. His father had said, "If Baal is a god, let him contend for himself." Baal never did anything to Gideon, so the name became a badge of honor: the man who fought Baal and lived.

passages.saying: camped beside the spring of Harod
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse gives the setting for the battle that follows.
layers.text: After the signs of the fleece, Gideon rose early and camped with his army by the spring of Harod, with the Midianite camp to the north in the valley.

layers.evidence: Gill, Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say Harod means trembling and tie it to the fearful men sent home in verse 3. Clarke gives the same meaning but links it to the Midianites' panic; Keil and Delitzsch think the spring was named after a town.
layers.text: Harod means trembling. At this spring the LORD had Gideon send home everyone who was "fearful and trembling," and the word for trembling, chared, comes from the same root. Fittingly, 22,000 men turned back there.

passages.saying: they killed Oreb at the rock of Oreb and Zeeb at the winepress of Zeeb
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse closes the pursuit of Midian after Gideon's night attack.
layers.text: The men of Ephraim captured the two Midianite princes, Oreb and Zeeb, killed them, and brought their heads to Gideon across the Jordan.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, Barnes and Gill all say Isaiah 10:26 recalls this victory over Midian, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible cross-reference this verse there.
layers.text: Centuries later Isaiah pointed back to this day. He promised that the LORD would strike Assyria "as when He struck Midian at the rock of Oreb," a sudden and complete rescue like Gideon's.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch give the meanings raven and wolf. Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch say the rock and the winepress were named after the princes killed there, and Gill suggests the rock took its name from Oreb's death.
layers.text: Oreb means raven and Zeeb means wolf, fierce names for two raiding princes. Each was killed at a spot that took his name from that day, the rock of Oreb and the winepress of Zeeb.

passages.saying: He had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse marks Jair's wealth and standing in a quiet period.
layers.text: Jair the judge had thirty sons, each riding his own donkey, a mark of rank in that day, and each with a town of his own in Gilead. Those towns were still called by Jair's name when the book was written.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the unusual form for towns was chosen because it sounds like the word for donkeys just before it.
layers.text: Some see a play on sound here. Jair's thirty sons rode on thirty donkeys (ayarim) and had thirty towns, also written ayarim. The usual word for towns is arim, but here it may take a form chosen to match the word for donkeys.

layers.evidence: Gill and Clarke both explain Havvoth-jair as the villages of Jair.
layers.text: Havvoth-jair means the villages of Jair. The verse says the towns were still known by that name when it was written.

passages.saying: Please say Shibboleth
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the account of the fighting at the Jordan fords in Judges 12:4-6.
layers.text: The men of Gilead held the fords of the Jordan. Each man trying to cross was told to say Shibboleth. Ephraimites could not make the sh sound and said Sibboleth, so they were caught and killed. In all 42,000 Ephraimites fell at that time.

layers.evidence: Gill says shibboleth signifies a stream, at which they then were; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the word was naturally suggested by the place. Clarke notes it can also mean an ear of grain and that the two forms differ only in their first letter.
layers.text: The test word was well chosen. Shibboleth can mean a flowing stream (it can also mean an ear of grain), so at the river crossing each man was in effect asked to name the stream he hoped to cross. One sound, s for sh, gave an Ephraimite away.

passages.saying: Why do you ask my name
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the angel's answer to Manoah's request in verse 17.
layers.text: Manoah asked the angel of the LORD his name, so that they could honor him when his promise came true. The angel would not give it. He said his name was beyond comprehension, too high for people to grasp.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Genesis 32, set Jacob's unanswered question beside the angel's reply to Manoah's similar question. Clarke notes that some Septuagint copies add which is wonderful at Genesis 32:29, apparently taken from Judges 13:18.
layers.text: The angel's reply "Why do you ask my name" is word for word, in Hebrew too, what Jacob heard when he asked the name of the One who wrestled with him (Genesis 32:29). Some see in both scenes God Himself appearing in human form and keeping His name hidden.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say peli is not a proper name but describes his nature, a predicate belonging to God alone, and compare Isaiah 9:6. Clarke and the Companion Bible tie it to Isaiah's Wonderful, and Gill calls it one of the names of Christ.
layers.text: The word behind "beyond comprehension" is peli, wonderful. It is not a proper name but describes his nature, which only God has. Isaiah uses a word from the same root for the promised Child, Wonderful Counselor (Isaiah 9:6), and many see the Son of God here.

passages.saying: the LORD did a marvelous thing
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Verse 20 explains the wonder: the flame rose from the altar and the angel went up in it.
layers.text: Manoah offered a young goat and a grain offering to the LORD on a rock. As he and his wife watched, the LORD did a marvelous thing. Verse 20 tells what it was: the flame went up from the altar, and the angel of the LORD went up in it.

layers.evidence: Gill says the angel did wondrously, agreeably to his name Wonderful; Clarke says he acted according to his name; Matthew Henry says the Lord's name is wonderful and by his wonderful works he makes himself known. Barnes, on verse 18, also links the name with the deed.
layers.text: The angel had just said his name was peli, wonderful. Now the LORD does a wonder (mafli, from the same Hebrew root): the flame rises from the altar and the angel goes up in it. The deed matches the name.

passages.saying: With the jawbone of a donkey I have piled them into heaps
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Samson's short victory song after the battle at Lehi in verse 15.
layers.text: After striking down a thousand Philistines with the jawbone of a donkey, Samson sang a short song of victory. So poor a weapon shows that the strength came from God, not from Samson.

layers.evidence: Barnes calls it a play upon the word, three times repeated, meaning both ass and heap; Gill calls it an elegant play on words; Keil and Delitzsch say the form for heap was chosen for its likeness to chamor; Bullinger's Figures of Speech and Companion Bible class it as Antanaclasis.

cites.at: E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech Used in the Bible (1898), Ploce (Word-Folding)

layers.text: Samson's song is a pun. In Hebrew chamor means donkey, and a word with the same sound means heap. So he says, in effect, with a donkey's jawbone I made donkey-heaps of them, a heap, two heaps. The pun also treats the Philistines as no better than donkeys.

passages.saying: he named that place Ramath-lehi
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the close of the account of the battle at Lehi.
layers.text: When Samson finished his song, he threw the jawbone from his hand and named the place Ramath-lehi after what had happened there.

layers.evidence: Barnes notes the margin reading, the casting away of the jaw-bone, with allusion to Samson casting it out of his hand; Clarke gives the lifting up or casting away of the jaw-bone. The verb ramah, to throw, is the one used in Exodus 15:1.
layers.text: Some also hear a second sense in Ramath. The Hebrew verb ramah means to throw (as in Exodus 15:1), so the name can sound like the throwing of the jawbone, which fits Samson tossing it from his hand as he named the place.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch render the name the jaw-bone height; Barnes gives the height or hill of Lehi, or of the jaw-bone; Clarke gives the lifting up of the jaw-bone. Lehi is the same word as the jawbone Samson has just thrown away.
layers.text: Lehi means jawbone, and Ramath means a height. So Ramath-lehi is the hill of the jawbone, a name that kept alive the memory of Samson's victory with a donkey's jawbone.

passages.saying: That is why he named it En-hakkore
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse tells how God answered Samson's prayer of verse 18 with water from a split hollow.
layers.text: Samson, close to dying of thirst after his victory, had cried out to the LORD. God split open a hollow at Lehi and water poured out. Samson drank, his strength returned, and he named the spring En-hakkore. The spring was still there when the book was written.

layers.evidence: Gill renders the name the fountain of him that was calling, Keil and Delitzsch the crier's well, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown the supplication well, Clarke the well of the implorer, and Bullinger's Companion Bible the Caller's Fount. All tie it to Samson's cry in verse 18.
layers.text: En-hakkore means the spring of the one who called. In verse 18 Samson called out (qara) to the LORD, and the name is built from that same Hebrew verb. Each time people spoke the spring's name, they recalled a prayer that God had answered.

layers.evidence: Barnes says the word means a mortar (Proverbs 27:22) and was the name of a mortar-shaped basin among the cliffs of Lehi. Matthew Henry notes the place was called Lehi from the jawbone.
layers.text: The hollow God split open is called in Hebrew the maktesh, the word for a mortar, a bowl in which grain was pounded. It seems to have been the name of a mortar-shaped basin in the rocks at Lehi, a place name that means jawbone.

passages.saying: suddenly the wicked men of the city surrounded the house
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse describes the mob at the door of the old man who had taken in the Levite.
layers.text: While the Levite and his host were enjoying their evening, wicked men of Gibeah surrounded the old man's house. Pounding on the door, they demanded that he bring out his guest so they could abuse him.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call it the very same demand the Sodomites made of Lot and say the old man acted as Lot had done; Gill notes the men of Sodom used the same word, know; Clarke points to Genesis 19:5; Bullinger's Companion Bible notes, Like Sodom.
layers.text: The scene closely mirrors Sodom in Genesis 19. There too the men of the city surrounded the house and demanded that the guests be brought out so they could have relations with them, and in the next verses the old man, like Lot, offers his own daughter. A town in Israel has become like Sodom.

passages.saying: there was a famine in the land
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse sets the time and the trouble that open the book of Ruth.
layers.text: In the days of the judges a famine struck the land of Israel. A man from Bethlehem in Judah left with his wife and two sons to live for a time in the country of Moab.

layers.evidence: Gill says Bethlehem had its name from the fruitfulness of the place and the plenty of bread in it, and yet the famine was here. In Hebrew bet means house and lechem means bread.
layers.text: Bethlehem means house of bread, a name that spoke of a fruitful place with plenty of food. Some see an irony as the book opens: famine strikes the house of bread, and a family leaves it to look for food in Moab.

passages.saying: Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Naomi left Bethlehem in a famine with her husband and two sons. About ten years later all three are dead, and she comes home with only her widowed daughter-in-law Ruth. When the women ask, "Can this be Naomi?" she answers out of grief.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: No'omi (H5281), Mara (H4755) and hemar, he has made bitter (H4843), all in 1:20. Naomi comes from a root meaning pleasant; TBESH gives my delight for Naomi and bitterness for Mara. The book lets her lament stand without rebuke.
layers.text: Naomi means "pleasant" or "my delight." Mara means "bitterness," and she explains it with the same root: the Almighty "has dealt quite bitterly with me." Her new name is a lament, and the Bible does not hide her complaint against God.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: reqam, empty (H7387), in Ruth 1:21 and 3:17, the only two places the word occurs in Ruth. John Currid (The Gospel Coalition) on 3:16-18: the same word Naomi used in 1:21; now she will no longer be empty

cites.at: John Currid, Ruth commentary, The Gospel Coalition

layers.text: "I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty," she says; empty is reqam. Later Ruth brings home barley and says Boaz told her, "Do not go back to your mother-in-law empty-handed." The same word, reqam. Her emptiness is starting to be filled.

cites.at: John Currid, Ruth commentary, The Gospel Coalition

layers.text: The story comes full circle. The women who asked, "Can this be Naomi?" now bless the LORD and say, "A son has been born to Naomi." No one ever calls her Mara; the book keeps calling her Naomi. Her grandson Obed will be King David's grandfather.

passages.saying: Spread the corner of your garment over me, for you are a kinsman-redeemer.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Ruth, a widow from Moab, asks Boaz to marry her and act as her family's kinsman-redeemer. He does, and their son Obed becomes King David's grandfather.

cites.at: Ligonier Ministries, A Risky Proposal (Tabletalk devotional)

layers.text: Boaz had prayed that Ruth be rewarded by the LORD, "under whose wings you have taken refuge." Now she asks him to spread his "wing" over her: kanaph means both wing and the corner of a garment. She asks Boaz to become the answer to his own prayer.

layers.evidence: Name meanings from TBESH
layers.text: Naomi means "my delight" and Mara "bitterness." Back in Bethlehem she tells the women, "Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me." The book ends with the LORD giving her a redeemer who "will renew your life."

cites.at: John Currid, Ruth commentary, The Gospel Coalition

layers.text: A kinsman-redeemer (go'el) was the near relative who bought back family land, and a related law had a man marry his dead brother's widow so that "his name will not be blotted out." Boaz does both at once, though exactly how these laws applied is debated.

The prophets use the same words for God. He is Israel's Redeemer (go'el), and in Ezekiel He says, "I spread My cloak over you," with the word kanaph, and "you became Mine." Ruth's request speaks the language of God's covenant love.

cites.at: Angie Velasquez Thornton, 3 Ways Ruth Foreshadows Christ, The Gospel Coalition Canada

layers.text: Matthew names Boaz and Ruth in Jesus' family line. Some Christians see Boaz the kinsman-redeemer as a picture of Christ the Redeemer, though the New Testament does not draw the Boaz link itself.

passages.saying: may your house become like the house of Perez
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse closes the blessing spoken over Boaz's marriage to Ruth in verses 11 and 12.
layers.text: The elders and people at the town gate bless Boaz. They pray that through the children the LORD will give him by Ruth, his family will become as great as the family of Perez, the son Tamar bore to Judah.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch tie the blessing to Genesis 38 and note that Boaz's ancestors came from Perez; Bullinger's Companion Bible points to Genesis 38:29. Gill and Wesley add that Tamar, like Ruth, was of another nation, yet Perez's family became one of the five families of Judah.
layers.text: The blessing looks back to Genesis 38, where Tamar bore Perez to Judah. Perez was Boaz's own forefather, and his family grew into a great clan of Judah. Tamar too is taken to have been a woman from outside Israel, like Ruth, whom God blessed with a lasting family.

passages.saying: no razor shall ever come over his head
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse records the vow Hannah made as she prayed at the house of the LORD in Shiloh.
layers.text: Grieving that she had no child, Hannah made a vow at Shiloh. If the LORD would look on her sorrow and give her a son, she would give him back to the LORD for his whole life, and no razor would ever touch his head.

layers.evidence: Gill (citing Numbers 6:5), Clarke, Keil and Delitzsch, Wesley and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown all read no razor as the mark of a Nazirite, and Gill, Clarke and Wesley stress that this was to be for life.
layers.text: Uncut hair was the sign of a Nazirite, a person set apart to the LORD under the vow described in Numbers 6. In the law that vow lasted for a set time, but Hannah gives her son to be a Nazirite for his whole life, as well as a servant at the LORD's house.

layers.evidence: Gill says the boy was to be a perpetual Nazarite, as Samson was, and Keil and Delitzsch point to Judges 13:5. The Hebrew of the razor clause (morah, razor) matches Judges 13:5 word for word, while Numbers 6:5 uses another word for razor.
layers.text: Hannah's promise repeats, word for word in Hebrew, what the angel said before Samson's birth: no razor shall come over his head. Like Samson, her son would be a Nazirite from birth to the end of his life.

passages.saying: Because I have asked for him from the LORD
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse records Samuel's birth as the answer to Hannah's prayer in verse 11.
layers.text: The LORD remembered Hannah. In due time she conceived and gave birth to a son, and she named him Samuel, because she had asked the LORD for him.

layers.evidence: Clarke reads the name as a contracted form of shaul me-El, asked of God, and Wesley glosses it Asked of God; Gill notes the reason given would better fit the name Saul (asked). Keil and Delitzsch and Barnes take Samuel as heard of God, with Hannah's words explaining why she chose it. All tie the name to her answered prayer.
layers.text: Hannah explains the name Samuel by her prayer: she asked (sha'al) the LORD for him. The name sounds like asked of God, though others take it more strictly to mean heard of God. Either way, the boy's name kept alive the memory of a prayer God had answered.

passages.saying: Though the boy was still young
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse describes Hannah keeping her vow once the boy was weaned.
layers.text: When Samuel was weaned, Hannah took him up to the house of the LORD at Shiloh, bringing a bull, flour and wine for the offerings, though he was still very young.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech sets out the Hebrew, the child was a child, used first of Samuel and then of a child of tender age; his Companion Bible marks it as a play on words. Keil and Delitzsch explain na'ar here as a tender boy.

cites.at: E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech Used in the Bible (1898), Ploce (Word-Folding)

layers.text: The Hebrew ends by repeating one word: and the boy (na'ar) was a boy (na'ar). Some see a play here: the first time the word names Samuel; the second says what he still was, a little child, stressing how young he was when Hannah brought him to the LORD's house.

passages.saying: I prayed for this boy
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Hannah speaks to Eli as she hands over the child in verses 26 to 28.
layers.text: Presenting the young Samuel to Eli at Shiloh, Hannah reminds him that she is the woman who once prayed there. This is the boy she prayed for, and the LORD has given her what she asked.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists verses 27 and 28 under Paronomasia, setting out she'elathi, sha'alti, hish'iltihu and sha'ul. Keil and Delitzsch render the end, I also make him one asked of the Lord, and explain the verb as making a person asked.

cites.at: E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech Used in the Bible (1898), Paronomasia (Rhyming-Words)

layers.text: Hannah's words keep returning to one Hebrew root, sha'al, to ask. The LORD granted her request (she'elah) that she asked (sha'alti). In verse 28, where English says dedicate, the same root comes back: she makes him asked of the LORD, and all his life he is sha'ul, asked for.

passages.saying: I now dedicate the boy to the LORD
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Hannah's own words as she presents Samuel at the tabernacle.
layers.text: Hannah gives the boy she prayed for back to the LORD. He will belong to the LORD and serve Him for his whole life, and they worship the LORD there.

layers.evidence: Clarke shows the same root sha'al in verse 27 (I asked) and verse 28 (he is asked, or lent, to the LORD), and Bullinger's Companion Bible calls verses 27 and 28 a paronomasia, a play on that root. Keil and Delitzsch explain that the verb in verse 28 means to make the boy one asked (sha'ul) of the LORD.
layers.text: Hannah plays on the Hebrew verb sha'al, to ask. She asked the LORD for this boy, and He gave her what she asked. Now, with the same verb, she gives him back as one asked for the LORD (sha'ul), His for as long as he lives.

passages.saying: The LORD brings death and gives life
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of Hannah's song of praise.
layers.text: Hannah praises the LORD as the one who holds life and death. He can bring a person down to the grave and raise them up again.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, on Hannah's song, point this line to Deuteronomy 32:39, and on Deuteronomy 32:39 they cite 1 Samuel 2:6 as the same thought. Gill also refers the reader to his note on Deuteronomy 32:39. Both verses use the Hebrew verbs for putting to death and making alive.
layers.text: Hannah's words match what God Himself says in the Song of Moses: I bring death and I give life. The same two Hebrew verbs stand in both places, and some read her song as taking up God's own claim that life and death are in His hand alone.

passages.saying: The LORD will judge the ends of the earth and will give power to His king. He will exalt the horn of His anointed.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TBESH, the Septuagint, the NET Bible notes, the Talmud, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Hannah, childless and taunted by her rival, prays for a son and then gives him to the LORD's service. Her song of thanks praises a God who reverses fortunes: "He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap."

layers.evidence: Judges 21:25. TAHOT: mashiach occurs earlier only in Leviticus 4:3, 4:5, 4:16 and 6:22, of the priest. Ellicott and JFB on 1 Samuel 2:10 call this the first passage to speak of His Anointed, the Messiah. Septuagint: the horn of his christos
layers.text: Israel had no king yet, but Hannah ends with "His king" and "His anointed." Mashiach, the word behind Messiah, had so far been used only of "the anointed priest"; this is its first use for a king. The Greek Old Testament has christos.

layers.evidence: NET Bible note on 1 Samuel 1:20: a sound-play, not a strict etymology. TAHOT: sha'al (H7592) in 1:20, 1:28, 8:10 and 12:17. Keil and Delitzsch on 1:20 and 1:28; Gill on 1:20 and Fix and Vannoy (The Gospel Coalition) on the link with Saul

cites.at: S. A. Fix and J. Robert Vannoy, 1 Samuel commentary, The Gospel Coalition

layers.text: Hannah explains Samuel's name with a sound-play: "Because I have asked for him from the LORD" (sha'al, to ask). In 1:28 she calls him sha'ul, "asked" (BSB "dedicated"), spelled like the name Saul. Later Israel is "asking him for a king," and gets Saul.

layers.evidence: Ellicott, JFB, Benson and Poole on Luke 1:46; Gill and the Pulpit Commentary on 1 Samuel 2:1
layers.text: Mary's song in Luke 1 is modeled on Hannah's. Hannah: "My heart rejoices in the LORD"; Mary: "my spirit rejoices in God my Savior!" Hannah's God "humbles and He exalts"; Mary's "has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble."

layers.evidence: Fix and Vannoy (The Gospel Coalition) note the frame. TAHOT: qeren, horn, in 1 Samuel 2:10 and 2 Samuel 22:3; mashiach in 2:10 and 22:51.

cites.at: S. A. Fix and J. Robert Vannoy, 1 Samuel commentary, The Gospel Coalition

layers.text: Hannah's song and David's song frame the books of Samuel. Both call God the Rock, sing of a "horn," and end with "His king" and "His anointed." Zechariah takes up the picture for Jesus: God "has raised up a horn of salvation for us" in David's house.

layers.evidence: Ellicott and Barnes on 1 Samuel 2:26 compare Luke 2:52
layers.text: Luke describes the boy Jesus in words close to those used of the boy Samuel. Samuel "continued to grow in stature and in favor with the LORD and with man"; Jesus "grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man."

layers.evidence: Talmud Megillah 14a, paraphrased. Keil and Delitzsch on 1 Samuel 2:10: David's line culminated in the Messiah; Pulpit: looking onwards to the Messiah, David's greater Son. TAHOT: qeren in 16:13 and 2:10; pakh, flask, in 10:1
layers.text: Hannah's son anointed Saul from "a flask of oil" but David with "the horn of oil," and Jewish tradition reads her "horn" as a prophecy of David's lasting line. Commentators see that line reaching forward to the Messiah.

passages.saying: sleeping with the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the report old Eli heard about his sons.
layers.text: Eli is very old. He hears of all the wrong his sons are doing to Israel, including that they are sleeping with the women who serve at the entrance of the tabernacle.

layers.evidence: Clarke says the Hebrew here is similar to Exodus 38:8 and, on that verse, that the women in both places were the women who guarded the tabernacle. Gill on Exodus 38:8 calls 1 Samuel 2:22 a parallel passage. Keil and Delitzsch point to Exodus 38:8 and say the sons profaned the sanctuary. Both verses use the same verb, tsava, for the women's serving.
layers.text: These women are described in almost the same words as Exodus 38:8, the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, whose mirrors were made into the bronze basin. They served at God's sanctuary, so Eli's sons were defiling God's house itself.

passages.saying: Why then do you kick at My sacrifice and offering
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the prophet's rebuke of Eli and his sons.
layers.text: Through a prophet, God rebukes Eli. His sons treat God's sacrifices with contempt, and Eli honors them more than God by letting the family grow fat on the best of Israel's offerings.

layers.evidence: Gill on Deuteronomy 32:15 explains Israel's kicking as disobedience to God's laws and refers to 1 Samuel 2:29 for the same kicking. On 1 Samuel 2:29 he calls it a metaphor from well-fed, fat cattle that kick at their own owners. The Hebrew verb ba'at (kick) is the same in both verses.
layers.text: The Hebrew verb for kick (ba'at) is found in only one other place in the Old Testament, the Song of Moses, where Jeshurun grew fat and kicked. Eli's house does the same: well fed on God's offerings, it kicks at them like a pampered animal that turns on the owner who feeds it.

passages.saying: The glory has departed from Israel
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Israel took the ark of the covenant, the sacred chest that stood for God's presence, into battle to "save us from the hand of our enemies." They lost, the ark was captured and the priest Eli's sons died. Dying in childbirth, his daughter-in-law named her son.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: I-khavod (H0350) and kavod, glory (H3519), in 4:21; galah, go into exile (H1540), in 4:21 and 4:22. TBESH: no glory. The first part, i, can mean not or where?, so both senses are proposed.

cites.at: S. A. Fix and J. Robert Vannoy, 1 Samuel commentary, The Gospel Coalition

layers.text: Ichabod, i-khavod, means "no glory" or, as many read it, "where's the glory?" Her words explain it: "The glory has departed from Israel." Departed is galah, the verb for going into exile. The glory has been carried off like a captive.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: kaved, heavy (H3515), in 4:18; kavad, honor (H3513), in 2:29-30; kavod, glory (H3519), in 4:21-22. All share the root k-b-d, which has to do with weight. The warning in 2:27-30 comes through a man of God. Fix and Vannoy (The Gospel Coalition) trace this thread from 2:30 through chapters 4 to 6.

cites.at: S. A. Fix and J. Robert Vannoy, 1 Samuel commentary, The Gospel Coalition
S. A. Fix and J. Robert Vannoy, 1 Samuel commentary, The Gospel Coalition

layers.text: Glory, kavod, comes from a root meaning heavy. Eli died because he was "old and heavy" (kaved). Through a prophet God had warned him, "You have honored your sons more than Me," and "I will honor those who honor Me." Honor, too, comes from the "heavy" root.

layers.evidence: Psalm 78:60 names Shiloh, where the ark had stood (1 Samuel 4:3-4), and the next verse is widely read as the ark's capture: God's strength and splendor given into captivity.
layers.text: A psalm looks back on this day: God "abandoned the tabernacle of Shiloh" and "delivered His strength to captivity, and His splendor to the hand of the adversary." The same psalm ends with God choosing David to shepherd His people.

passages.saying: Thus far the LORD has helped us
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Samuel's act after the victory over the Philistines.
layers.text: After the LORD routed the Philistines, Samuel set up a stone as a memorial. He gave it a name that confessed the LORD had helped Israel up to that day.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Keil and Delitzsch, and Wesley all give the meaning stone of help. Keil and Delitzsch add that the stone was a standing memorial that the Lord had thus far helped His people, joining the name to Samuel's words.
layers.text: Ebenezer means stone of help, from even (stone) and ezer (help). Samuel explains the name with a verb from the same root, azar, to help: Thus far the LORD has helped us. The stone was a lasting reminder of God's help.

passages.saying: Now appoint a king to judge us like all the other nations
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the elders' request to the aging Samuel.
layers.text: Because Samuel is old and his sons are dishonest, Israel's elders ask him to give them a king to rule them, as the nations around them have.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the request resembles the law of the king in Deuteronomy 17:14 so closely, down to the phrase like all the nations, that the allusion is unmistakable. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, on Deuteronomy 17:14, say Moses there foretold the change that came in 1 Samuel 8.
layers.text: The elders' request echoes Moses' words in Deuteronomy, where he foresaw Israel saying, Let us set a king over us like all the nations around us. What Moses foretold now happens, in nearly the same words.

passages.saying: He took a pair of oxen, cut them into pieces
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse, which describes a solemn summons to war.
layers.text: Saul cut a pair of oxen into pieces and sent them through Israel as a call to arms: anyone who did not march behind Saul and Samuel would have his oxen cut up the same way. The terror of the LORD fell on the people, and they turned out together.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Keil and Delitzsch all point to Judges 19:29; Barnes says Saul probably acted in imitation of it. Both verses use natach (cut in pieces) and the same Hebrew phrase for all the territory of Israel.
layers.text: Saul's summons echoes the Levite in the days of the judges, who cut up his concubine and sent the pieces throughout the territory of Israel to rouse the tribes. Both verses use the same Hebrew verb for cutting in pieces (natach). This time the sign gathers Israel to rescue Jabesh-gilead.

passages.saying: I witnessed what the Amalekites did to the Israelites
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own wording and the command that follows it in 15:3.
layers.text: Through Samuel, the LORD of Hosts tells Saul that He has taken note of how the Amalekites ambushed Israel on the way up from Egypt. This is the ground for the command in the next verse to destroy Amalek.

layers.evidence: Clarke, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Keil and Delitzsch and the Companion Bible point to Exodus 17:8; Clarke, Wesley and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also cite Deuteronomy 25:18, and Matthew Henry's Concise cites Exodus 17:14 and Deuteronomy 25:19. Clarke notes the sentence was carried out over four hundred years later.
layers.text: God's words look back to the Amalekite attack at Rephidim soon after Israel left Egypt, to Moses' charge to remember how they fell on Israel's weary stragglers, and to God's vow to blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven. Saul is now sent to carry out that old sentence.

passages.saying: Saul grabbed the hem of his robe, and it tore
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse; the robe that tore was Samuel's, seized by Saul.
layers.text: As Samuel turned to leave, Saul grabbed the edge of the prophet's robe to hold him back, and the robe ripped.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch tie the verb for the robe tearing in 15:27 to Samuel's explanation in 15:28 and call the tearing a sign of the kingdom being torn away. Gill says Samuel, seeing his mantle rent, foretold that the kingdom would be rent from Saul in like manner.
layers.text: The robe tore (qara), and Samuel took up the same Hebrew verb at once: "The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today." The accidental rip in Samuel's robe became a picture of the kingdom being torn away from Saul.

passages.saying: the Glory of Israel does not lie or change His mind
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's contrast between God and man.
layers.text: Samuel tells Saul that God's sentence will stand. God, the Glory of Israel, does not lie and does not change His mind the way a human being does.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say Samuel refused Saul's request in these words of Balaam; Gill says the sense of the verse agrees with and is confirmed by Numbers 23:19. Both verses use nacham for changing one's mind.
layers.text: Samuel's answer echoes Balaam's words in the wilderness: "God is not a man, that He should lie, or a son of man, that He should change His mind." God held to His word of blessing then, and He holds just as firmly to His word of judgment on Saul now.

passages.saying: man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own contrast between outward appearance and the heart.
layers.text: When Samuel was impressed by Jesse's eldest son Eliab, the LORD told him not to judge by looks or height. People see what is on the outside, but God sees the heart.

layers.evidence: Gill says Eliab's stature was like Saul's; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Samuel fell into the same error as before (10:24); Matthew Henry's Concise notes that Saul's countenance and stature had recommended him. The word for height (gavoah) also describes Saul in 9:2.
layers.text: God's warning about height looks back to Saul, Israel's first king, who impressed everyone because he stood a head taller than any of the others. Samuel was about to judge Eliab the same way, but this time God was choosing a king by the heart.

passages.saying: That is why that place is called Sela-hammahlekoth
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the report of the Philistine raid in 23:27.
layers.text: Saul had nearly trapped David when news of a Philistine raid forced him to break off the chase and turn back. The place where this happened was given a name to remember it.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Wesley and the Companion Bible all render the name rock (or cliff) of divisions; Gill and Wesley explain it as the place where Saul was separated from David. Keil and Delitzsch prefer the reading rock of slipping away.
layers.text: Sela-hammahlekoth means rock of divisions, or rock of separation. It was named for the spot where Saul was pulled away from David just as David was nearly in his grasp.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch derive the name from chalaq in the sense of smooth and judge this better supported than rock of divisions.
layers.text: Others read the name as rock of slipping away, from a Hebrew word meaning smooth. On this reading it is the place where David slipped out of Saul's hands and escaped.

passages.saying: His name means Fool, and folly accompanies him.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: David's men had guarded the flocks of Nabal, a rich man "harsh and evil in his dealings." When David asked for food, Nabal insulted him, and David set out with 400 men to kill every male in Nabal's household. Nabal's wife Abigail rode out to stop him.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: Naval (H5037) and nevalah, folly (H5039), in 25:25; naval, fool (H5036), in Psalm 14:1. Benson: a fool not by nature but through pride and insolence; Keil and Delitzsch: folly goes with ungodliness. Ellicott takes the name as probably a nickname earned by his folly; Abigail hears only one sense.
layers.text: His own wife says it: Nabal means "fool," and folly, nevalah, goes with him. In Hebrew a nabal is not slow-witted but someone who lives as if God and others do not count: "The fool says in his heart, ‘There is no God.’"

layers.evidence: TAHOT: nivlei, skins of (H5035), in 25:18; betset hayyayin mi-Naval, when the wine had gone out from Nabal, in 25:37. Some commentators see a play between nevel and Naval; the text does not point it out.
layers.text: Some hear a second pun. Abigail packs "two skins of wine," and a skin or jar is nevel, close to Nabal. Where our English says "when Nabal was sober," the Hebrew says the wine had gone out of Nabal. On this reading the fool ends as an emptied wineskin.

passages.saying: Your glory, O Israel, lies slain on your heights.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the lament itself, which names Saul and Jonathan (1:23) and places their death on Mount Gilboa (1:21).
layers.text: David's lament for Saul and Jonathan begins here. The king and his son, the pride of Israel, lie dead on the heights of Mount Gilboa. The refrain that runs through the song is heard for the first time: "How the mighty have fallen!"

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: literally the gazelle, the Eastern type of beauty. The Companion Bible, in its note on 1:18, gives the line as Thy hart, Israel. Keil and Delitzsch disagree and read the word simply as ornament, meaning Saul and Jonathan. In 2 Samuel 2:18 the same Hebrew word, tsevi, in the plural, means gazelles.
layers.text: The Hebrew word for glory here, tsevi, is spelled and sounds the same as the word for gazelle, used of swift Asahel in 2 Samuel 2:18. Some read the line as mourning the fallen as Israel's gazelle, the graceful animal that stood for beauty in the East.

passages.saying: Abner son of Ner, the commander of Saul’s army, took Saul’s son Ish-bosheth
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on 2:8-11, where Abner makes Ish-bosheth king over Israel while the house of Judah follows David.
layers.text: After Saul died, Abner, the commander of his army, took Saul's son Ish-bosheth east across the Jordan to Mahanaim and made him king over Israel. This set up a rival kingdom to David, who reigned over Judah at Hebron.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch and the Companion Bible: Ish-bosheth means man of shame. With Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown they identify him with the Esh-baal of 1 Chronicles 8:33, with bosheth, shame, written in place of Baal. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch compare Hosea 9:10.
layers.text: Ish-bosheth means man of shame. In 1 Chronicles 8:33 the same son of Saul is called Esh-baal. Bosheth, shame, was written in place of Baal, the name of a shameful idol. Gideon's name Jerubbaal is changed the same way in 2 Samuel 11:21.

passages.saying: So this place, which is in Gibeon, is called Helkath-hazzurim.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on 2:12-16: twelve men from each side were matched in a contest at the pool of Gibeon, and they all fell together.
layers.text: At the pool of Gibeon, Abner and Joab each sent out twelve young men to fight. Each man seized his opponent by the head and drove his sword into his side, so they all fell together. The place was named after that fight.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch and Barnes: field of the sharp edges; Keil and Delitzsch compare Psalm 89:43, where the same word, tsur, is the edge of a sword. Gill and Wesley: field of rocks, men who would not give way.
layers.text: Helkath-hazzurim means field of the sharp edges, a name that remembers the swords that struck down all twenty-four men at once. Another reading is field of rocks, for men who stood like rock and died on the spot where they fought.

passages.saying: the LORD has burst out against my enemies before me
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on 5:17-20: the Philistines came against the newly anointed king, David asked the LORD, and the LORD gave the victory.
layers.text: When the Philistines came up to attack the new king, David asked the LORD whether to fight and was promised victory. After defeating them he gave the LORD the credit, saying the LORD had broken through his enemies like a flood.

layers.evidence: Gill, Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Keil and Delitzsch, Wesley and the Companion Bible all tie Mount Perazim in Isaiah 28:21 to this victory. Barnes and Keil and Delitzsch: the strange thing is that God would now act against His own people.
layers.text: Isaiah 28:21 looks back to this day: "the LORD will rise up as at Mount Perazim." But this time He would burst out against His own people in Jerusalem, not against their enemies. That is why Isaiah calls it His strange work.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Barnes, Wesley and Keil and Delitzsch all explain Baal-perazim as master or possessor of breaches, named from David's words that the LORD broke through his enemies like a breach of waters.
layers.text: David says the LORD has burst out, parats, against his enemies like a flood bursting, perets, through its banks. So the place is named Baal-perazim, master of burstings-through. The name gives the LORD the credit for the victory.

passages.saying: so he named that place Perez-uzzah, as it is called to this day.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on 6:6-8: Uzzah took hold of the ark when the oxen stumbled, and God struck him down beside it.
layers.text: As the ark was being brought up to the City of David, Uzzah took hold of it when the oxen stumbled, and God struck him dead. David was angry and grieved, and he named the place for what had happened there.

layers.evidence: Gill, Wesley and Keil and Delitzsch: Perez-uzzah means the breach or rent of Uzzah. Barnes points the reader back to the naming of Baal-perazim in 5:20, where the same verb parats and noun perets are used.
layers.text: Perez-uzzah means the breaking out against Uzzah: the LORD had broken out, parats, in a breaking out, perets, against him. It is the same word that named Baal-perazim, where the LORD broke out against David's enemies (2 Samuel 5:20).

passages.saying: He will build a house for My Name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESH, the Septuagint, the Dead Sea Scroll 4Q174 (Intertextual Bible), F. F. Bruce, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: King David, settled in a palace of cedar, wants to build a temple for the ark of God. Through the prophet Nathan, God turns the offer around: David's son will build the temple, and God will build David a dynasty and establish its throne forever.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: bayit (H1004) 15 times in 2 Samuel 7. TBESH: house, also household, family. The closing lesson is Keil and Delitzsch's on 7:11; Gill and Benson make the same turn
layers.text: The chapter turns on bayit, "house," used 15 times. David offers God a house, a temple; God answers, "He Himself will establish a house for you," a dynasty. One commentator draws the lesson: God must build a man's house before the man can build God's.

layers.evidence: Solomon adds: I have built the house for the Name of the LORD (1 Kings 8:20). Benson and Gill on 2 Samuel 7:14: the discipline clause fits Solomon, not Christ
layers.text: The first fulfillment is Solomon, who dedicated the temple saying, "Now the LORD has fulfilled the word that He spoke." The promise even allows for his failures: "When he does wrong, I will discipline him."

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch on 1 Chronicles 17:13: the omission comes from reading David's seed as the Messiah; Ellicott: probably not a mere abridgment; Barnes: the writer is not about to record Solomon's sins
layers.text: Chronicles retells the promise without "When he does wrong," and where Samuel has "Your house and kingdom," it reads "My house and My kingdom." Some commentators say Chronicles reads the son as the Messiah; others, that it simply passes over Solomon's sins.

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary on Hebrews 1:5: a primary and partial fulfillment in Solomon; Gill and Bengel: spoken of Solomon, but belonging to Christ. Barnes on 2 Samuel 7:14: Hebrews 1:5 applies it to Christ
layers.text: Hebrews quotes "I will be His Father, and He will be My Son" of Christ, and the angel tells Mary her son will have "the throne of His father David" and "His kingdom will never end!" Commentators see in Solomon only a first, partial fulfillment.

layers.evidence: 4Q174 (4QFlorilegium) 1.10-13 on 2 Samuel 7:11-14, read with Amos 9:11 through the shared verb qum (TAHOT; BSB restore), in the Intertextual Bible translation. Herbert Bateman (JETS 38/1, 1995): the shared "I will raise up" links the two, and the scroll expects a future Davidic King-Messiah, the shoot of David.

cites.at: Herbert W. Bateman IV, "Two First-Century Messianic Uses of the OT: Heb 1:5-13 and 4QFlor 1.1-19," JETS 38/1 (1995), pp. 15-16

layers.text: The Dead Sea Scrolls show some Jews reading this as a promise of a coming king. One scroll applies it to the Branch of David and links "I will raise up" to Amos's "I will restore the fallen tent of David," the same verb in Hebrew. Acts 15:16 quotes Amos.

layers.evidence: Numbers 12:7. The Reformation Study Bible on Hebrews 3:6: Moses was in the house, Christ is over it, and God's house is His people (2 Samuel 7:16). Keil and Delitzsch and Benson on 1 Chronicles 17:14: spoken only of the Messiah. Ellicott on Hebrews 3:6: Moses faithful as a servant in God's house, Christ as a son over it.
layers.text: Hebrews sets Moses, faithful "in all My house," beside the Son: "Christ is faithful as the Son over God’s house." In 1 Chronicles 17:14 God promises to set David's son over His house and His kingdom forever, words that older commentators say fit only the Messiah.

passages.saying: Who was the one to strike Abimelech son of Jerubbesheth?
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on 11:14-21: David had ordered Uriah placed where he would be killed, and Joab now reports the losses near the wall.
layers.text: Joab sends word to David of losses near the wall of Rabbah. He expects the king to be angry and to recall how Abimelech died near a wall, so he tells the messenger to add that Uriah the Hittite is dead too, the news David was waiting for.

layers.evidence: Gill, Keil and Delitzsch and Barnes all read the question as pointing to Abimelech's death in Judges 9. Barnes adds that it shows the records of that period were known and read in David's day.
layers.text: Joab recalls Judges 9:53, where a woman at Thebez dropped a millstone from the tower onto Abimelech's head. The old story warned soldiers not to go near a besieged wall, and Joab expects David to raise it against him.

layers.evidence: Gill: Jerubbesheth is Jerubbaal, that is Gideon (Judges 6:32), with Besheth, shame, in place of Baal, the name of a shameful idol. Keil and Delitzsch, on 2 Samuel 2:8, note the same change beside Ish-bosheth.
layers.text: Jerubbesheth is Gideon. In Judges 6:32 he is named Jerubbaal, "Let Baal contend with him." Here the Baal part of the name is replaced by besheth, shame, because Baal was a shameful idol.

passages.saying: to name him Jedidiah because the LORD loved him
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own wording, read with verse 24, as Gill explains it.
layers.text: After Solomon was born, the LORD sent word through Nathan the prophet that the child should also be called Jedidiah, because the LORD loved him.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible notes that yedid, beloved, in Psalm 127:2 was Solomon's name Jedidiah, given by the LORD in 2 Samuel 12:25. Bullinger's Figures of Speech says the same word is used in the psalm and that the psalm relates to Solomon, as its title shows.

cites.at: E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech Used in the Bible (1898), Ellipsis (Omission)

layers.text: Psalm 127, a psalm of Solomon, says He gives sleep to His beloved. The Hebrew word for beloved there is yedid, the word inside Solomon's God-given name Jedidiah, so the line seems to look back to Solomon himself.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke and Wesley all explain Jedidiah as beloved of the Lord, and Matthew Henry and Bullinger say the same. Barnes adds that the name shares its root, to love, with the name David.
layers.text: Jedidiah means beloved of the LORD. It joins yedid, beloved, with Yah, a short form of God's name, so the name says what verse 24 says, that the LORD loved the child. It also echoes his father David's name, which carries the same idea of love.

passages.saying: such a thing should never be done in Israel
