layers.text: The ancient path points back to the world before Noah's Flood. In the next verse these men have their foundations swept away by a flood, recalling the day the fountains of the great deep burst forth and that ungodly generation was destroyed.

passages.saying: Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the two matching lines of the verse, part of Job's praise of God's power in verses 5 to 14.
layers.text: Job says nothing is hidden from God. Even Sheol, the realm of the dead, lies open before Him, and Abaddon, the place of destruction, has nothing to cover it from His sight.

layers.evidence: Barnes says the Hebrew word means destruction, then the place of destruction, and points to Revelation 9:11; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown gives the abode of destruction and Revelation 9:11; Clarke calls Abaddon the place where destruction reigns. The Companion Bible also notes the Hebrew Abaddon.
layers.text: Abaddon means destruction. Here it names the place of the dead, set beside Sheol. Revelation 9:11 gives the same Hebrew name to the angel of the Abyss, whose name in Greek is Apollyon.

passages.saying: by His understanding He shattered Rahab
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the two matching lines: God's power over the sea and His wisdom in striking down what is proud.
layers.text: Job praises God's rule over the sea. By His power He stirs up the sea, and by His wisdom He strikes down Rahab, the proud one. Nothing in creation is too wild or too proud for Him to master.

layers.evidence: Clarke calls it a manifest allusion to the Red Sea crossing and the overthrow of Pharaoh; Gill reports that some take it of the Red Sea and of Egypt. Barnes says there is no allusion here to the dividing of the sea, and Keil and Delitzsch say the writer of Job purposely avoids references to Israel's history.
layers.text: Some readers hear the Exodus here: God divided the Red Sea and broke proud Egypt, the nation Isaiah calls Rahab (Isaiah 51:9-10). Others take the verse more generally, of God taming the raging sea.

layers.evidence: Gill and Clarke both note that the word behind the King James rendering the proud is Rahab. Gill calls it one of the names of Egypt (Psalm 87:4), and Clarke calls it the very name by which Egypt is called in Isaiah 51:9.
layers.text: This Rahab is not the woman of Jericho, whose name is a different Hebrew word. Rahab here means pride, so older versions say the proud. The Bible also uses it as a poetic name for proud Egypt (Psalm 87:4; Isaiah 51:9).

passages.saying: the breath of God remains in my nostrils
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the oath of verses 2 to 4, where breath in the nostrils stands for life itself.
layers.text: Job takes an oath. As long as he has breath in him, the breath God gave him, his lips will not speak wickedness or deceit (verse 4). Breath in the nostrils here simply means being alive.

layers.evidence: Clarke says Job appears to allude to the creation of Adam; Barnes thinks the language probably alludes to God breathing into man (Genesis 2:7); Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says it shows Job knew the living soul was breathed into man by God. Gill also cites Genesis 2:7.
layers.text: Job's words recall the creation of man, when God breathed the breath of life into his nostrils (Genesis 2:7). Job uses the same Hebrew words for breath and nostrils, showing he knew his life was breathed into him by God.

passages.saying: the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the poem's question of where wisdom can be found (verses 12 and 20) and this closing answer.
layers.text: After asking where wisdom can be found, the poem gives God's answer to man: true wisdom is to fear the Lord, and true understanding is to turn away from evil.

layers.evidence: Gill says Job here shows himself one who feared God and eschewed evil, as Job 1:1 testifies; Wesley says Job meant to show he had always counted it his best wisdom to fear God and depart from evil. The Hebrew repeats fear, turn and evil.
layers.text: This answer echoes the first verse of the book, where Job is described as "fearing God and shunning evil" (Job 1:1). The wisdom God gives to man is the very life Job had been living.

passages.saying: I have become like dust and ashes
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the picture in the verse and on Job sitting among the ashes in his illness (Job 2:8).
layers.text: Job says God has thrown him down into the mud. He has become like dust and ashes, brought as low and as worthless in the eyes of others as a man can be.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists dust (aphar) and ashes (v'epher) under Paronomasia, or rhyming words, at Genesis 18:27 and adds: See also Job 30:19. Gill notes this is the phrase by which Abraham expressed his lowliness before God. Clarke, on Genesis 18:27, calls aphar vaepher words very similar in sound.

cites.at: E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech Used in the Bible (1898), Paronomasia (Rhyming-Words)

layers.text: In Hebrew, dust and ashes is a pair of sound-alike words, afar and efer. Abraham used the same pair of himself before God (Genesis 18:27), and Job uses it again when he repents (Job 42:6). It pictures how small and low a person is.

passages.saying: if I have covered my transgressions like Adam
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Job's closing oath of innocence in chapter 31.
layers.text: Job insists that he never covered up his sins or hid his guilt in his heart. He did not try to look righteous by keeping his wrongs secret.

layers.evidence: Clarke calls this a most evident allusion to the Fall, when Adam hid among the trees and blamed his wife; Keil and Delitzsch translate like Adam and point to Adam's hiding himself; Wesley says, as Adam did in Paradise. Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also lean toward this reading rather than as men do.
layers.text: Job looks back to Adam in the garden. After he sinned, Adam hid from the LORD God among the trees and then blamed his wife (Genesis 3:8, 12). Job says he never covered his wrongs the way Adam did.

passages.saying: let briers grow instead of wheat
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the oath of verses 38 to 40 and the closing note that the words of Job are ended.
layers.text: Job ends his oath of innocence. If he has wronged his land or the tenants who work it, let briers and stinking weeds grow where his wheat and barley should be. With this, Job's words to his friends are finished.

layers.evidence: Gill says respect seems to be had to the original curse upon the earth (Genesis 3:18), when fruitful land is turned to barrenness for sin; Barnes also points this line to Genesis 3:18.
layers.text: Job's wish that briers would spring up instead of grain recalls the curse on the ground after Adam's sin, when God said it would yield thorns and thistles (Genesis 3:18). Job calls that kind of curse on his own field if he is guilty.

passages.saying: Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on verses 2 and 3, which give the two reasons for Elihu's anger.
layers.text: A new speaker, the younger man Elihu, now grows angry. He is angry with Job for justifying himself rather than God, and in the next verse with the three friends for condemning Job without an answer.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch and Wesley give Elihu as my God is He, and Keil and Delitzsch give Barachel as may God bless; Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown give Barachel as God blesses and say the names show the piety of the family. Gill and the Companion Bible agree.
layers.text: The name Elihu means my God is He, and his father's name, Barachel, means God blesses. Names built on the name of God like these point to a family that knew and honored the true God.

passages.saying: the breath of the Almighty gives me life
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on verses 4 to 7, where Elihu says he was formed from clay just like Job.
layers.text: Elihu reminds Job that he is only a fellow creature. God's Spirit made him and the Almighty's breath gives him life, so Job can answer him freely, as one man to another.

layers.evidence: Gill says the allusion is to the creation of man, when God breathed into him the breath of life; Clarke calls it another plain allusion to Genesis 2:7, shown by the words nishmath and techaiyeni; Barnes calls it an evident allusion. Keil and Delitzsch also read verses 4 and 6 in harmony with Genesis 2:7.
layers.text: Elihu's words recall the creation of man, when God formed him from the dust and breathed the breath of life into his nostrils (Genesis 2:7). The same Hebrew word for breath is used, and in verse 6 Elihu adds that he too was formed from clay.

passages.saying: withdraw His Spirit and breath
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on verses 13 to 15, where Elihu argues from God's care for all creation to His justice.
layers.text: Elihu says every living thing depends on God. If He chose to take back His Spirit and breath, all flesh would perish together and people would return to dust. That He keeps giving life shows He is not unjust.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible notes that breath here is the Hebrew neshamah and says compare Genesis 2:7; Gill speaks of the breath God breathes into man and can take away; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown points the words about all flesh perishing to Genesis 3:19. Job 34:15 uses the same Hebrew words for dust and return as Genesis 3:19.
layers.text: Elihu's words echo Genesis. The breath God could take back is the breath of life He breathed into man (Genesis 2:7), and the return to dust in the next verse recalls God's word to Adam, "to dust you shall return" (Genesis 3:19).

passages.saying: Therefore, men fear Him, for He is not partial to the wise in heart
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the close of Elihu's speech, which calls for reverence before God's majesty.
layers.text: Elihu ends his speech by saying that people should stand in awe of God. God is not impressed by those who think themselves wise, so the right response to His greatness is humble reverence, not argument.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch note the assonance of yere'uhu (they fear Him) and yir'eh (He sees) and try to keep it in their translation: men regard Him with reverence, He has no regard for the wise of heart.
layers.text: Some hear two Hebrew words echoing each other here: people fear Him (yere'uhu), but He does not regard (yir'eh, literally see) the wise in heart. The likeness in sound may set human awe of God against God's refusal to be impressed by human wisdom.

passages.saying: when I fixed its boundaries and set in place its bars and doors
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on God's questions to Job about who set the sea its limits (Job 38:8-11).
layers.text: God asks Job who set limits on the sea. God alone marked out its boundaries and shut it in as if with bars and doors, so that its waves cannot pass the line He drew.

layers.evidence: Clarke says Job 38:10 refers to the decree of Genesis 1:9 that the waters be gathered into one place. Gill, on Genesis 1:9, points to Job 38:10 for the same work of making a place for the sea.
layers.text: God's words about fixing the sea's boundaries look back to creation, when He commanded the waters under the sky to gather into one place so that dry land could appear (Genesis 1:9). The sea keeps to its bed because of that first command.

passages.saying: The wings of the ostrich flap joyfully
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on God's survey of wild creatures, which shows Job the wisdom of their Maker.
layers.text: God points Job to the ostrich. Her wings flap with joy, yet they are no match for the stork's. Her odd habits, described in the verses that follow, show the wisdom of the God who made her.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call chasidah here a play on the stork's name, meaning pious. JFB calls the stork the pious bird, a symbol of parental love, which the ostrich lacks when she deserts her young. Barnes says the stork's name means the pious one, from its tenderness to its young, and that the verse contrasts the two birds' care for their young.
layers.text: The stork's Hebrew name, chasidah, means the pious or devoted one, for the stork was known for caring for its young. The verse sets the ostrich beside her, and the next lines show the ostrich is anything but devoted: she leaves her eggs on the ground and treats her young harshly.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say renanim means a shrill, quavering cry and is a name for the female ostrich. JFB says it means the crying bird, from its night cries, and that both birds here are called by descriptive names. Barnes derives it from a verb for a tremulous, shrill sound and says the bird is named from its cry.
layers.text: Here the ostrich is called renanim, a poetic name rather than its usual one. It comes from a word for a ringing, quavering cry, so it means something like the shrill criers, after the loud cries the ostrich is known for.

passages.saying: Look at Behemoth, which I made along with you
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on God's second speech, which sets two great creatures before Job.
layers.text: God tells Job to look at Behemoth, a huge creature that God made just as He made Job. For all its strength, it eats grass like an ox. If Job cannot master this creature, he is in no position to govern the world.

layers.evidence: Gill and Clarke call Behemoth the plural of behemah, beast, and Gill says it denotes the chiefest of beasts. Keil and Delitzsch say the form, read as Hebrew, means the beast above all, the giant of beasts. Matthew Henry says the name signifies beasts. JFB and Keil and Delitzsch also mention a possible Egyptian name, water-ox, behind the form.
layers.text: Behemoth is the plural form of the ordinary Hebrew word for beast (behemah). Used of one animal, the plural marks it as the beast of beasts, the greatest of all. Some think the form may also echo an Egyptian name meaning water ox.

passages.saying: Can you pull in Leviathan with a hook
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on God's challenge to Job to capture the great creature of the waters.
layers.text: God asks whether Job could haul in Leviathan with a fishhook or bind its tongue with a rope. The question expects the answer no: this creature is far beyond any man's power to capture.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch, who take Leviathan here as the crocodile, say the poet uses the verb timshok to play on the crocodile's Egyptian and Arabic name, timsah.
layers.text: The first word of the verse, timshok (can you pull in), sounds like timsah, the name for the crocodile in Egyptian and Arabic. If Leviathan here is the crocodile, as many think, some hear God's question already echoing the creature's own name.

layers.evidence: JFB calls Leviathan literally the twisted animal, and Keil and Delitzsch call the name a word for twisted monsters. Gill and Clarke derive its first part, levi, from joining or coupling; Gill links this to the close joining of its scales.
layers.text: The name Leviathan comes from a Hebrew root meaning to twist or to join. It pictures a creature that coils itself in folds, or, as others take it, one whose scales are joined so tightly that nothing can pass between them (41:15-17).

passages.saying: He named his first daughter Jemimah, his second Keziah, and his third Keren-happuch.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse in its setting, Job 42:12-15, where the LORD restores Job after his trials.
layers.text: After his trials, God restored Job and gave him seven sons and three daughters. Only the daughters are named, and the next verse says no women in the land were as beautiful, and that Job gave them an inheritance among their brothers.

layers.evidence: Barnes, Wesley and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown take Jemimah as day (the Septuagint renders it Day); Keil and Delitzsch read dove. All agree Keziah is cassia. Barnes, Gill, Keil and Delitzsch and JFB read Keren-happuch as a horn of eye-paint (stibium); Clarke and Wesley take it as plenty.
layers.text: The names are pictures of beauty. Jemimah is usually taken to mean day, as after Job's long night, though some read dove. Keziah means cassia, a fragrant spice. Keren-happuch most likely means horn of eye-paint, a small horn of the dark powder women used on their eyes.

passages.saying: You are My Son; today I have become Your Father.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, the Septuagint, Jerome, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Psalm 2:7: ancient Near Eastern adoption language from covenants of grant, in which a lord rewarded a faithful subject with the status of son and an inheritance.
layers.text: Kings plot "against the LORD and against His Anointed One," but God has installed His King on Zion, calls him Son and promises him the nations. This is royal adoption language, used of David's line: a faithful subject made a son, with an inheritance.

layers.evidence: Bengel on Acts 4:27: Herod answers to the psalm's kings and Pilate to its rulers; Gill and JFB apply the psalm to Jesus. TAHOT and TAGNT: mashiach (H4899), christos (G5547), chriō (G5548).
layers.text: When the apostles are threatened, the church prays this psalm as current events: Herod and Pilate conspired "against Your holy servant Jesus, whom You anointed." The psalm's "Anointed One" is mashiach (Messiah), in Greek christos (Christ).

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary on Acts 13:33: this use of the psalm is best explained by Romans 1:4. Poole: Christ did not begin to be Son at the resurrection but was then shown to be.
layers.text: Paul hears the king's "today" as resurrection day: God kept His promise "by raising up Jesus." In Romans, Jesus is "declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection," shown to be Son then, not made Son. Hebrews quotes it too.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Luke 3:22: the words recall Psalm 2:7 and Isaiah 42:1; one Greek manuscript (D), several Latin ones and some church fathers quote Psalm 2:7 in full, against the weight of the manuscripts. Ellicott and Pulpit on Matthew 3:17.
layers.text: At Jesus' baptism the voice from heaven says, "You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased," recalling this psalm and Isaiah's Servant, "in whom My soul delights." In Luke, a few old copies read the psalm's "today I have become Your Father" instead.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Psalm 2:9: the Septuagint reads the consonants as ra'ah (shepherd) rather than ra'a' (break); nafats (smash) in the next line favors break. TAGNT: poimainō in Revelation 2:27, 12:5, 19:15 and 7:17.
layers.text: The Hebrew letters of "You will break them with an iron scepter" can also read "you will shepherd," as the Greek Old Testament took it. Revelation quotes it so (BSB "rule"), and the Lamb "will be their shepherd." But "shatter them like pottery" favors "break."

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Psalm 2:12: bar for son occurs in Hebrew only in Proverbs 31:2; the Septuagint, followed by the Vulgate, has lay hold of discipline. Keil and Delitzsch and the NET Bible notes report the reading pure, and Keil and Delitzsch hold to Kiss the Son. Jerome, Apology against Rufinus 1.19: Adore the Son in his commentary, Worship purely in his Psalter.

cites.at: Jerome, Apology against Rufinus 1.19

layers.text: "Kiss the Son" uses bar, Aramaic for son, where verse 7 has the Hebrew ben; elsewhere Hebrew has bar only in Proverbs 31:2. Some read "pure"; the Greek urges taking hold of discipline. Jerome rendered it both ways, as adoring the Son and as worshiping purely.

passages.saying: Shine the light of Your face upon us, O LORD.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the contrast in Psalm 4:6-7 between the many who look for good and David's joy in God's favor.
layers.text: Many people ask who can show them what is good. David answers with a prayer for God's favor, pictured as the light of His face shining on His people. That favor gives him more joy than a rich harvest of grain and wine (verse 7).

layers.evidence: Gill, Keil and Delitzsch and Bullinger's Companion Bible all tie this prayer to the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26. Keil and Delitzsch note that it blends the blessing's shining face and lifted face into one request; Bullinger notes that no priest was with David to bless him. Hebrew: nasa (lift up) and or (light, shine) in both.
layers.text: In Hebrew David asks God to lift up the light of His face, echoing the priests' blessing: "may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you" and "may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you." David blends the two wishes into one prayer.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch: this spelling of the verb nasa (lift up) with a samekh, nesah, is found nowhere else and mixes it with a verb meaning to raise high, the root of nes (banner), so the light of God's face may also be a banner of victory. They offer this as a possibility.
layers.text: The Hebrew word for lift up is spelled here in an unusual way, nesah, which looks like nes, a banner. If the spelling is deliberate, David also asks God to raise the light of His face over His people like a banner of victory to rally around.

passages.saying: what is man that You are mindful of him, or the son of man that You care for him?
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB and its footnotes, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Psalm 8:5: these terms allude to mankind's royal status as God's vice-regents.
layers.text: Looking at "the moon and the stars," David marvels that God cares for frail humans at all, yet has crowned them "with glory and honor" and made them rulers over the animals, as in Genesis 1. These are royal words: humans rule on God's behalf.

layers.evidence: TBESH: enosh, man, mortal man; adam, man, human being. Barnes on Hebrews 2:9: we do not see mankind with the dominion the psalm describes.
layers.text: Hebrews quotes this and admits the gap: "Yet at present we do not see everything subject to him. But we see Jesus." In the psalm "son of man" (ben adam) means a human being, like enosh, "mortal man." What God promised humanity is already true of one man.

layers.evidence: BSB footnote on Psalm 8:5: or than God, or than the heavenly beings; see also the Septuagint. NET Bible notes: Hebrews 2:7 follows the Septuagint. TBESG (Abbott-Smith) on brachy ti cites Hebrews 2:7, 9 for both senses. Bengel and Gill on Hebrews 2:7 read time; Barnes, JFB and Ellicott, rank.
layers.text: In "a little lower than the angels" the Hebrew has elohim, "God" or "the heavenly beings"; Hebrews follows the Greek "angels." Its Greek for "a little" can mean slightly or for a short time, so some read Jesus' lowering as brief, others as a matter of rank.

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary on 1 Corinthians 15:27: words spoken of man in general are transferred to the federal Head of humanity. Ellicott: all things are put under man, and in a higher sense under the Son of Man.
layers.text: Paul joins "You have placed everything under his feet" to Christ's reign: "He must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death." The rule given to humanity belongs, in a higher sense, to Christ, the new Adam.

layers.evidence: BSB footnote on Psalm 8:2: literally strength; the Septuagint has praise, cited in Matthew 21:16. Abbott-Smith (TBESG) marks Matthew 21:16 as the Septuagint's wording. Pulpit Commentary on Matthew 21:16: words first applied to Jehovah, which Jesus claims as addressed to Himself.
layers.text: Children shout "Hosanna to the Son of David!" and leaders object. Matthew gives Jesus' answer in the Greek Old Testament's words: "From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise." The Hebrew has "strength." Jesus accepts praise meant for God.

passages.saying: You made him ruler of the works of Your hands
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Psalm 8:4-8, where David marvels at the honor God gives to frail man.
layers.text: David marvels that God has made frail humans rulers over His creation and placed every creature under their feet. It is a royal honor, and the New Testament sees it fully realized in Jesus (Hebrews 2:8-9).

layers.evidence: Barnes says the allusion is to Genesis 1:26, 28. Keil and Delitzsch say the psalm's words about putting all things under man's feet paraphrase the rule (radah) given there. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown note that the creatures listed in Psalm 8:7-8 match those named in Genesis 1:26-28.
layers.text: This looks back to creation, when God made man "to rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air." The creatures the psalm lists next, sheep, oxen, wild beasts, birds and fish, are the same kinds placed under human rule in Genesis 1.

passages.saying: On the wicked He will rain down fiery coals and sulfur
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Psalm 11:4-7, where the LORD on His heavenly throne tests the righteous and judges the wicked.
layers.text: Friends urge David to flee, but he trusts the LORD, who watches from His throne in heaven. The wicked will meet God's judgment, pictured as a storm of fire, sulfur and scorching wind poured out as their share.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Barnes and Wesley all see the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah behind this verse. Both verses use the Hebrew verb matar (rain down) with esh (fire) and gophrit (sulfur).
layers.text: The picture comes from Sodom and Gomorrah, when "the LORD rained down sulfur and fire" from heaven. The psalm uses the same Hebrew words for rain, fire and sulfur. What God did to those wicked cities shows what awaits all who persist in wickedness.

passages.saying: When the LORD restores His captive people
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the Hebrew idiom who will give, meaning oh that, and on Zion as God's dwelling place.
layers.text: David longs for God to send salvation to Israel from Zion, where He dwells. When the LORD turns back the captivity or deep trouble of His people, Jacob, that is Israel, will rejoice and be glad.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible marks bringeth back the captivity as a paronomasia; Bullinger's Figures of Speech says every passage where God turns the captivity of His people uses two similar words; Keil and Delitzsch say the verb form was chosen for the alliteration with shevut, which they derive from a verb meaning to take captive.

cites.at: E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech Used in the Bible (1898), Paronomasia (Rhyming-Words)

layers.text: In Hebrew, restores His captive people is shuv shevut, literally turn the captivity, two similar-sounding words. The same sound play appears wherever Scripture speaks of God turning the captivity of His people, as in Deuteronomy 30:3.

passages.saying: For You will not abandon my soul to Sheol, nor will You let Your Holy One see decay.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, Josephus, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Psalm 16:10: the psalmist speaks of himself, confident that God will prevent him from dying.
layers.text: David trusts the LORD as his "chosen portion," so he is sure God will not hand him over to the grave but show him "the path of life," with "eternal pleasures at Your right hand." He is confident God will keep him from death.

At Pentecost Peter quotes the psalm and argues it cannot mean David: "David died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day." As a prophet, David foresaw "the resurrection of the Christ, that He was not abandoned to Hades, nor did His body see decay."

layers.evidence: Josephus, Antiquities 7.15.3 (Whiston): Hyrcanus the high priest opened one room of David's tomb and took out three thousand talents; many years later King Herod opened another.
layers.text: David's tomb was a landmark. Nehemiah marks repairs "opposite the tombs of David," and an ancient historian says a high priest and later King Herod each took treasure from a room of it. Everyone knew where David lay. But "God has raised this Jesus to life."

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Psalm 16:10: shachat, pit, often a title for Sheol. TBESH H7845: Pit, another name of Sheol. TBESG (Abbott-Smith) G1312: corruption of the grave; in the Septuagint chiefly for shachat.
layers.text: "Decay" is the Hebrew shachat, "pit," a name for the grave; the Greek Old Testament has diaphthora, "corruption." Both promise rescue from death. Paul draws the contrast: David "saw decay. But the One whom God raised from the dead did not see decay."

layers.evidence: Ellicott and JFB on Psalm 16:10: chasid is one who receives God's grace and shows it. Ellicott on Acts 13:34: the Greek for mercies is the adjective translated holy in the next verse; Pulpit: hosia stands for the Hebrew chasadim. Gill: the blessings are made sure only by His resurrection.
layers.text: Paul links two verses by one Greek word. Isaiah's "loving devotion promised to David" (chesed) is in Greek the "holy" (hosia) blessings; the psalm's "Holy One" is chasid, one who shows chesed, in Greek hosios. The promises are sure in God's risen Holy One.

passages.saying: Keep me as the apple of Your eye
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the apple of the eye meaning the pupil, which a person guards most carefully, and on the picture of a bird sheltering its young.
layers.text: David asks God to guard him as carefully as a person guards the pupil of his own eye, and to hide him under His wings as a bird shelters its young.

layers.evidence: Barnes says both comparisons are found in Deuteronomy 32:10-12 and the psalmist probably had that passage in view; Keil and Delitzsch call Deuteronomy 32:10 the primary passage for the apple of the eye and trace the wings to the eagle figure of the same song.
layers.text: Both pictures likely come from the Song of Moses, where God guarded Israel as the apple of His eye and, like an eagle, spread His wings over His young (Deuteronomy 32:10-11). David asks God to protect him with the same care He showed Israel in the wilderness.

passages.saying: Then the earth shook and quaked
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the context of the psalm, where God comes from His temple to answer David's cry for help.
layers.text: David describes God coming to rescue him with the force of a mighty earthquake: the earth and the foundations of the mountains shook because God burned with anger against his enemies.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible and Bullinger's Figures of Speech list vattigash and vattirash as a paronomasia, rendered shaked and quaked; Keil and Delitzsch note that gaash rhymes with raash and that the same verb then returns in another form.

cites.at: E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech Used in the Bible (1898), Paronomasia (Rhyming-Words)

layers.text: In Hebrew, shook and quaked are vattigash and vattirash, two rhyming verbs, something like shaked and quaked. The first verb comes back later in the verse, they were shaken, as if the earth keeps on rocking.

passages.saying: He drew me out of deep waters
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on deep or many waters as a common Old Testament picture of overwhelming trouble.
layers.text: God reached down from heaven, took hold of David, and pulled him out of overwhelming troubles, pictured as deep waters about to drown him.

layers.evidence: Gill says the words may allude to Moses, named from being drawn out of the water, and that this is the only other use of that Hebrew word. Keil and Delitzsch note the verb occurs elsewhere only in Exodus 2:10 and agree with Luther's reading, He hath made a Moses of me.
layers.text: The Hebrew verb for drew me out, mashah, is very rare. Apart from this song (repeated in 2 Samuel 22:17) it appears only in Exodus 2:10, where Pharaoh's daughter names Moses because she drew him out of the water. David pictures God rescuing him from the waters as He rescued Moses.

passages.saying: My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: David cries out to a God who seems silent while enemies surround him, then turns to praise: God has listened, and the nations will worship.
On the cross Jesus cries the psalm's first line in Aramaic: "Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?"

layers.evidence: On Matthew 27:47, Ellicott and Benson lean to a mishearing; Barnes, Gill and Matthew Henry to mockery; the Pulpit Commentary calls it an undecided question.
layers.text: Some bystanders say He is calling Elijah. Commentators differ on whether they misheard "Eloi" (my God) or mocked Him. Either way, the cry was the opening line of a psalm.
The psalm's details return at the cross: mockers shake their heads and say God should deliver Him, and soldiers divide His garments and cast lots, which John says fulfilled Scripture.

The psalm does not end in despair. Its second half praises God among "my brothers," words Hebrews puts in Jesus' mouth, and it ends with all nations turning to the LORD. Many readers think quoting the first line called the whole psalm to mind.

layers.evidence: STEPBible's TAHOT gives the Leningrad Codex reading ka'ari and notes the Judean Desert reading ka'aru
layers.text: The BSB reads "they have pierced my hands and feet." The traditional Hebrew text has ka'ari, "like a lion," while a manuscript found in the Judean Desert reads ka'aru, "they dug." Christians link the verse to the nail wounds, but the wording is a real textual question.

passages.saying: The earth is the LORD’s, and the fullness thereof
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse states God's ownership of the earth outright, and verse 2 grounds it in His creating the world.
layers.text: The whole earth and everything in it belong to the LORD, and so do the world and all the people who live in it. He owns it all because He made it.

layers.evidence: Gill, Keil and Delitzsch and Bullinger's Companion Bible all note that Paul quotes this verse in 1 Corinthians 10:26, where he applies it to food sold in the market.
layers.text: Paul quotes this verse in 1 Corinthians 10:26. Since the earth and all it holds belong to the Lord, believers may eat food sold in the market without anxious questions, while still caring for the conscience of others.

passages.saying: for I am lonely and afflicted
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain words of the prayer and the reason David gives for it.
layers.text: Feeling alone and weighed down with trouble, David asks the LORD to turn toward him and show him grace.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the repeated sounds of ani ani are deliberately kept; Bullinger lists the verse among his examples of paronomasia, or rhyming words, rendering it afflicted am I.

cites.at: E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech Used in the Bible (1898), Paronomasia (Rhyming-Words)

layers.text: The verse ends with a sound play in Hebrew. Afflicted is ani and I is ani, two different words that sound almost alike. So the line closes ani ani, afflicted am I, and the doubled sound presses home how low David felt.

passages.saying: The LORD sits enthroned over the flood
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of the LORD enthroned, which closes the psalm's description of the storm.
layers.text: The LORD sits on His throne over the flood, and He reigns as King forever. The raging storm the psalm has just described is under His rule, and that gives His people comfort.

layers.evidence: Gill, Keil and Delitzsch and Bullinger's Companion Bible note that mabbul is used elsewhere only of Noah's Flood and read the verse as recalling it. Barnes grants that use of the word but takes the verse of storm rains.
layers.text: The Hebrew word for flood here, mabbul, is used elsewhere in the Bible only for Noah's Flood (Genesis 6 to 11). The psalm recalls that the LORD sat as Judge and King at that Flood, and He still rules every storm as King forever.

passages.saying: By the word of the LORD the heavens were made
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the parallel lines of the verse, where word and breath both stand for God's command.
layers.text: God made the heavens and all the stars simply by speaking. His word and the breath of His mouth were enough to create them, without effort or delay.

layers.evidence: Clarke says the verse evidently refers to the creation account of Genesis 1; Barnes points to Genesis 1:3 and 1:6; Keil and Delitzsch call God's word His almighty Let there be and point to the history of Creation, and Gill ties the Word to God's speaking on the six days of creation.
layers.text: This verse looks back to Genesis 1, where God made each thing simply by speaking, beginning with light. Verse 9 says the same thing again: when God speaks, creation comes into being and stands firm.

layers.evidence: Gill takes the Word here as Christ and the breath as the Holy Spirit, the third Person of the Trinity; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says there may be an allusion to the Son and the Holy Spirit.
layers.text: Christian teachers have seen the Trinity at work here. The word of the LORD points to the Son, who is called the Word through whom all things came to be (John 1:1-3), and the breath of His mouth points to the Holy Spirit.

passages.saying: He piles up the waters of the sea
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's two pictures of God's control over the waters of the sea.
layers.text: God gathers the waters of the sea like a heap and stores the deep waters as in storehouses. He holds the seas in their place, a striking sign of His power.

layers.evidence: Gill ties the verse to the third day of creation (Genesis 1:9). Keil and Delitzsch note the same expression at the Red Sea and the Jordan, but say this verse speaks of a miracle of creation.
layers.text: The picture looks back to the third day of creation, when God gathered the waters under the sky into one place (Genesis 1:9). Behind piles up is ned, Hebrew for a heap, the word used when the Red Sea stood up like a wall for Israel (Exodus 15:8). Here it shows God's power in creation.

passages.saying: You give them drink from Your river of delights
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's pictures of a feast in God's house and a flowing river.
layers.text: Those who take refuge in God are richly fed from the plenty of His house, and He gives them drink from a river of joys, a supply that is full and never runs dry.

layers.evidence: Clarke reads the phrase as the river of thy Eden and sees a reference to the river of Genesis 2:10; Keil and Delitzsch call it a paradisaic river of delights; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says it may allude to Eden.
layers.text: The Hebrew word for delights here is a form of eden, which is spelled just like the name of the garden of Eden. So the river of God's delights recalls the river that flowed out of Eden to water the garden (Genesis 2:10), a taste of paradise restored.

passages.saying: Many will see and fear and put their trust in the LORD
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse; Barnes explains that many learn of the rescue and come to reverence and trust God.
layers.text: God gave David a new song of praise for his rescue. When many people see what God has done for him, they will stand in awe of the LORD and put their trust in Him.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible and Figures of Speech (both Bullinger) mark yir'u and v'yira'u as a Paronomasia, rendering it peer and fear; Keil and Delitzsch note the alliteration in these verbs. Bullinger compares Psalm 52:6, where the same pair recurs.

cites.at: E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech Used in the Bible (1898), Paronomasia (Rhyming-Words)

layers.text: In "Many will see and fear," the two Hebrew verbs sound almost alike: yiru (they will see) and yirau (they will fear). The sound may carry the thought, as seeing what God has done turns into fearing Him. In English one could say peer and fear.

passages.saying: but my ears You have opened
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's contrast between sacrifices and an opened ear; Barnes explains that God preferred obedience to sacrifice.
layers.text: David says that what God most wanted was never the animal sacrifices and offerings in themselves, but an ear opened to hear and obey Him. Hebrews 10 applies these words to Christ, who came to do God's will.

layers.evidence: Clarke says the words are better rendered my ears hast thou bored and that the allusion is evidently to the servant law of Exodus 21; Wesley reads it the same way, as devotion to perpetual service. Barnes and Gill prefer the sense of an ear opened to hear, so this reading is not universal.
layers.text: The Hebrew for opened literally means dug or bored. Many read this as a picture of the servant in the Law whose ear was pierced at the doorpost when he chose to serve his master for life (Exodus 21:6). It speaks of willing, lifelong obedience to God.

passages.saying: Even my close friend whom I trusted, the one who shared my bread, has lifted up his heel against me.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the Septuagint, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes on Psalm 41:9: the figure is a horse that turns and kicks the one who fed it; the Pulpit Commentary reads it the same way.
layers.text: Sick in bed, David hears his enemies ask, "When will he die and be forgotten?" Worse, a trusted friend who ate at his table has turned against him, like a horse kicking the one who fed it. David asks God to "raise me up."

At the Last Supper Jesus applies the verse to Judas: "The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me." Soon after, "He dipped the morsel and gave it to Judas." The friend who shared the psalmist's bread now sits at Jesus' own table.

layers.evidence: The Septuagint of Psalm 41:9 has esthiō; John 13:18 has trōgō (TAGNT), used of eating Christ's flesh in John 6 and elsewhere only in Matthew 24:38. Ellicott on John 6:54: the same word as in John 13:18, simply eating, its literal sense not to be pressed. The psalm's Hebrew has the ordinary akal (TAHOT), so the link to John 6 is in John's Greek.
layers.text: In John's Greek the word for "shares" (eats) is trōgō, not the Greek psalm's verb. John also uses it in "Whoever eats My flesh and drinks My blood has eternal life," though it was an everyday word. The betrayer ate with "the bread that came down from heaven."

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary on Psalm 41:9: Ahithophel almost certainly intended; Poole and Barnes agree. Ellicott on Matthew 27:5: apanchō is the Septuagint's word in 2 Samuel 17:23. TAGNT: G0519 occurs only in Matthew 27:5.
layers.text: Many take David's false friend to be Ahithophel, who sided with Absalom and later "hanged himself." Matthew says Judas "went away and hanged himself," with a verb used nowhere else in the New Testament: the Greek Old Testament's word for Ahithophel.

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary, Barnes, Gill and Benson on John 18:1 recall David's flight from Absalom; Benson calls David here a type of Christ.
layers.text: Betrayed by Ahithophel, David "crossed the Kidron Valley" and climbed the Mount of Olives weeping. Betrayed by Judas, Jesus "went out with His disciples across the Kidron Valley" to the same hill. Some recall David's flight here, though John himself does not point it out.

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary on John 13:19: instead of shaking their faith, it will prove He was taken by no surprise. Ellicott: they will find in it confirmation of their faith in Him as the Messiah.
layers.text: Jesus names the betrayal in advance on purpose: "I am telling you now before it happens, so that when it comes to pass, you will believe that I am He." What could have shaken their faith becomes a reason for it.

layers.evidence: Bengel on John 13:18 compares aqev in Genesis 3:15. TAHOT tags both words H6119.
layers.text: "Heel" is aqev, the word of the first promise, where the serpent "will strike his heel" but the woman's seed "will crush your head." Some set the two verses side by side, and John notes that when Judas took the morsel, "Satan entered into him."

passages.saying: Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own images of hyssop, washing and snow; Barnes explains it as a prayer to be made entirely clean.
layers.text: David asks God to cleanse him from his sin so completely that he will truly be clean, washed whiter than snow.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the verse recalls the hyssop sprinkling of the leper and of one defiled by a dead body (Leviticus 14; Numbers 19); Gill and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown add the Passover hyssop of Exodus 12:22, and Barnes, Clarke and Wesley also tie it to these rites.
layers.text: Hyssop was the small plant used to put the Passover blood on the doorposts and, under the Law, to sprinkle a healed leper and anyone made unclean by touching the dead (Numbers 19:18). David asks God Himself to do for his heart what those rites pictured.

layers.evidence: Barnes notes that purge is from chata, to sin, which in this form means to atone or expiate, and he cites Luther's rendering Unsin me with hyssop; the Companion Bible gives Thou wilt sin-cleanse me, or un-sin me.
layers.text: The Hebrew word for purify here is the ordinary verb meaning to sin, used in a form that means to take sin away. So David is literally asking God to un-sin him, removing his guilt completely, as the sin offering pictured.

passages.saying: The righteous will see and fear
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own words; Barnes explains the fear as reverence at God's justice.
layers.text: When God brings the boastful evildoer down, the righteous will see His judgment and stand in reverent awe of Him. They will mock the man who did not make God his refuge but trusted in his wealth.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch point out the play of sounds here and compare Psalm 40:3, where Bullinger's Figures of Speech also lists the same see and fear sound pair and refers to this verse.

cites.at: E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech Used in the Bible (1898), Paronomasia (Rhyming-Words)

layers.text: In Hebrew, will see (yiru) and fear (yirau) sound almost the same, so seeing God's judgment flows straight into fearing Him. The same sound pair appears in Psalm 40:3, where many see what God has done, fear Him and trust Him.

passages.saying: When God restores His captive people, let Jacob rejoice
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own words; Barnes reads it as the people's earnest longing for deliverance.
layers.text: The psalm closes with a longing for God's salvation to come out of Zion. When God brings His captive people back, Jacob and Israel will rejoice and be glad.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists this verse, with Psalm 14:7 and many prophetic promises, among the places where turn and captivity are paired as two similar words.

cites.at: E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech Used in the Bible (1898), Paronomasia (Rhyming-Words)

layers.text: In Hebrew, the phrase translated restores His captive people pairs two similar words: shuv, to turn back, and shevut, captivity. The same sound pair appears in Psalm 14:7 and in many of God's promises to bring His captive people back.

passages.saying: O Lord, confuse and confound their speech
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own words; Clarke explains it as a prayer that the enemies' counsel be divided.
layers.text: David asks the Lord to throw his enemies' speech and plans into confusion so that they cannot agree, because he sees violence and strife in the city.

layers.evidence: Gill, Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Wesley and Keil-Delitzsch all see the confusion of tongues at Babel in Genesis 11 behind this prayer; Gill and Barnes call it an allusion.
layers.text: The prayer to confuse and divide their speech recalls Babel, where the LORD came down and confused the builders' language so they could not understand one another. David asks God to bring the same kind of confusion on the plotters in the city.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the verb divide looks back to Babel and to Genesis 10:25, that swallow up was chosen in remembrance of the Babel verb confuse, and that divide is pointed as it is for the sake of similarity of sound.
layers.text: The two Hebrew commands sound alike: balla, swallow up or confuse, and pallag, divide. Both recall Genesis: balla echoes balal, the word for God confusing the language at Babel, and pallag is the verb used when the earth was divided in Peleg's days.

passages.saying: Put my tears in Your bottle
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own picture; Barnes explains it as God keeping account of David's flights from place to place.
layers.text: Hunted from place to place, David trusts that God has kept count of every move he has made. He asks God to keep his tears as if in a bottle, sure that they are already written in God's book.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call it a play in sound, the Companion Bible marks a paronomasia on nodi and ben'odeka, and Bullinger's Figures of Speech says the likeness of sound shows that the tears our wanderings cause are noted by God.

cites.at: E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech Used in the Bible (1898), Paronomasia (Rhyming-Words)

layers.text: In Hebrew, my wanderings (nodi) and Your bottle (nod, a skin bottle) sound nearly the same. The play may tie them together: the tears that David's homeless wandering cost him are noticed and kept by God.

passages.saying: ambushing the innocent in seclusion, shooting suddenly, without fear
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own picture of an ambush; Barnes explains that they fear neither God nor man.
layers.text: The wicked lie in hiding and shoot at the innocent without warning. They strike suddenly and boldly, with no fear of being found out and no fear of God.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call the second word an assonance with the first, the Companion Bible marks a paronomasia on yoruhu and yira'u, and Bullinger's Figures of Speech lists the verse with its other examples of words that sound alike.

cites.at: E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech Used in the Bible (1898), Paronomasia (Rhyming-Words)

layers.text: In Hebrew, they shoot at him (yoruhu) and they do not fear (yirau) sound alike. The echo sets the attackers' sudden arrows right beside their complete lack of any fear of God.

passages.saying: He turned the sea into dry land
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own words; Barnes reads it as a display of God's power to deliver His people.
layers.text: The psalm calls everyone to see God's mighty works. He made a dry path through the sea and brought His people across the water on foot, and there they rejoiced in Him.

layers.evidence: Gill, Barnes and Keil-Delitzsch identify the sea as the Red Sea crossing of Exodus 14, and the Companion Bible and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown agree.
layers.text: The first line looks back to the Red Sea, where the LORD drove back the sea with a strong east wind and made it dry land, and Israel went through the sea on dry ground.

layers.evidence: Gill, Barnes and the Companion Bible take the river as the Jordan crossing of Joshua 3, and Keil-Delitzsch speak of both the Red Sea and the Jordan being laid dry; Gill notes that the Targum also reads Jordan.
layers.text: The Hebrew word behind waters is river (nahar), and it most likely recalls the Jordan, which Israel crossed on dry ground under Joshua to enter the promised land. The verse joins the two crossings that began and ended the journey from Egypt.

passages.saying: May God be gracious to us and bless us
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse and on verse 2, which gives the purpose of the prayer.
layers.text: The psalm opens by asking God to be gracious to His people, to bless them, and to look on them with favor. The next verse gives the purpose: that God's ways and His salvation would become known among all nations.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the psalm begins with words of the priest's blessing in Numbers 6:24-26, and Gill, Clarke, Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown point to the same blessing. Both passages use chanan (be gracious), barakh (bless) and or (make shine) with panim (face).
layers.text: This prayer takes up the blessing God gave the priests to speak over Israel in Numbers 6: "may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you." Here God's people pray that blessing for themselves, so that His salvation may reach all nations.

passages.saying: His enemies are scattered, and those who hate Him flee His presence
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse, whose two halves say the same thing in parallel.
layers.text: The psalm opens with God rising up to act. When He does, His enemies cannot stand before Him: they scatter and run from His presence, while the righteous rejoice before Him (verse 3).

layers.evidence: Barnes calls this an obvious reference to Moses' words in Numbers 10:35, and Clarke, Keil and Delitzsch, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible also tie it to that verse. The verbs qum (arise), puts (scatter) and nus (flee), and the words for enemies and haters, all repeat Moses' prayer.
layers.text: These words repeat the prayer Moses spoke each time the ark set out on the march: "Rise up, O LORD! May Your enemies be scattered; may those who hate You flee before You." The psalm sings that same cry as God goes before His people again.

passages.saying: when You went out before Your people, when You marched through the wasteland
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of verses 7 and 8 and the exodus story they recall.
layers.text: The psalm looks back to the exodus, when God Himself went at the head of His people and led them through the desert, and to Sinai, where the earth shook and the sky poured rain at His coming (verse 8).

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the poet repeats the words of Deborah in Judges 5:4; Gill says verses 7 and 8 seem borrowed from her song; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes the phrase that Sinai, as in Judges 5:5. Shared Hebrew: yatsa (go out), tsa'ad (march), ra'ash (shake), nataph (pour down) and Sinai.
layers.text: Verses 7 and 8 closely follow Deborah's victory song, which says, "when You went out from Seir, when You marched from the land of Edom, the earth trembled, the heavens poured out rain." Both songs then speak of God as the One of Sinai, the God of Israel.

passages.saying: zeal for Your house has consumed me, and the insults of those who insult You have fallen on me.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, the Septuagint, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: JFB, introduction to Psalm 69: referred to seven times in the New Testament as prophetical of Christ and the gospel times.
layers.text: David, sinking into "deep waters," cries to God. He suffers "for Your sake": his devotion to God's house has made him "a stranger to my brothers." Yet the psalm ends in praise. The New Testament quotes it again and again of Christ.

layers.evidence: Ellicott on John 2:17: the change from past to future is itself significant. Bengel: His zeal at last cost Him His life. TAGNT: the future kataphagetai is in all major Greek texts; the Textus Receptus has the past.
layers.text: When Jesus clears the temple, His disciples remember the line "Zeal for Your house will consume Me." The psalm says "has consumed"; John has the future, "will consume." Some hear His death in that change: His zeal would cost Him His life.

Paul quotes the second half to teach patience with weaker believers: "even Christ did not please Himself." The insults aimed at God fell on Christ, so the strong can "bear with the shortcomings of the weak."

layers.evidence: Septuagint (Rahlfs) of Psalm 69:21: cholē and oxos. Benson, Gill and the Pulpit Commentary on Psalm 69:21 see it fulfilled at the cross; Gill cites Matthew 27:48. Benson and Gill also cite Psalm 22:15.
layers.text: David's enemies "poisoned my food with gall and gave me vinegar to quench my thirst," in Greek cholē and oxos. On the cross Jesus said "I am thirsty" to fulfill Scripture and was given oxos, sour wine; Matthew says He was first offered wine "mixed with gall."

layers.evidence: TAHOT: chinnam (H2600) in Psalm 69:4, Psalm 35:19 and Job 2:3; John 15:25 has dōrean (G1432). NET Bible notes on Job 2:3: chinnam means gratis, without cause.
layers.text: Jesus applies the psalm's "Those who hate me without cause" to His own enemies: "They hated Me without reason." Psalm 35:19 has the same Hebrew. The key word is chinnam, "for nothing," the word God uses of Job's undeserved suffering.

layers.evidence: Gill and Barnes on Psalm 69:25 note that Acts 1:20 applies it to Judas. JFB and Poole on Psalm 69 read David, suffering in God's cause, as a type of Christ; Matthew Henry reads its curses as prophecies of the destruction of Christ's persecutors.
layers.text: Peter applies verse 25 to Judas, turning "their place" into "his place." Older commentators read David, who suffered for God's sake, as a type of Christ, and the psalm's curses as falling on those who rejected Him.

passages.saying: May the righteous flourish in his days and prosperity abound
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse within the psalm's prayer for the king.
layers.text: The psalm prays that in this king's days the righteous would flourish and peace and well-being would overflow without end, until the moon itself is gone.

layers.evidence: Gill says the abundance of peace here alludes to the name of Solomon, which signifies peace, and on 1 Chronicles 22:9 he again explains Solomon as meaning peace. The word rendered prosperity in this verse is shalom.
layers.text: This psalm is titled Of Solomon, and his name, Shelomoh, comes from the same root as shalom, peace, a link God Himself made in 1 Chronicles 22:9. Some hear the prayer that shalom, here rendered prosperity, would abound in his days as an echo of the king's own name.

passages.saying: In him may all nations be blessed
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse, the climax of the psalm's prayer for the king.
layers.text: The psalm closes its prayer for the king by asking that his name would last as long as the sun, that all nations would find blessing through him, and that they would call him blessed.

layers.evidence: Barnes points to Genesis 12:3 and 22:18 and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown to Genesis 12:3 and 18:18; the Companion Bible says the verse confirms the promise to Abraham; Gill calls Christ the seed of Abraham in whom all nations are blessed, citing Genesis 22:18. The verb barakh (bless) with all the goyim (nations) matches Genesis 22:18.
layers.text: This prayer takes up God's promise to Abraham: "through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed." The psalm asks for that promise to come true through the king, and Christians see it fulfilled in Christ, Abraham's offspring.

passages.saying: You divided the sea by Your strength
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse and on verse 12, which calls God the King who has worked salvation from ancient times.
layers.text: In a lament over the ruined sanctuary, the psalmist takes courage from what God did long ago: by His strength He split the sea and smashed the heads of the monsters in its waters.

layers.evidence: Barnes says the allusion is evidently to the Red Sea crossing of Exodus 14:21; Gill and the Companion Bible point to the same verse, and Clarke, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Keil and Delitzsch also read it of the Red Sea. Most of them take the sea monsters as Pharaoh and his army.
layers.text: This recalls the night God split the Red Sea for Israel, when "the waters were divided" (Exodus 14:21). The sea monsters whose heads He smashed are taken as a picture of Pharaoh and his army, drowned in that same sea.

passages.saying: His tent is in Salem, His dwelling place in Zion
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on Salem being the old name of Jerusalem (Genesis 14:18) and on its pairing with Zion in the same line.
layers.text: God has made His home among His people. His tent is in Salem, an old name for Jerusalem, and His dwelling place is on Zion. From there, as the next verse says, He broke the weapons of those who came against the city.

layers.evidence: Barnes says the name properly means peace, notes the Septuagint renders it in peace here, and suggests the old name may have been chosen to recall the peace God restored to the invaded city. Gill also notes the Septuagint's in peace and compares Hebrews 7:2, where king of Salem means king of peace.
layers.text: Salem, the old name of Jerusalem, means peace; Hebrews 7:2 explains king of Salem as king of peace. The psalm may use the old name on purpose, for in the city of peace God shattered the arrows, shield and sword and put an end to war.

passages.saying: Your path led through the sea, Your way through the mighty waters
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the picture in the verse and on verse 20, where God leads His people like a flock.
layers.text: The psalmist remembers how God made a path through the sea and the mighty waters for His people. God was plainly at work, yet no one could trace His footprints. His ways are beyond our tracking, but He led His people safely like a flock (verse 20).

layers.evidence: Gill, Barnes, Keil and Delitzsch and the Companion Bible all identify the sea here as the Red Sea crossing. Gill, Wesley and the Companion Bible explain the hidden footprints by the waters returning over the path. Both passages speak of the yam (sea) and the mayim (waters).
layers.text: This looks back to the night God parted the Red Sea and Israel walked through on dry ground (Exodus 14:21-22). Afterward the waters flowed back, so no footprints could be found. Verse 20 names Moses and Aaron, the leaders God used at that time.

passages.saying: Let Your hand be upon the man at Your right hand
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wording of the verse and the prayer that follows; the man is taken as Israel (Keil and Delitzsch, Wesley), its king (Barnes) or the Messiah (Gill, Clarke, Henry).
layers.text: The psalmist asks God to rest His hand on the one He has placed at His right hand, the place of honor, and made strong for Himself, so that Israel will not turn away again (verse 18). Interpreters take this man as Israel, its king, or the promised Messiah.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call the phrase a play upon the name of Benjamin, named in verse 2; Wesley and Gill note that Benjamin means son of the right hand, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the phrase may allude to Benjamin (Genesis 35:18). The words are yamin (right hand) and ben (son).
layers.text: The man at Your right hand (yamin) and the son (ben) echo the name Benjamin, which means son of the right hand (Genesis 35:18). Benjamin is named among the tribes in verse 2. The wording pictures one dearly loved and set in the place of honor beside God.

passages.saying: I am the LORD your God, who brought you up out of Egypt
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse read with verse 9, which forbids any foreign god.
layers.text: God reminds Israel that He alone is their God, the one who rescued them from Egypt, so they must bow to no foreign god (verse 9). He invites them to open their mouths wide and promises to fill them with all they need.

layers.evidence: Gill calls these words the preface to the Ten Commandments and says the first commandment is urged in the verse before; Barnes points to Exodus 20:2. Both verses have anokhi (I), the LORD's name and Mitsrayim (Egypt).
layers.text: "I am the LORD your God, who brought you up out of Egypt" echoes the words that open the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:2). The verse before restates the first commandment, so the psalm calls Israel back to the covenant God made with them at Sinai.

passages.saying: with honey from the rock I would satisfy you
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on verses 13 to 16, where God's gifts depend on Israel listening to Him.
layers.text: The psalm ends with what God longed to give His people if they would only listen to Him: the finest wheat and honey from the rock, the richest food of the land. Their own refusal kept these gifts from them.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch read the line as looking back to the gifts of Deuteronomy 32:13 and say God would renew the gifts of the redemption under Moses. Barnes points to Deuteronomy 32:13-14, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown links that passage's finest wheat to this verse. Both use devash (honey), chelev (fat, finest) and chittah (wheat).
layers.text: The finest wheat and honey from the rock echo the Song of Moses, which tells how God fed Israel with honey from the rock and the choicest wheat (Deuteronomy 32:13-14). God was ready to give again the rich gifts of Moses' day, if His people would listen.

passages.saying: As they pass through the Valley of Baca, they make it a place of springs
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on verses 5 to 7, which describe pilgrims on the road to God in Zion.
layers.text: Pilgrims whose hearts are set on going up to God in Zion pass through a dry, barren valley, yet for them it becomes a place of springs, and the autumn rain covers it with pools. Their hope in God turns hard country into refreshment.

layers.evidence: Barnes says Baca means weeping and is also a tree named for its weeping drops; Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible read it as weeping, the latter noting that all the ancient versions do. Keil and Delitzsch take it as a tree name, since the usual words for weeping differ, so the link is one of sound.
layers.text: Baca sounds like the Hebrew word for weeping, and the ancient translations call it the valley of weeping. The pilgrims' faith turns this valley of tears into a place of springs, a picture of sorrow changed into refreshment on the way to God.

passages.saying: a compassionate and gracious God, slow to anger
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the contrast with the enemies of verse 14 and the prayer of verse 16.
layers.text: Facing proud and ruthless men who seek his life (verse 14), the psalmist rests on who God is: compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, and rich in loving devotion and faithfulness. On that ground he asks God to turn to him and save him (verse 16).

layers.evidence: Gill says these words refer to Exodus 34:6; Keil and Delitzsch say the psalmist supports his prayer with the LORD's testimony about Himself there; the Companion Bible also compares it. Both verses use rachum (compassionate), channun (gracious), erekh appayim (slow to anger), chesed and emet.
layers.text: These words repeat what the LORD proclaimed about Himself when He passed before Moses on Mount Sinai (Exodus 34:6). The psalmist prays God's own description of Himself back to Him and builds his plea for help on it.

passages.saying: I will mention Rahab and Babylon among those who know Me
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself, which names foreign nations as those who know the LORD and as born in Zion.
layers.text: God names foreign nations, among them old enemies such as Egypt and Babylon, as people who know Him. Of each one it will be said that it was born in Zion, as though it had become a citizen of God's own city.

layers.evidence: Barnes, Wesley, the Companion Bible and Bullinger's Figures of Speech all explain Rahab here as a name for Egypt meaning pride or haughtiness. Gill and the Companion Bible note that it is a different Hebrew word from the name of Rahab of Jericho.
layers.text: Rahab here is a poetic name for Egypt. The Hebrew word rahav means pride or arrogance, a fitting name for the proud nation that once enslaved Israel. In Hebrew it is spelled differently from the name of Rahab of Jericho, though the two look alike in English.

passages.saying: I have made a covenant with My chosen one
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and the next one, where God states the covenant and oath He gave to David.
layers.text: The psalmist recalls God's own words: He made a covenant with David, His chosen servant, and swore to him that David's offspring and throne would last for all generations.

layers.evidence: Barnes and JFB point to 2 Samuel 7:11-16 as the promise meant, Keil and Delitzsch call these lines the sum of the promises in 2 Samuel 7, and the Companion Bible notes that 2 Samuel 7 gives the terms of the oath without the word swear.
layers.text: God's sworn covenant with David looks back to Nathan's promise in 2 Samuel 7. Both passages promise David's offspring (zera) and throne (kisse), and both use the verb kun, establish, for God making them last forever. That chapter never says swear, but the psalm treats the promise as an oath.

passages.saying: You crushed Rahab like a carcass
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself, which praises the strength of God's arm against His enemies.
layers.text: The psalmist praises God's power. He crushed Rahab, a name for Egypt, as easily as a dead body is trampled, and He scattered His enemies with His strong arm.

layers.evidence: Gill, Barnes and Keil and Delitzsch all take Rahab as Egypt and the crushing as God's work at the Exodus and the Red Sea. Gill adds that Israel saw the Egyptians lying dead on the shore.
layers.text: The crushing of Rahab looks back to the Exodus, when God broke Pharaoh's army in the Red Sea. Afterward "Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the shore" (Exodus 14:30), like the slain body the psalm describes.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Figures of Speech says Egypt is called Rahab because of its pride, and Gill says Rahab signifies the proud and insolent one.

cites.at: E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech Used in the Bible (1898), Polyonymia (Many Names)

layers.text: The name Rahab means pride or arrogance. Calling Egypt by this name shows the proud power that defied God and enslaved His people lying crushed before Him.

passages.saying: I will attend to their transgression with the rod
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on verses 30 to 33, where God speaks of disciplining David's sons without withdrawing His love.
layers.text: If David's sons forsake God's law, He will punish their sin with the rod and with blows. Yet the next verse promises that He will not take away His loving devotion from David.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call verses 30 to 33 a paraphrase of 2 Samuel 7:14. Gill reads the rod as the rod of men, as in 2 Samuel 7:14, and the Companion Bible says to compare 2 Samuel 7:14. Both verses pair shevet, rod, with nega, blow.
layers.text: These words repeat God's promise about David's son in 2 Samuel 7:14, where He said He would discipline him with the rod of men and with blows. Both verses use the same Hebrew pair, shevet (rod) and nega (blow or stroke).

passages.saying: Lord, You have been our dwelling place through all generations
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself, which confesses God as His people's dwelling place in every generation.
layers.text: Moses' prayer opens by confessing that in every generation the Lord Himself has been the true home and refuge of His people, even when they had no settled home of their own.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call the word dwelling place here Deuteronomic and point to Deuteronomy 33:27, and JFB also refers it to Deuteronomy 33:27. The psalm has ma'on; Moses' blessing has me'onah, a form of the same word.
layers.text: This prayer of Moses calls the Lord our dwelling place (ma'on). Moses' blessing on Israel uses a form of the same word: "The eternal God is your dwelling place" (Deuteronomy 33:27). Both picture God Himself as His people's home.

passages.saying: You return man to dust
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself, which sets man's return to dust against God's eternity in the verses around it.
layers.text: Unlike the eternal God, people do not last. At His word they die and return to dust, generation after generation.
