layers.evidence: JFB, Gill, Wesley and Barnes all tie this verse to God's sentence on Adam in Genesis 3:19. Both verses use the verb shuv, return, and Gill and the Companion Bible note that the psalm says sons of Adam.
layers.text: This echoes God's sentence on Adam: "For dust you are, and to dust you shall return" (Genesis 3:19). Both verses use the verb shuv, return, and the psalm calls people sons of adam, the word that is also Adam's name.

passages.saying: do not harden your hearts as you did at Meribah
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse itself, which warns against repeating Israel's unbelief in the wilderness.
layers.text: God warns His people not to make their hearts stubborn and unbelieving, as their ancestors did in the wilderness when they quarreled with Him and put Him to the test.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke and JFB explain Meribah as named for Israel's contention and Massah for their tempting of God, as told in Exodus 17:7. Barnes notes the same two names there.
layers.text: Meribah means quarrel and Massah means testing. Moses gave the place these names because the Israelites quarreled (riv) and tested (nasah) the LORD there (Exodus 17:7). The psalm uses the names to recall that sin.

passages.saying: They shall never enter My rest
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse and its setting in the wilderness wanderings described in the verses before it.
layers.text: Because that generation kept rebelling, God swore in His anger that they would not enter the rest He had promised, the land of Canaan.

layers.evidence: Gill says the form of the oath was "as truly as I live" and points to Numbers 14:21. JFB says the Hebrew reads literally "if they", part of the form of swearing, and compares Numbers 14:30. In both verses the oath is im (if) with bo (enter).
layers.text: This oath looks back to Numbers 14. There the LORD swore, "As surely as I live," that the grumbling generation would die in the wilderness and not enter the land, except Caleb and Joshua. Both oaths use the same Hebrew form, im (if) with bo (enter), a way of swearing they will never enter.

passages.saying: all the gods of the nations are idols
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes explains that the gods of the nations are mere idols with no real existence as gods.
layers.text: The gods the other nations worship are worthless idols, with no real existence as gods. The LORD is the true God, for He is the One who made the heavens.

layers.evidence: Bullinger marks a paronomasia (a play on similar-sounding words) here in both the Companion Bible and Figures of Speech, and Adam Clarke says that instead of being Elohim they are elilim. Keil and Delitzsch derive elilim from the Hebrew word for not.

cites.at: E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech Used in the Bible (1898), Paronomasia (Rhyming-Words)

layers.text: In Hebrew the gods (elohim) of the nations are idols (elilim). Elilim means nothings or worthless things, and it sounds like elohim. The line may mock the idols: people call them elohim, but they are really elilim.

passages.saying: He made known His ways to Moses
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes explains the verse as another ground of praise: God revealed His will to Moses and acted on behalf of Israel.
layers.text: God revealed His ways to Moses and showed His mighty acts to the people of Israel. This is one more reason the psalmist calls on his soul to bless the LORD.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the psalmist has Moses' prayer of Exodus 33:13 in mind and that the confession in verse 8 is drawn from Exodus 34:6; Gill also ties the verse to Exodus 33:13. Both verses use the same verb, make known (yada), and the same noun, ways (derekh).
layers.text: This recalls Moses' prayer at Sinai, "please let me know Your ways" (Exodus 33:13). God answered by passing before Moses and proclaiming His name, and the next verse of the psalm repeats His words: "compassionate and gracious, slow to anger" (Exodus 34:6).

passages.saying: He knows our frame; He is mindful that we are dust
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes explains that God knows we are made of dust and frail, and gives this as the reason He pities us.
layers.text: God knows how we are made and remembers that we are only dust. Because He knows how frail we are, He has compassion on those who fear Him, as a father has on his children.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch tie our frame to the form man has from God the Creator in Genesis 2:7, and Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and the Companion Bible all point the word dust back to Genesis 2:7. Frame (yetser) comes from the verb formed (yatsar), and dust (aphar) is the same word in both verses.
layers.text: Our frame (yetser) is the form God gave us, from the verb yatsar, to form. With dust (aphar) it looks back to the moment when "the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground" (Genesis 2:7). The One who made us from dust remembers how frail we are.

passages.saying: You covered it with the deep like a garment
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes explains that God covered the earth with the waters of the deep as if a garment had been spread over it.
layers.text: God covered the earth with deep waters as if He were spreading a garment over it, so that the waters stood even above the mountains.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke and Barnes all read this as the waters that covered the earth at creation (Genesis 1:2); Barnes notes that tehom is the same Hebrew word and points to Genesis 1:9. Wesley and Keil and Delitzsch agree. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown instead reads these verses as the Flood.
layers.text: The deep (tehom) is the same word as in Genesis 1:2, where "darkness was over the surface of the deep." The psalm retells creation: at God's rebuke the waters fled to their place and dry land appeared, as when God gathered the waters into one place (Genesis 1:9).

passages.saying: You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Barnes explains that he would be a priest after the manner of Melchizedek, not from the tribe of Levi, and points to Hebrews 5 to 7.
layers.text: God has sworn an oath He will not take back: the King whom David calls my Lord will be a priest forever, a priest like Melchizedek rather than from the tribe of Levi. The letter to the Hebrews applies this to Jesus Christ.

layers.evidence: Gill notes that Melchizedek is mentioned only in Genesis 14:18 and Hebrews; Barnes says this priest would resemble Melchizedek in uniting priest and king; Keil and Delitzsch say the priesthood is joined to the kingship as it was in Melchizedek. Both verses use kohen, priest: Genesis of Melchizedek, the psalm of the King.
layers.text: This reaches back to Genesis 14:18, the only earlier mention of Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, who brought bread and wine to Abram. Like him, the promised King will be both king and priest, and His priesthood will last forever.

layers.evidence: Gill says the meaning of his name, King of righteousness and King of peace, agrees with Christ; Clarke explains that salem signifies peace and tsedek righteousness. Hebrews 7:2 gives the same meanings.
layers.text: Melchizedek joins malki, king, with tsedek, righteousness, so his name means king of righteousness. He ruled Salem, which means peace. Hebrews 7:2 draws out both meanings, and both fit the Messiah, the righteous King who brings peace.

passages.saying: He raises the poor from the dust
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse, which Barnes explains as God raising the lowly to honor.
layers.text: God lifts up people from the lowest places in life, the poor in the dust and the needy on the rubbish heap, and gives them honor. It is one of the reasons the psalm gives for praising Him.

layers.evidence: The Hebrew of Psalm 113:7 and 1 Samuel 2:8 is nearly identical. Keil and Delitzsch say the thoughts of verses 7 and 8 are transplanted from Hannah's song, with her own rise from sorrow in view. The Companion Bible and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cross-reference 1 Samuel 2:8, and Clarke calls verse 9 nearly the words of Hannah.
layers.text: Verses 7 and 8 repeat, almost word for word, the song Hannah sang after God gave her Samuel: "He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap" (1 Samuel 2:8). Verse 9, where a barren woman becomes a joyful mother, recalls Hannah's own story.

passages.saying: The LORD is my strength and my song
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse, as Barnes explains it.
layers.text: The psalmist says the LORD is the one who makes him strong, the one he sings about, and the one who has saved him.

layers.evidence: The Hebrew of Psalm 118:14 and Exodus 15:2 is the same word for word. Keil and Delitzsch say the verse is taken from Exodus 15:2, and Gill says the psalmist borrowed these words from the song of Moses. The Companion Bible and Bullinger's Figures of Speech also point to Exodus 15:2.
layers.text: This line comes from the song Moses and Israel sang after crossing the Red Sea (Exodus 15:2). The Hebrew is the same word for word, so a later rescue is praised in the very words Israel sang at the Red Sea.

passages.saying: Pray for the peace of Jerusalem
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse, which Barnes explains as a prayer for the city's welfare.
layers.text: Pilgrims are urged to pray for Jerusalem's peace and welfare, asking that those who love the city may prosper.

layers.evidence: Clarke notes a remarkable alliteration with the letter shin; Keil and Delitzsch say the words for prosper and prosperity alliterate with shalom and accord with the name of Jerusalem; the Companion Bible and Bullinger's Figures of Speech list it as Paronomasia.
layers.text: In Hebrew this prayer is full of sh and l sounds: pray (sha'alu) for the peace (shalom) of Jerusalem (Yerushalayim), may they prosper (yishlayu). Verse 7 adds peace (shalom) and prosperity (shalvah). Each word echoes the sound of the city's own name.

passages.saying: Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse, which Barnes explains as our dependence on God in every undertaking.
layers.text: Building a house or guarding a city is wasted effort unless the LORD Himself does the work. Every human undertaking depends on Him.

layers.evidence: Clarke says ben (son) and bath (daughter) come from banah, to build, because sons and daughters build up a household, and that building a house can mean having many children. Gill likewise reads the house as a family built up by children, as verse 3 goes on to say.
layers.text: In Hebrew, build (banah) and sons (banim) sound alike, and a family can be called a house that children build up (Ruth 4:11). So the house the LORD must build in verse 1 can also mean a family, which leads into the sons He gives in verse 3.

passages.saying: we found it in the fields of Jaar
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the psalm's setting: the search for a worthy dwelling for the ark in verses 5 to 8.
layers.text: The singers remember the search for the ark of the covenant. They heard of it at Ephrathah and found it in the fields of Jaar, where it had long been left, before it was brought up to a fitting dwelling place for the LORD.

layers.evidence: Gill and Wesley say Kiriath-jearim signifies city of woods, and JFB glosses it the same way; Keil and Delitzsch take Jaar as a short, poetic name for that town. Clarke and Bullinger's Companion Bible also read Jaar as Kiriath-jearim. Jaar is ya'ar, forest; Kiriath-jearim is qiryat ye'arim.
layers.text: Jaar means forest. It is a short name for Kiriath-jearim, which means city of forests, the wooded town where the ark remained a long time (1 Samuel 7:1-2) until David brought it up to Jerusalem.

passages.saying: Arise, O LORD, to Your resting place
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the ark as the sign of God's presence and on the settled place prepared for it.
layers.text: The people ask the LORD to go up, with the ark that stood for His mighty presence, into the resting place prepared for Him, a settled home where the ark would no longer be moved from place to place.

layers.evidence: Bullinger's Companion Bible says the cry Arise, LORD is according to Numbers 10:35, and his note on Psalm 68:1 calls those words the formula used when the ark set out. Both verses use qum (arise) with the ark (aron).
layers.text: The cry Arise, O LORD may take up the words Moses spoke whenever the ark set out in the wilderness: “Rise up, O LORD! May Your enemies be scattered” (Numbers 10:35). Now the ark that traveled with Israel is asked to go up to its resting place.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Barnes, JFB and Bullinger's Companion Bible all note that Solomon used these words at the dedication of the temple (2 Chronicles 6:41). Both verses share arise (qum), ark (aron) and strength (oz).
layers.text: Almost the same words close Solomon's prayer at the dedication of the temple: “arise, O LORD God, and enter Your resting place, You and the ark of Your might” (2 Chronicles 6:41).

passages.saying: It is like fine oil on the head
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the comparison of brotherly unity with the holy anointing oil.
layers.text: The joy of God's people living together in unity is like the fragrant anointing oil poured so richly on the high priest's head that it ran down his beard to the collar of his robes.

layers.evidence: Gill (citing Exodus 29:7), Wesley, and Keil and Delitzsch (citing Leviticus 8:12) all tie the oil to the anointing poured on Aaron's head when he was consecrated; Barnes and Bullinger's Companion Bible agree. Both verses name oil (shemen), head (rosh) and Aaron.
layers.text: The picture recalls the day Aaron was consecrated as high priest, when Moses poured the holy anointing oil on his head (Leviticus 8:12; Exodus 29:7). Unity among God's people is as precious and holy as that oil, flowing from his head down his beard to the collar of his robe.

passages.saying: May my prayer be set before You like incense
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the comparison of prayer with the incense and offerings of the sanctuary.
layers.text: David asks God to receive his prayer as pleasing incense rising before Him, and his hands lifted up in prayer as an evening offering at the sanctuary.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch identify the evening offering (minchah) with the grain offering added to the daily evening lamb in Exodus 29:38-42; Gill gives this as one reading, citing Exodus 29:38; Clarke reads the word as the minchah that went with the evening burnt offering. Both verses use minchah (offering) and erev (evening).
layers.text: The evening offering is the grain offering that went with the lamb offered every day at twilight (Exodus 29:38-41), closing the day's worship. David asks God to accept his hands lifted in prayer like that daily offering.

passages.saying: O LORD, what is man, that You regard him
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the wonder at God's care for frail man, set beside verse 4.
layers.text: David marvels that the LORD should take notice of man at all and give him a thought, since man is weak and his days pass like a shadow.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call the verse a variation of Psalm 8:4 (8:5 in Hebrew) with other verbs; Barnes says the thought is the same; Gill, Clarke and Bullinger's Companion Bible point to Psalm 8:4. Both verses use mah (what) with adam and enosh (man), the two words in swapped order.
layers.text: The psalm takes up the question of Psalm 8:4, “what is man that You are mindful of him,” with different verbs: here God knows man and takes account of him. In Psalm 8 the wonder rises from the vast heavens; here it rises from man's frailty, as verse 4 shows.

passages.saying: let us swallow them alive like Sheol
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the robbers' boast in verses 11 to 14.
layers.text: A father warns his son against robbers who invite him to join their ambush. They boast that they will destroy their victims suddenly and completely, as the grave swallows up the living.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call swallowing them alive an allusion, in fact and in expression, to the fate of Korah's company (Numbers 16:30, 33), and JFB cites Numbers 16:33. Both verses use bala (swallow), chay (alive) and Sheol.
layers.text: The boast echoes the judgment on Korah's company, when the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the rebels so that they went down alive into Sheol (Numbers 16:30-33). The robbers want their victims to vanish just as completely, leaving no trace.

passages.saying: when distress and anguish overwhelm you
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's storm and whirlwind pictures of sudden judgment.
layers.text: Wisdom warns that those who refuse her will be overtaken by sudden ruin. Dread will come on them like a storm and disaster like a whirlwind, with distress and anguish pressing in.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call tsarah and tsuqah alliterating words, meaning narrowness and distress, and note that Proverbs is fond of such sound-rhymes.
layers.text: Distress and anguish renders two Hebrew words that open with the same sound, tsa-rah and tsu-qah. The first pictures a narrow, cramped place and the second pressing distress; some hear the matching sounds as driving the warning home.

passages.saying: do not reject the discipline of the LORD
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the meaning of musar, discipline that corrects and instructs.
layers.text: A father urges his son not to reject the LORD's discipline or resent His correction. The hard things God sends to correct His children are meant to teach and train them.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call Job 5:17 the original passage behind these verses and say Proverbs borrows its thought. Both lines join musar (discipline) with al tim'as (do not reject). Gill, Barnes and JFB also point to Job 5:17.
layers.text: In Hebrew this line uses the same key words as Eliphaz's counsel to Job: "so do not despise the discipline of the Almighty" (Job 5:17). Proverbs takes up that truth and adds why: the LORD disciplines as a father who loves his son.

passages.saying: as does a father the son in whom he delights
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's comparison of the LORD to a loving father.
layers.text: The LORD's correction is a sign of His love. He disciplines those He loves, just as a father corrects the son who is his delight.

layers.evidence: Gill explains the verse in the words of Deuteronomy 8:5 and points the reader to it. Both verses picture the LORD as a father disciplining a son (ben).
layers.text: The picture of the LORD correcting His people as a father corrects his son may echo Moses' words to Israel in the wilderness: "just as a man disciplines his son, so the LORD your God disciplines you" (Deuteronomy 8:5).

passages.saying: She is a tree of life to those who embrace her
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's tree of life picture and its promise of blessing.
layers.text: Wisdom gives life to those who hold on to her. Those who embrace her and keep hold of her are truly blessed.

layers.evidence: Clarke, Keil and Delitzsch, Wesley, Gill, Barnes and JFB all link this to the tree of life in Eden. Both verses use the phrase ets chayyim, tree of life.
layers.text: Wisdom is called a tree of life, the same Hebrew phrase used for the tree in the middle of Eden (Genesis 2:9). The life that was lost when man was shut out from that tree is offered again to all who take hold of God's wisdom.

passages.saying: Bind them always upon your heart
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's picture of binding and tying the teaching.
layers.text: A son is told to keep his parents' godly teaching close at all times, as if it were tied to his heart and worn around his neck.

layers.evidence: Gill sees an allusion to the law's command to bind God's words on head and arm, and Clarke names Deuteronomy 6:6-8 as the command alluded to. Keil and Delitzsch say the figure recalls the tefillin, the scripture boxes bound on hand and forehead. Both verses use qashar, to bind.
layers.text: Binding the teaching on the heart echoes Moses' command about God's words: keep them on your heart and bind them on your hand and forehead (Deuteronomy 6:6-8). The proverb uses the same verb, bind, and ties the parents' teaching to the heart itself, to be kept there always.

passages.saying: When you walk, they will guide you
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's three scenes of walking, sleeping and waking.
layers.text: The godly teaching a son keeps will go with him everywhere. It guides him on the road, guards him in his sleep, and speaks to him when he wakes.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch note that going, lying down and rising up come in the same order as in the Shema at Deuteronomy 6:7. Both verses use halakh (walk) and shakhav (lie down).
layers.text: Walking, lying down and waking come in the same order as in Moses' command to talk of God's words "when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up" (Deuteronomy 6:7). The verse seems to draw its picture from that command.

passages.saying: Tie them to your fingers
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's pictures of tying and writing.
layers.text: The son is told to keep wisdom's teaching always at hand and deep within, as close as something tied to his fingers and as lasting as writing on his heart.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch explain binding on the fingers by the hand tefillin, the scripture boxes worn on the hand in keeping with Deuteronomy 6:8. The Companion Bible sets Deuteronomy 6:8 beside the verse. Both verses use qashar, to bind.
layers.text: Tying the teaching to the fingers recalls Moses' command about God's words: "Tie them as reminders on your hands" (Deuteronomy 6:8). The son is to keep wisdom's teaching just as close, bound to his fingers and written on his heart.

passages.saying: I hate arrogant pride, evil conduct, and perverse speech
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own definition of the fear of the LORD.
layers.text: Wisdom says that to fear the LORD is to hate evil. She hates pride, wicked ways and twisted speech.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call ge'ah vega'on a paronomasia that expresses pride in its whole compass, and Gill notes that the two Hebrew words are very much the same.
layers.text: Arrogant pride translates two Hebrew words that sound almost alike, ge-ah and ga-on, both meaning pride. Pairing them sweeps in pride of every kind, the first thing Wisdom names among the things she hates.

passages.saying: Then I was a skilled craftsman at His side, and His delight day by day, rejoicing always in His presence.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB and its footnotes, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, the Septuagint, the Wisdom of Solomon, Athanasius, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Wisdom is pictured as a woman calling out "beside the gates to the city." She says she was with God before creation, "I was there when He established the heavens," and promises, "whoever finds me finds life."

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Proverbs 8:22: two Hebrew roots qanah, to possess and to create (Genesis 14:19; Deuteronomy 32:6). BSB footnote: or possessed. Athanasius, Discourse II Against the Arians 1 and 11.

cites.at: Athanasius, Discourse II Against the Arians 1

layers.text: "The LORD created me" uses qanah, which can mean "to possess" or "to create," as when God is "Creator of heaven and earth." Arius read "created" to make the Son a creature; Athanasius said it speaks of the Word becoming man. Both read Wisdom as the Son.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Proverbs 8:30: master craftsman or nursing child; craftsman has the most support (Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac). TBESH: amon, skilled workman; sachaq, to laugh, play.
layers.text: "Skilled craftsman" is amon, a rare word: "master craftsman" or "nursing child." A child fits Wisdom being "brought forth," but craftsman has more support. "Rejoicing" is sachaq, "to laugh, play": Wisdom delights before God and "in the sons of men."

layers.evidence: Septuagint (Rahlfs) of Proverbs 8:23: en archē. Benson, Gill and Poole on John 1:1 point to Proverbs 8.
layers.text: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God" recalls Genesis 1 and also Wisdom, at God's side "from the beginning, before the earth began." The Greek of 8:23 even has John's opening words, en archē. But John goes further: "the Word was God."

layers.evidence: TAGNT: apaugasma occurs in the New Testament only at Hebrews 1:3. TBESG (Abbott-Smith) G0541: in the Septuagint only at Wisdom of Solomon 7:26, a book not in the Hebrew Bible, where Wisdom is the apaugasma of eternal light and the eikōn of God's goodness. Ellicott, Gill and JFB on Hebrews 1:3 compare it; JFB and Gill also point to Colossians 1:15.
layers.text: Hebrews calls the Son "the radiance of God’s glory." The Greek Old Testament has that word only in the Wisdom of Solomon, a book outside the Hebrew Bible: Wisdom is the radiance of eternal light and image of God's goodness. Paul calls the Son God's "image."

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary on Luke 11:49: He identifies Himself with the Wisdom of God; Barnes and Gill agree. Gill notes some have thought a lost book of that name is cited; Ellicott finds no trace of one.
layers.text: Paul calls Christ "the power of God and the wisdom of God." In Luke, Jesus quotes "the wisdom of God": "I will send them prophets and apostles." In Matthew He says it in His own voice: "I am sending you prophets." Many hear Him speaking as God's Wisdom.

passages.saying: Dishonest scales are an abomination to the LORD
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the contrast between dishonest scales and an accurate weight.
layers.text: God hates cheating in trade with rigged scales, but an honest weight pleases Him. Fair dealing in buying and selling matters to the LORD.

layers.evidence: Barnes calls the proverb an emphatic reproduction of the old rule of Deuteronomy 25:13-14; Clarke points to the law in Deuteronomy 25:13-16; the Companion Bible compares Leviticus 19:36 and Deuteronomy 25:13-15. Both verses say even shelemah, a full weight.
layers.text: This proverb repeats the Law of Moses. Deuteronomy 25:13-16 forbids keeping two different weights, demands a full and honest weight (even shelemah, the same words as the accurate weight here), and says the LORD hates those who cheat.

passages.saying: A man of many companions may come to ruin
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the contrast between many companions and one loyal friend.
layers.text: Having many so-called friends can bring a person to ruin. What really counts is one true friend whose loyalty is stronger even than family ties.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible and Bullinger's Figures of Speech both name a paronomasia between re'im, friends, and lehitro'ea, from the root meaning to break. Keil and Delitzsch take the verb from the root meaning to become brittle and note its alliteration with re'im.

cites.at: E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech Used in the Bible (1898), Paronomasia (Rhyming-Words)

layers.text: In Hebrew, companions are re'im and come to ruin is hitro'ea, which some take from a root meaning to be broken in pieces. The words sound alike: the many friends a man gathers may be the very ones who break him. Against them stands "a friend who stays closer than a brother."

passages.saying: To do righteousness and justice is more desirable to the LORD than sacrifice
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The verse sets right living beside offerings and ranks right living higher.
layers.text: God is more pleased when people do what is right and fair than when they offer sacrifices. Religious acts cannot make up for a life of wrongdoing.

layers.evidence: Clarke calls this verse the words of Samuel to Saul; Gill points to 1 Samuel 15:22 for the same teaching that moral duty is preferred to ceremonial sacrifice. Both verses use the same Hebrew word for sacrifice (zevach).
layers.text: This proverb echoes the prophet Samuel's rebuke of King Saul, who disobeyed God and then pointed to sacrifices he planned to offer. Samuel answered that "obedience is better than sacrifice." Doing what God asks matters more to Him than ritual.

passages.saying: Do not move an ancient boundary stone
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Boundary stones marked where one family's land ended and the next began.
layers.text: Do not shift the old stones that mark the edge of a neighbor's land. Moving them quietly was a way to steal part of someone else's field and inheritance.

layers.evidence: Clarke says these words of Solomon appear to be taken from Deuteronomy 19:14; Gill says moving a landmark broke that law. Both verses use the same Hebrew verb for move (nasag) and noun for boundary (gevul).
layers.text: This proverb repeats a command from the Law of Moses. There God forbade Israel to move a neighbor's boundary marker, set up by earlier generations to mark each family's share of the land He gave them.

passages.saying: Wisdom is too high for a fool
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The city gate was where elders met to judge and give counsel.
layers.text: Wisdom is out of a fool's reach. So when the leaders meet at the town gate to judge and give advice, he has nothing worth saying and keeps quiet.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say the poet probably chose this word for its double meaning: high things, and the costly gem named in Job 28:18. The Companion Bible likewise reads it as coral, a costly ornament the fool cannot reach.
layers.text: The Hebrew word for too high (ramot) is spelled here like ra'mot, a precious gem such as coral (Job 28:18). Both senses fit: to a fool, wisdom is out of reach and also too costly to be worth the effort of getting it.

passages.saying: If you faint in the day of distress, how small is your strength!
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Trouble tests strength, and giving up shows how little there was.
layers.text: If you give up as soon as trouble comes, your strength was small to begin with. Hard times show how strong a person really is.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch name a paronomasia between tsarah (distress) and tsar (narrow, small). Jamieson-Fausset-Brown bring it out literally: in the day of straits, strait is thy strength. Clarke notes that tsar means contracted.
layers.text: In Hebrew, distress (tsarah) and small (tsar) share the idea of being narrow or tight. The proverb plays on this: if you give way on a tight day, your strength turns out to be tight and small as well.

passages.saying: Do not answer a fool according to his folly
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: The warning is against arguing in the fool's own foolish manner.
layers.text: Do not reply to a fool by sinking to his level, with angry or insulting talk. If you do, you become a fool just like him.

layers.evidence: Barnes explains that the phrase means stooping to the fool's level in verse 4 but giving the fitting reply in verse 5. Keil and Delitzsch say that the second time it means as is due to his folly. Wesley's notes give the same two senses: imitating his folly, then answering as his folly requires.
layers.text: Verses 4 and 5 use the same words in two senses. Do not answer a fool by copying his foolish ways, or you become like him. Yet "answer a fool according to his folly," meaning as his folly deserves, so he does not think himself wise.

passages.saying: These are the words of Agur son of Jakeh
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's own title line; the speaker is otherwise unknown.
layers.text: These are the opening words of Agur son of Jakeh, a wise man known to us only from this chapter. He calls his words a burden, a weighty message, and begins by confessing to God that he is weary and worn out.

layers.evidence: Gill gives Ithiel as God with me, the Companion Bible as El is with me, Clarke as him who is God with me, and Keil-Delitzsch as perhaps God is with me. Keil-Delitzsch say that with changed vowels the letters read as a confession, I have wearied myself, O God, and Barnes gives the same reading.
layers.text: The name Ithiel means God is with me. With different vowels, the same Hebrew letters can also be read as a short sentence: I am weary, O God. This translation keeps the name the first time it appears and reads the sentence the second time.

passages.saying: Every word of God is flawless
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the image of refining metal in the Hebrew word for pure or refined.
layers.text: Everything God has said is pure and true, like metal refined in a furnace until no impurity is left. God Himself protects, like a shield, everyone who runs to Him for safety.

layers.evidence: Keil-Delitzsch say this proverb depends on Psalm 18 (their 18:31, English 18:30) and 2 Samuel 22:31 and is borrowed from it, with the name of God changed to Eloah. The Hebrew words for word, refined, shield and take refuge match.
layers.text: This line may echo David's song in Psalm 18:30 (also 2 Samuel 22:31): "the word of the LORD is flawless. He is a shield to all who take refuge in Him." The Hebrew words for word, flawless (literally refined) and shield are the same, but here God is called Eloah instead of the LORD.

passages.saying: Do not add to His words
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain warning against adding to God's words.
layers.text: No one should add their own ideas to what God has said. Anyone who does will be rebuked by God, and the additions will be shown to be false, proving that person a liar.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible calls this a solemn warning based on Deuteronomy 4:2. Keil-Delitzsch tie it to Deuteronomy 4:2 and say that precept is revived here and enforced again in Revelation 22:18-19. Both use the verb yasaph, to add.
layers.text: Do not add to His words repeats the warning Moses gave with the Law: You must not add to or subtract from what I command you (Deuteronomy 4:2). The same Hebrew verb for adding is used, and the same warning comes again at the close of the Bible in Revelation 22:18.

passages.saying: These are the words of the Teacher, the son of David
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the title line naming the son of David who reigned in Jerusalem.
layers.text: The book opens by naming its speaker: the Teacher, a son of David who was king in Jerusalem. This points to Solomon, who near the end of his life wrote down what he had learned for the benefit of others.

layers.evidence: Clarke derives Qoheleth from qahal, to gather or assemble, and notes the Septuagint's ekklesiastes, a speaker in an assembly. Barnes renders it Convener, one calling an assembly together to address it.
layers.text: Teacher translates Qoheleth, from qahal, to assemble: one who calls people together to address them. The Greek title Ecclesiastes, a speaker in an assembly, carries the same idea. The king gathers hearers so that he may teach them wisdom.

passages.saying: When you make a vow to God, do not delay in fulfilling it
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse, which commands prompt payment of vows made to God.
layers.text: A vow made to God must be kept, and kept without delay. God takes no pleasure in fools who make rash promises to Him and then put them off or forget them. Whatever you have vowed, pay it.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch say this passage on vows is, in thought and expression, the echo of Deuteronomy 23:21-23 (23:22-24 in Hebrew numbering), and compare the wording phrase by phrase. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown also point verse 5 to Deuteronomy 23:21 and 23.
layers.text: Some hear in this command an almost word-for-word echo of the Law of Moses: "If you make a vow to the LORD your God, do not be slow to keep it" (Deuteronomy 23:21). The Law also said that choosing not to vow is no sin, and the next verse here may echo that.

passages.saying: so he will depart again, naked as he arrived
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's plain comparison between birth and death.
layers.text: People come into the world with nothing and leave it the same way. However much a person gains by his work, he cannot carry any of it with him when he dies.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call this verse a reminiscence from Job 1:21, noting that it leaves out Job's harder word 'thither'. Gill and the Companion Bible also point to Job 1:21.
layers.text: This verse may echo Job's words after he lost everything: "Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I will return" (Job 1:21). The rich man, like Job, leaves the world as bare as he entered it, and none of his wealth goes with him.

passages.saying: Whatever exists was named long ago
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's statements about what was named and known long ago, and the One stronger than man.
layers.text: Everything that exists was settled and named by God long ago, and what man is, and what will happen to him, was known beforehand. Man is only a creature, so he cannot argue with God, who is far stronger than he.

layers.evidence: Gill says God called the first man Adam from adamah, the earth he was taken from. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say the Hebrew Adam means man of red dust, a name his Creator gave him for his frailty. Wesley likewise says God named man to show his mortal condition.
layers.text: The word for man here is adam. Some read the verse as pointing to that name: God called the first man Adam, from adamah, the ground he was taken from. His very name tells what he is, an earthly and frail creature, so he cannot argue with God, who is stronger than he.

passages.saying: A good name is better than fine perfume
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.evidence: Readers take the startling line in more than one way. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown and the Pulpit Commentary tie it to the first half: death is better for one who has a good name. Keil and Delitzsch hear the same lament as Ecclesiastes 4:2. The verse does not explain itself.
layers.text: The Teacher sets a good name above costly perfume, then says something startling: "one’s day of death is better than his day of birth." He explains that "death is the end of every man," and the living should take it to heart.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: shem, name (H8034), and shemen, oil (H8081), side by side, each with tov, good. The BSB renders shemen here as perfume. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown, Keil and Delitzsch, Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary all note the sound-play; Gill adds that a good name is more lasting.
layers.text: The proverb is a sound-play: tov shem mishshemen tov, a good name (shem) is better than good oil (shemen). Perfume was scented oil and costly, yet a good name is worth more. Many add that a name lasts when the scent is gone.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: shemen (H8081) and shemekha, your name (H8034), two words apart in Song of Solomon 1:3: shemen turaq shemekha, oil poured out is your name. The verse begins lereach shemanekha tovim, the fragrance of your oils is good, so tov, shemen and shem all meet here, as in Ecclesiastes 7:1.
layers.text: The Song of Solomon makes the same pun as praise: "your name is like perfume poured out." In Hebrew it is shemen, then shemekha, "your name." The two words sound so alike that Scripture pairs them twice, here and in Ecclesiastes 7:1.

passages.saying: like the crackling of thorns under the pot
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's simile of a quick thorn fire under a cooking pot.
layers.text: A fool's laughter is like a fire of thorns under a cooking pot: loud and crackling for a moment, then quickly gone. It makes much noise but does no real good.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown note a paronomasia in the Hebrew, sirim (thorns) and sir (pot). The Companion Bible names the figure Paronomasia, hassirim and hassir, and suggests nettles and kettles in English. Keil and Delitzsch copy the pun in German as Nessel and Kessel.
layers.text: In Hebrew, thorns are sirim and the pot is sir, two words that sound almost alike, as if English said nettles under the kettle. A thorn fire crackles loudly but soon burns out without cooking the meal. A fool's laughter is just as loud and just as empty.

passages.saying: there is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's plain statement that no one on earth is free from sin.
layers.text: No one on earth, not even the most righteous person, always does good and never sins. Everyone falls short and needs God's mercy.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call 1 Kings 8:46, in Solomon's prayer at the temple's dedication, the original and briefer form of this saying. Bullinger's Figures of Speech says that line became a proverb for its great truth and lists this verse among its uses. Gill also points to 1 Kings 8:46.

cites.at: E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech Used in the Bible (1898), Parœmia (Proverb)

layers.text: Solomon said nearly the same thing in his prayer at the dedication of the temple: "there is no one who does not sin" (1 Kings 8:46). Here that truth returns as a settled saying: even the best person on earth still sins.

layers.evidence: The Companion Bible says Romans 3:10-12 are taken from this verse together with Psalm 14:2-3 and 53:2-3.
layers.text: Paul begins his chain of Scriptures about sin in Romans 3:10 with "There is no one righteous, not even one." Some see his words drawing on this verse together with Psalms 14 and 53, to show that every person is a sinner before God.

passages.saying: God made men upright, but they have sought out many schemes
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's contrast between how God made man and what men have done since.
layers.text: The Teacher concludes that God made people upright, with nothing wrong in them. The evil in the world is not God's doing: people themselves turned aside and invented many ways of going wrong.

layers.evidence: Barnes calls the verse a definite allusion to the original state of man. Gill explains the uprightness by man's creation in God's image and likeness (Genesis 1:26). Wesley reads it of Adam and Eve, made upright after God's likeness, and their posterity. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown point to Genesis 2 and 3.
layers.text: This verse looks back to creation. God made man in His own image and likeness (Genesis 1:26), upright and free of sin. The many schemes came afterward, when Adam and Eve turned from God and their children followed. Sin is man's doing, not God's.

passages.saying: He who digs a pit may fall into it
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's everyday pictures of digging and of breaking through a wall.
layers.text: Ordinary work has hidden dangers. A man digging a pit may fall into it, and one breaking through a wall may be bitten by a snake hiding in its cracks. The wise person acts with care, knowing his own deeds can turn back on him.

layers.evidence: Gill calls these proverbial sayings and says the one who digs a pit for another falls into it himself, as Solomon's father David had observed in Psalm 7:15. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cite Psalm 7:15 and Proverbs 26:27. Keil and Delitzsch read this verse more as a warning of possible accidents.
layers.text: This saying echoes David in Psalm 7:15, where the wicked man digs a pit and then falls into the pit he made. Proverbs 26:27 says the same. Harm a person plans for others, or a reckless deed, can come back on the one who does it.

passages.saying: the spirit returns to God who gave it
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's two clauses, dust to the ground and spirit to God, read as body and soul parting at death.
layers.text: At death the body, made of dust, goes back to the earth it came from, and the human spirit goes back to God, who gave it in the first place. The spirit does not die with the body.

layers.evidence: Gill points to Genesis 3:19 and to the breath first given at creation; Clarke links the spirit to the breath God breathed into man's nostrils; Keil and Delitzsch cite Genesis 3:19. On Genesis 2:7 Jamieson-Fausset-Brown and Wesley cite this verse, and on Genesis 3:19 the Companion Bible links the two.
layers.text: This verse runs creation backward. God formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed life into him (Genesis 2:7), and said he would return to dust (Genesis 3:19). At death the dust goes back to the ground and the spirit to God who gave it.

passages.saying: your name is like perfume poured out
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the verse's comparison of the beloved's name to fragrant oil spread abroad.
layers.text: The bride praises her beloved. His perfumes smell sweet, and his very name, all that he is, is sweeter still, like perfume poured out to fill a room. No wonder the young women love him.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch call name and fragrance here a paronomasia that brings the comparison near Ecclesiastes 7:1. On that verse Jamieson-Fausset-Brown speak of the happy paronomasia of shem and shemen.
layers.text: In Hebrew, name (shem) and perfume (shemen) sound almost alike, so the comparison comes naturally: the beloved's name is like perfume poured out. The same pair appears in Ecclesiastes 7:1: "A good name is better than fine perfume".

passages.saying: like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the paired comparisons: dark like Kedar's tents, lovely like Solomon's curtains.
layers.text: The bride tells the women of Jerusalem that her skin is dark, yet she is lovely. She is dark like the black tents of the desert tribe of Kedar, and lovely like the rich curtains of King Solomon.

layers.evidence: Barnes says the word Kedar itself signifies dark or black, and the Companion Bible glosses Kedar as dark, adding that all Kedar's tents were black. Keil and Delitzsch think another root more likely but record the old reading from the Hebrew for being dark.
layers.text: Kedar was an Arab tribe whose tents were woven of black goat hair, and the name Kedar is taken to mean dark. So the bride who calls herself dark compares herself to tents whose very name speaks of darkness.

passages.saying: You are as beautiful, my darling, as Tirzah
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the comparison with Tirzah and Jerusalem, the leading royal cities of the north and the south.
layers.text: The king praises his bride. She is as beautiful as Tirzah and as lovely as Jerusalem, the two finest royal cities of the land, and as awe-inspiring as an army marching under its banners.

layers.evidence: Gill, Clarke, Barnes, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Keil and Delitzsch and the Companion Bible all give the name the sense pleasant, delightful or beautiful. The Companion Bible adds, hence the flattering comparison, and Gill traces it to a root meaning to be pleasing and accepted.
layers.text: Tirzah, a royal city in the north, has a name that means pleasant or delightful. So when the king says his bride is as beautiful as Tirzah, he likens her to a city whose very name is delight.

passages.saying: Come back, come back, O Shulammite!
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the fourfold call to come back and the bride's modest question in reply.
layers.text: As the bride turns to leave, she is called back again and again so that others may gaze at her beauty. She modestly asks why they would look at her, and the reply likens her to the dance of Mahanaim.

layers.evidence: Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say allusion is made to Jacob's Mahanaim, and Keil and Delitzsch read it as a look back to the angel camps of Genesis 32 (their verse 3 is the English verse 2). Barnes ties the name to that place, and Gill on Genesis 32:2 sees an allusion to it here.
layers.text: Mahanaim means two camps. Jacob gave that name to the place where God's angels met him, saying, "This is the camp of God." Calling the sight of the bride the dance of Mahanaim points back to that place and its story.

layers.evidence: Clarke calls it a feminine formed from Shelomoh, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown a feminine of Solomon, Prince of Peace. Keil and Delitzsch hold that the poet shaped it to match Solomon's name, and Gill and Wesley say she is called after her husband. Barnes and the Companion Bible link it to Shunem.
layers.text: Shulammite probably names her home town, Shulem or Shunem, but it sounds like a feminine of Solomon's name, Shelomoh. The bride bears a name that echoes her husband's, and both carry the sound of shalom, peace.

passages.saying: I belong to my beloved, and his desire is for me
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the bride's own words, which Barnes explains as all his affection having her for its object.
layers.text: The bride says she belongs wholly to her beloved, and she rests in knowing that all his love and longing are turned toward her.

layers.evidence: Adam Clarke notes that the word translated his desire is the very same as in Genesis 3:16, part of the woman's curse, and says here it seems to be reversed. Keil and Delitzsch say this line refers back to Genesis 3:16.
layers.text: The word for desire here, teshuqah, is the same rare word used in Genesis 3:16, where God tells the woman her desire will be for her husband and he will rule over her. Here the bride says his desire is for her, as if that sad line from the fall were turned around.

passages.saying: Set me as a seal over your heart, as a seal upon your arm. For love is as strong as death
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TBESH, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, the Mishnah (Joshua Kulp's translation), and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Song 8:6: the seal is a symbol of something especially dear and precious. The Pulpit Commentary: the signet ring was sometimes carried by a string on the breast, near the heart.
layers.text: The bride asks to be worn as a seal on her beloved's heart and arm, kept close as something precious. Love like this cannot be put out or bought: "Mighty waters cannot quench love; rivers cannot sweep it away." Earlier she sang, "My beloved is mine and I am his."

layers.evidence: TBESH: shalhevet, flame; Yah, a shortened form of the LORD's name. TAHOT glosses it a flame of the Lord. NET Bible notes: the Masoretes did not point it as the divine name; most likely an intensive. Ellicott: the only sacred name in the book, used as a superlative. Gill: a superlative, or a flame kindled by the Lord himself.
layers.text: "The fiercest blaze of all" is one Hebrew word, shalhevetyah: "flame" plus -yah, which may be Yah, short for God's name, its only trace in the Song. Many read it as a way of saying mightiest, as the BSB does; others hear a flame kindled by God.

layers.evidence: Jamieson, Fausset and Brown: the Jews explain the Song of the union of Jehovah and ancient Israel; the Targum on the Song reads it that way. Gill: the ancient Jews called it the Holy of Holies, citing Mishnah Yadayim 3:5, Rabbi Akiva (trans. Joshua Kulp, CC BY).
layers.text: Jewish readers long heard more than a love poem: the oldest readings take it as a picture of God and Israel. When rabbis debated which books were holy, Rabbi Akiva answered that all the writings are holy, but the Song of Songs is the holy of holies.

The prophets already picture God as Israel's husband: "I will betroth you to Me forever," in "loving devotion"; "as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you"; "I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride."

layers.evidence: Benson and Gill read the Song as Christ's marriage with the church, and Jamieson, Fausset and Brown note that Christians explain it of Christ and the Church.
layers.text: John the Baptist says, "The bride belongs to the bridegroom"; Jesus calls Himself the bridegroom; Paul applies marriage to "Christ and the church"; Revelation has "the marriage of the Lamb." Christians came to read the Song in this light.

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary on Song 8:6 recalls Paul in Romans 8. Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary: no waters can quench Christ's love to us.
layers.text: Christians hear in love "as strong as death" a love stronger still. Some recall Paul here: neither death nor life "will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord." Others add that no waters can quench Christ's love.

passages.saying: So I have become in his eyes like one who brings peace
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the bride's picture of herself as a wall, as Barnes explains it.
layers.text: The bride says she kept herself pure, firm as a wall with towers. Because of that she won favor in her beloved's eyes and came into a relationship of peace with him.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch ask why she says shalom (peace) here rather than the usual word for favor, and answer that she plays on the name Solomon, which she says in the next verse and which 1 Chronicles 22:9 ties to peace.
layers.text: The Hebrew says she became in his eyes like one who finds shalom, peace. The very next verse names Solomon, Shelomoh in Hebrew, a name built on that same word for peace. So the bride has found shalom with Shelomoh, the king whose name means peace.

passages.saying: Solomon had a vineyard in Baal-hamon
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT and TAGNT, and the commentaries named under each note.

layers.evidence: Rests on the plain wording of the verse, as John Wesley explains it.
layers.text: The bride tells of a vineyard Solomon owned at Baal-hamon. He let it out to keepers, and each of them was to pay him a thousand shekels of silver for its fruit.

layers.evidence: John Gill says the name signifies the master or lord of a multitude, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown gives it as owner of a multitude.
layers.text: The place name Baal-hamon means lord of a multitude, or owner of a crowd. Solomon's vineyard lies in a place whose very name speaks of great numbers.

passages.saying: He looked for justice, but saw bloodshed; for righteousness, but heard a cry of distress.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, and OpenBible.info cross-references.

layers.text: Isaiah sings about a vineyard its owner tended with every care, which still grew only sour grapes. Then he names it: the vineyard is Israel, and the fruit God wanted was justice.

The punchline is two pairs of sound-alike words: God looked for mishpat (justice) and found mispach (bloodshed), for tsedaqah (righteousness) and heard tse'aqah (a cry). Mispach occurs nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible, so its exact sense is not certain.

Tse'aqah is the cry God heard from the slaves in Egypt and the outcry against Sodom, and Isaiah has already called Jerusalem's rulers "rulers of Sodom." God's own people now cause the cry He once rescued them from.
Israel as God's vine is a running picture: "You uprooted a vine from Egypt; You drove out the nations and transplanted it."

Jesus retells this song as the parable of the tenants, with Isaiah's details: a planted vineyard, a wall, a wine vat, a watchtower. This time the owner sends his beloved son, and the leaders know the story is about them.
Jesus says, "I am the true vine." Where the vineyard of Isaiah 5 gave sour fruit, the true vine bears fruit, and those who remain in Him "bear much fruit."

passages.saying: If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, the Septuagint, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Two kings march on Jerusalem, and King Ahaz and his people tremble "like trees in the forest shaken by the wind." God sends Isaiah to say the invasion "will not happen." All turns on whether Ahaz will trust God, and he refuses even the sign God offers.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Isaiah 7:9: a wordplay designed to draw attention to the alternatives set before the king; ta'aminu is the Hiphil and te'amenu the Niphal of aman. TBESH H0539: Niphal made firm, sure; Hiphil to trust, believe.
layers.text: The warning uses one Hebrew verb twice: im lo ta'aminu ki lo te'amenu. Ta'aminu, "believe," and te'amenu, "be made firm," are two forms of aman. The pun sets the king's two choices side by side, and the BSB keeps the echo: "stand firm" and "stand at all."

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch on Isaiah 7:9: the same play upon words is in 2 Chronicles 20:20. Ellicott: an affirmative way of putting Isaiah's words to Ahaz. Maclaren: believing and being established are two forms of the same root-word.
layers.text: Earlier, King Jehoshaphat faced an invasion with the same pair: "Believe in the LORD your God, and you will be upheld" (ha'aminu, te'amenu), Isaiah's warning put positively. His people sang, and "the LORD set ambushes" against the invaders.

layers.evidence: TAHOT: the first occurrence of H0539 is Genesis 15:6 (vehe'emin). Keil and Delitzsch: aman is to be firm and to confirm, in Hiphil to trust, believe. Gill: this is the first time we read of believing.
layers.text: Aman first appears in the Bible when "Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness," the verse Paul quotes in Romans and Galatians. Isaiah's pun shows what the word holds: in Hebrew, believing God and being made firm share one root.

layers.evidence: Septuagint of Isaiah 28:16: ho pisteuōn ep' autō ou mē kataischynthē. TAHOT: ha-ma'amin is H0539.
layers.text: Isaiah's stone in Zion uses the word again: ha-ma'amin, "the one who believes will never be shaken." The Greek Old Testament reads "put to shame," and Paul and Peter quote it of Christ: "the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame."

layers.evidence: TBESG G0281: amen, from aman, be firm. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch: Isaiah 65:16 is literally the God of Amen, and Ellicott hears an echo of it in Revelation 3:14. Keil and Delitzsch link it to 2 Corinthians 1:20. Barnes: Amen means true, certain, faithful.
layers.text: Amen comes from the same root, "be firm." Isaiah's "God of truth" is literally the God of Amen, and Jesus takes Amen as His title: "the Amen, the faithful and true Witness." So, Paul says, all God's promises are "Yes" in Christ.

passages.saying: Behold, the virgin will be with child and will give birth to a son, and will call Him Immanuel.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, Ligonier articles, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Two kings march on Jerusalem, and King Ahaz and his people tremble "like trees in the forest shaken by the wind." Isaiah offers him any sign he wants; Ahaz refuses to ask, so the Lord gives a sign anyway: a son to be called Immanuel.

layers.evidence: TBESH H6005: Immanuel, God with us. TAHOT writes the name as two words in 7:14 and 8:8, the same two words (H5973, H0410) that end 8:10.
layers.text: Immanuel is Hebrew for "God with us," as Matthew translates. Isaiah keeps sounding the name: the Assyrian flood will cover "your entire land, O Immanuel!" and the next oracle ends, "For God is with us," in Hebrew the same two words, immanu el.

layers.evidence: Pulpit Commentary, giving Bishop Lowth's view: a double bearing and a double fulfillment. JFB: partly the immediate event, fully the Messiah. Gill: a sign of present deliverance. NET Bible notes on Isaiah 7:14 and 7:16.
layers.text: The sign had a near horizon. Before the boy could "reject evil and choose good," the two kings' lands would be laid waste, and soon Assyria took Damascus. Isaiah's next son gets a similar timetable (8:4). So many readers see a double fulfillment, near and far.

layers.evidence: Ellicott: almah strictly denotes one of marriageable age. Barnes: the word is used of Rebekah, and the Septuagint has parthenos. Gill: the Jewish translators of the Septuagint so rendered it long before Matthew. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown: from a root to lie hid. TBESG (Abbott-Smith) G3933: parthenos renders almah at Genesis 24:43 and Isaiah 7:14.
layers.text: Matthew quotes this verse of Jesus' birth. Isaiah's word almah means a young woman of marriageable age, and the Greek Old Testament had already rendered it parthenos, "virgin," here and for Rebekah in Genesis 24:43. Its root means hidden, of a maiden kept from men's gaze.

layers.evidence: Barnes and Ellicott on Isaiah 9:6: the name is applied to the LORD Himself in 10:21. Keil and Delitzsch: the same person as the son of the virgin in chapter 7. TAHOT: El Gibbor is H0410 and H1368 in both verses.
layers.text: Two chapters on, the child returns: "unto us a son is given," named "Mighty God," El Gibbor, who will "reign on the throne of David." A chapter later Isaiah uses El Gibbor of the LORD Himself: a remnant will return "to the Mighty God."

layers.evidence: Gerald Bilkes and Gerrit Scott Dawson (Ligonier) tie Jesus' closing promise in Matthew 28:20, "I am with you always," to His name Immanuel, God with us (Matthew 1:23).

cites.at: Gerald Bilkes, Immanuel (Ligonier)
Gerrit Scott Dawson, I Am with You Always (Ligonier)

layers.text: Matthew gives the name near his start, "God with us," and Jesus' last words echo it: "surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age." In between He promises, "where two or three gather together in My name, there am I with them."

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Hebrews 2:13: the words are from Isaiah 8:18, with Isaiah representing Christ. The Pulpit Commentary: Isaiah is himself a sign, a type of the Immanuel to come. Gill and Jamieson, Fausset and Brown also trace the words to Isaiah 8:18.
layers.text: Isaiah says he and his children are "signs and symbols in Israel," and Hebrews puts his words in Christ's mouth: "Here am I, and the children God has given Me." The prophet's sign-children become a picture of Christ and the family He brings to God.

passages.saying: He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, the Targum of Isaiah, and commentaries on Bible Hub.

layers.text: Isaiah describes the LORD's servant suffering for wrongs that are not His own. Watch the pronouns: the wounds are His, the transgressions are ours, and the peace and the healing come to us.

layers.evidence: Peter's word is molops, a bruise or wound left by a blow (TBESG, from Abbott-Smith). It is the word the Greek Old Testament uses here, and it appears nowhere else in the New Testament. Isaiah's chabburah is a bruise or welt (TBESH). Ellicott on Isaiah 53:5 links Peter's use to the slaves he addressed, who were scourged.
layers.text: Peter quotes this line to household servants who could be beaten even for doing good: "By His stripes you are healed." Isaiah's "we" becomes "you," and Peter's word for stripes means a welt, a mark many of his readers knew on their own backs.

layers.evidence: Isaiah 53:4 has choli, sickness, and makob, pain (TBESH); the Greek Old Testament renders the first as sins. Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary on Matthew 8:17: Matthew follows the Hebrew; Barnes: the word for griefs properly means diseases of the body.
layers.text: The New Testament reads this song two ways at once. Matthew quotes 53:4 of Jesus' healings, where the Hebrew speaks of sickness. The Greek Old Testament made it sins, and Peter writes, "He Himself bore our sins." The Servant carries both.

"Crushed" is the Hebrew daka, and it returns five verses later: "it was the LORD’s will to crush Him." Onlookers thought God was striking Him (53:4). The chapter answers that He was crushed for our iniquities, and that even this served God's purpose.

layers.evidence: Gill, the Pulpit Commentary and Ellicott on Luke 22:37.
layers.text: On His last night Jesus applies the chapter to Himself: "this Scripture must be fulfilled in Me," He says, and quotes 53:12, "He was numbered with the transgressors." The next day He was crucified between two criminals.

layers.evidence: Gill on Acts 8:34 reports Jews who apply the passage to the people of Israel in general. See also Barnes and the Pulpit Commentary on Acts 8:34.
layers.text: An Ethiopian official asked, "who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?" Isaiah calls Israel God's servant (49:3), and medieval Jewish commentators read the song that way. Yet this Servant is "stricken for the transgression of My people." Philip answered with Jesus.

layers.evidence: Targum Jonathan on Isaiah 52:13 and 53:5 (English translation of 1871, on Sefaria). TBESH lists both senses of chalal, to pierce and to profane
layers.text: An early Jewish paraphrase in Aramaic, the Targum, names the Servant of 52:13 as the Messiah. In 53:5 it reads the word for "pierced" as "profaned" and applies it to the sanctuary. The Hebrew letters allow both senses.

passages.saying: I am watching over My word to accomplish it.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, OpenBible.info cross-references, the NET Bible notes, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Young Jeremiah protests, "I am only a child!" God touches his mouth, puts His words there, and sends him "to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and plant." Then He asks, "Jeremiah, what do you see?"

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Jeremiah 1:12: the almond blossoms in January or February and is the harbinger of spring. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown: literally the wakeful tree, waking from winter's sleep before the others. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch note the play on the name.
layers.text: Jeremiah sees "a branch of an almond tree," shaqed, and God answers that He is shoqed, "watching." The almond is the first tree to blossom after winter, so its name means something like "the wakeful tree." God is awake over His word.

layers.evidence: NET Bible notes on Amos 8:2: qets (end) sounds like qayits (summer fruit). Keil and Delitzsch on Amos 8:2: qets is chosen to form a paronomasia with qayits. Poole on Jeremiah 1:11 links the almond rod to Amos's summer fruit.
layers.text: Amos had a vision built the same way: "Amos, what do you see?" "A basket of summer fruit," qayits. Then God says the end, qets, "has come for My people Israel." Both visions turn an everyday object into a message through the sound of its name.

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Jeremiah 31:28 recalls the wakeful or watching tree. TAHOT: all three forms are H8245.
layers.text: The almond's verb returns beside the new-covenant promise: "Just as I watched over them to uproot and tear down," so "I will watch over them to build and to plant," the two tasks of Jeremiah's call. God watches over rebuilding as He watched over judgment.

layers.evidence: Ellicott, Barnes and Gill on Hebrews 8:8: the quotation in Hebrews 8:8-12 is from Jeremiah 31:31-34.
layers.text: Three verses later comes what He is watching to build, "a new covenant": "I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts." Hebrews quotes the whole passage and says of Jesus, "the covenant He mediates is better."

passages.saying: And this is His name by which He will be called: The LORD Our Righteousness.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TBESH and TBESG, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Judah's rulers have been shepherds who "destroy and scatter the sheep of My pasture." God promises to "raise up for David a righteous Branch," a King who "will administer justice and righteousness in the land."

layers.evidence: TBESH H6667: Zedekiah, Jehovah is righteous, the last king of Judah, renamed from Mattaniah by Nebuchadnezzar. Ellicott: the reigning king's name implied the same thought, and his reign was a miserable failure.
layers.text: Judah's last king was Zedekiah, a name the king of Babylon gave him, meaning the LORD is righteous. Yet "Zedekiah did evil in the sight of the LORD." He bore a name close to the promised one and failed it; the true King will be "The LORD Our Righteousness."

layers.evidence: TBESH H6780: a sprout or shoot, used of the Messiah from David's tree. Keil and Delitzsch: tsemach denotes the Messiah. Poole ties it to the Branch of Jeremiah 33:15, and Ellicott to the Branch of Zechariah 3:8 and 6:12.
layers.text: "Branch" is tsemach, a sprout: the future King springing from David's family tree. Jeremiah repeats it, "I will cause to sprout for David a righteous Branch," and after the exile Zechariah hears, "I am going to bring My servant, the Branch."

layers.evidence: Ellicott on Jeremiah 23:6: in 33:16 the same name is given to Jerusalem. Gill and Jamieson, Fausset and Brown on 33:16: Christ and His church are one, so they share the name.
layers.text: When Jeremiah repeats the promise, the name moves from the King to His city: Jerusalem "will dwell securely, and this is the name by which it will be called: The LORD Our Righteousness." The King and His people share one name.

layers.evidence: Barnes and Poole see the King called Yahweh, and Poole links the name to 1 Corinthians 1:30. Keil and Delitzsch: he by whom Jahveh deals righteousness. Ellicott applies it to imputed righteousness.
layers.text: Christians have long read the name of Christ, whom Paul calls "our righteousness," in whom "we might become the righteousness of God." Some hear the King called the LORD Himself; others, the one through whom the LORD gives righteousness.

passages.saying: I saw One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven. He approached the Ancient of Days and was led into His presence.
passages.source: Drafted with AI help (Claude) from the BSB, STEPBible TAHOT, TAGNT and TBESH, OpenBible.info cross-references, and older commentaries named under each note.

layers.text: Daniel sees four beasts rise from the sea, explained as "four kings who will arise from the earth." Then the Ancient of Days takes His throne, and one like a son of man comes with the clouds and is given an everlasting kingdom.

layers.evidence: TBESH: bar, son; enash, man, human being. Keil and Delitzsch: like a man, not a beast; clouds are the chariot on which God comes to judge (Psalm 104:3; Isaiah 19:1).
layers.text: In Aramaic "son of man" is bar enash, simply a human being. After the beasts comes a human figure, yet he arrives with "the clouds of heaven," and in Scripture clouds carry God Himself: "the LORD rides on a swift cloud." Human, and coming as God comes.

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott on Daniel 7:14: in biblical Aramaic pelach is used only of the service and homage due to God. All 10 biblical uses are religious, though later Aramaic (Targum Onkelos) also uses it of farm work. Barnes on Daniel 7:14 compares Matthew 28:18.
layers.text: He is given a kingdom so "that the people of every nation and language should serve Him." The Bible uses this verb, pelach, only for religious service, as in "the God whom we serve." Jesus' last words echo the scene: all authority "has been given to Me."

layers.evidence: Gill on Mark 14:62, and Benson and Keil and Delitzsch on Daniel 7:13, tie Jesus' answer to this verse; His words also echo Psalm 110:1.
layers.text: Asked at His trial if He is the Christ, Jesus answers "I am," joining this verse to Psalm 110: "you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven." The high priest tears his clothes and cries blasphemy.

layers.evidence: TAGNT: the Son of Man occurs 80 times in the Gospels (NA28). TAHOT: ben adam occurs 94 times in Ezekiel; Ellicott: above ninety times. Matthew Henry's Concise: Christ usually called Himself the Son of man. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown: the title implies His lowliness and His exaltation.
layers.text: Son of Man was Jesus' favorite name for Himself, used about 80 times in the Gospels. It could sound humble: God calls Ezekiel "son of man" more than 90 times. But Jesus used it with authority: "the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins."

layers.evidence: Keil and Delitzsch report some who read the figure as the people of Israel. Gill: the Messiah, as most Christian interpreters allow.
layers.text: The angel's explanation shares the kingdom: "the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom." Some medieval Jewish and modern commentators read the figure as Israel; most Christian interpreters see the Messiah, who shares His kingdom with His people.

layers.evidence: Gill, Barnes and Poole on Revelation 1:14: the description matches the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7:9.
layers.text: John sees "One like the Son of Man" whose hair is "white like wool, as white as snow," as Daniel described the Ancient of Days. The one who came to the throne shares the look of the One on it. And "He is coming with the clouds."

passages.saying: I will say to those called ‘Not My People,’ ‘You are My people,’ and they will say, ‘You are my God.’
